docs.title: 1. The CLI (@capsule/cli) ✅ Done
docs.text:
This is the backbone. All native complexity lives here, not in the developer's project.

# ── Project setup ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
capsule init                              # scaffold a new project (interactive template selection)
capsule init --template react-ts          # scaffold with a specific template
capsule init --template vue-ts            #   available: react-ts | vue-ts | svelte-ts | vanilla-ts
capsule init --template github:org/tmpl   # community template from GitHub
capsule add android                       # add Android platform
capsule add ios                           # add iOS platform (Phase 4+)
capsule sync                              # regenerate .capsule/ wrappers from capsule.lock
capsule sync --frozen-lockfile            # CI mode — fails if lock is out of date
capsule update                            # update capsule shell to latest compatible version

# ── Development ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
capsule dev                               # start dev server(s) + hot reload
                                          # starts Vite/ng for client
                                          # starts Node.js server process if src/server/routes/ exists
                                          # runs adb reverse for all ports
capsule dev --tunnel                      # HTTPS tunnel for physical devices / corporate WiFi
capsule dev --tunnel --qr                 # same + display QR code for instant device pairing
capsule dev --qr                          # LAN mode + QR code (no tunnel)
capsule dev --port 3000                   # custom Vite port (default: 5173)

# ── Build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
capsule build android                     # debug build
                                          # runs Vite/ng build (client bundle)
                                          # runs esbuild (server bundle, if src/server/routes/ exists)
capsule build android --release           # signed release APK
capsule build android --release --format aab  # signed AAB (required for Play Store)
capsule build android --release --format apk  # signed APK (for direct/enterprise install)
capsule build ios                         # debug build (Phase 4+, requires macOS)
capsule build ios --release               # signed release IPA (Phase 4+)

# ── Run & test ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
capsule run android                       # deploy to running emulator or connected device
capsule run android --device <id>         # target specific device (from adb devices)
capsule run ios                           # deploy to iOS simulator or device (Phase 4+)

# ── Signing & publishing ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
capsule sign android                      # configure Android keystore credentials (Phase 8+; Fastlane automation in Phase 9 DX)
capsule sign ios                          # configure iOS certificates via Fastlane Match (Phase 8+; Fastlane automation in Phase 9 DX)

capsule publish android                          # upload to defaultTrack (Phase 8)
capsule publish ios                              # upload to TestFlight (Phase 8)

# ── Version management ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
capsule version                           # show current versionName and buildNumber
capsule version bump patch                # 1.4.2 → 1.4.3  (also increments buildNumber)
capsule version bump minor                # 1.4.2 → 1.5.0
capsule version bump major                # 1.4.2 → 2.0.0
capsule version set 2.0.0                 # set explicit version (also increments buildNumber)

# ── OTA updates (CodeSync) ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
capsule codesync publish                         # push new web bundle to production channel (Phase 2+)
capsule codesync releases                        # list all releases on current channel
capsule codesync rollback                        # revert to previous bundle on current channel
capsule codesync pause                           # emergency stop — halt current rollout
capsule codesync rollout <percent>               # adjust gradual rollout percentage (0–100)
capsule codesync devices                         # fleet summary (active devices, OS breakdown)

Key behavior: capsule update reads capsule.config.ts, bumps the shell AAR/XCFramework version in capsule.lock, and regenerates the thin platform wrappers. That is the entire SDK update — no code changes required.

docs.title: 2. Single Config (capsule.config.ts) ✅ Done
docs.text:
The complete defineConfig interface — every field the CLI understands:

import { defineConfig } from '@capsule/cli'

export default defineConfig({

  // ── Identity ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  appId:   'com.yourcompany.app',   // reverse-domain — must match Play/App Store listing
  appName: 'My App',                // display name on device home screen

  // ── Version (managed by `capsule version` commands — do not hand-edit buildNumber) ──
  version: {
    name:        '1.0.0',   // human-readable semver shown in stores
    buildNumber: 1          // monotonic integer, auto-incremented by `capsule publish`
  },

  // ── Android ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  android: {
    minSdk:     26,    // Android 8.0 — minimum supported Android version
    targetSdk:  35,    // Android 15 — primary target (must match store requirements)
    compileSdk: 35,    // SDK used to compile (usually == targetSdk)

    permissions: [     // short names — CLI expands to android.permission.*
      'CAMERA',
      'POST_NOTIFICATIONS'
    ],

    signing: {         // ── all values from env vars, never hardcoded ──
      storeFile:     process.env.CAPSULE_KEYSTORE_PATH,  // path to .jks file
      storePassword: process.env.CAPSULE_KEYSTORE_PASS,
      keyAlias:      process.env.CAPSULE_KEY_ALIAS,
      keyPassword:   process.env.CAPSULE_KEY_PASS
    },

    publish: {         // ── Play Store automation (Phase 8) ──
      serviceAccountKey:     process.env.PLAY_STORE_JSON_KEY,
      serviceAccountKeyData: process.env.PLAY_STORE_JSON_KEY_DATA,
      defaultTrack: 'internal',
      packageName:  'com.yourcompany.app'
    }
  },

  // ── iOS (Phase 4+) ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ios: {
    /** @experimental Available in Phase 4 (iOS support) */
    deployment: '16.0',
    bundleId:   'com.yourcompany.app',
  },

  // ── Community integrations ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  plugins: [
    '@capsule-community/google-maps',
    '@capsule-community/stripe',
    './capsule-plugins/my-integration',
    {
      path:  './capsule-plugins/vendor-sdk',
      trust: 'unverified'
    }
  ],

  // ── CodeSync OTA updates (Phase 2+) ──────────────────────────────────────
  codeSync: {
    enabled:          true,
    url:              process.env.CODESYNC_URL,
    apiKey:           process.env.CODESYNC_API_KEY,
    channel:          process.env.CHANNEL || 'production',
    strategy:         'background',
    checkOnForeground: true,
    mandatory:         false
  },

  // ── Web layer ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  web: {
    mobileReset: true,   // inject ~150-byte mobile CSS reset into built index.html
  },

  // ── Server (Phase 2+) — optional, activated by src/server/routes/ presence ──
  server: {
    timeout: 3000,   // ms before splash error screen (default: 3000)
    // No port config — port is derived from appId hash, invisible to developer
  }
})

The CLI reads this and generates build.gradle, AndroidManifest.xml, and Info.plist. Developers never touch those files directly.

docs.title: 3. The Native Capsule (the key investment)
docs.text:
Android — A Kotlin library (AAR) published to Maven: - CapsuleRuntime coordinator owns: CapsuleServer, QuickJSEngine, SplashController, bridge (Phase 2+) - CapsuleActivity is a thin shell that delegates entirely to CapsuleRuntime - JS bridge registration via JavascriptInterface - Handles deep links, back button, keyboard, safe area insets - Dev mode: loads from http://10.0.2.2:5173 (ADB port forward) — Vite client + Node.js server - Prod mode: loads from http://127.0.0.1:{port}/ (CivetWeb embedded server) (Phase 2+)

iOS — A Swift package (XCFramework) (Phase 4+): - Same CapsuleRuntime interface, different implementations - The same CivetWeb server, compiled through SwiftPM instead of the NDK - QuickJS compiled for iOS (same C source) - WKWebView instead of Android WebView - Bridge via WKScriptMessageHandler

Critical: These are compiled binaries shipped by the Capsule team. Version 2.0.0 of the capsule = Android targetSdk 35. Version 2.1.0 = targetSdk 36. Developers just bump the version number.

Shell dispatch is registry-based, not hardwired. The bridge dispatcher inside the binary routes method calls through a mutable override map before falling back to built-in handlers. This is what enables the capsule override command — developer-written fixes register into this map at app startup via the generated wrapper, without recompiling the shell. The registry pattern is a first-class design requirement of the shell's internal architecture, not an afterthought.

docs.title: 4. The Bridge API (Web-First Philosophy)
docs.text:
All platform capabilities live in @capsule/core. No separate plugin installs for hardware or OS APIs.

// Everything is imported from @capsule/core — no separate packages to install
import { camera, geolocation, push, haptics, bluetooth, nfc, biometrics } from '@capsule/core'

// Use directly — tree-shaking removes anything you don't import
const photo    = await camera.capture({ quality: 0.9, facing: 'back' })
const position = await geolocation.getCurrentPosition()
await push.requestPermission()
await haptics.impact('medium')

// Standard Web APIs still work as-is — no bridge needed
navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(...)   // web standard, also works
navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({ video: true })

Unused capabilities (bluetooth, nfc, etc.) are tree-shaken from the release build by R8 (Android) and the iOS linker. Importing camera does not include nfc in your binary.

Bridge protocol is JSON-RPC 2.0 over the native bridge (see known-issues.md Issue 2 for full spec): 

WebView → Native:  { jsonrpc: '2.0', id: '<uuid>', method: 'camera.capture', params: { quality: 0.8 } }
Native → WebView:  { jsonrpc: '2.0', id: '<uuid>', result: { path: '/tmp/img.jpg' } }
Native → WebView:  { jsonrpc: '2.0', method: 'push.messageReceived', params: { ... } }  // event (no id)

Bridge = events only. The Bridge (JavascriptInterface) handles all native push, events, and real-time updates. HTTP (the embedded CivetWeb server) handles all request/response data flows. These two channels never mix.

Four bridge implementations (same @capsule/core API in all contexts): - CapsuleBridge — WebView + native shell (production) ✅ - WebBridge — browser dev fallback (all 6 APIs work in browser) ✅ - FakeBridge — unit tests ✅ - QuickJSBridge — server route handlers, Phase 2

TypeScript types are auto-generated from a bridge manifest. No stringly-typed calls. Errors are typed via a Capsule error code registry (1xxx–5xxx).

docs.title: 5. Hot Reload Architecture
docs.text:
capsule dev android

Process 1: Vite/ng dev server (port 5173)
  → hot reload for client code
  → adb reverse tcp:5173 tcp:5173

Process 2: Node.js server process (port 3001, if src/server/routes/ exists)
  → runs the same TypeScript route handlers
  → watches src/server/routes/ for changes
  → adb reverse tcp:3001 tcp:3001

Developer runs one command. Two processes are invisible.

Physical device:
  → Same WiFi: load from machine's LAN IP
  → USB: ADB reverse port forward
  → Corporate WiFi / different network: capsule dev --tunnel

Hot reload scope: - JS / CSS / HTML / asset changes → instant HMR via Vite (<50ms) - Server route changes → Node.js process restarts (fast, watched by dev command) - Source plugin .kt / .swift changes → full native rebuild required (capsule build android). The CLI detects .kt/.swift changes during capsule dev and prints a warning.

docs.title: 6. File-Based Server Routing (Phase 2+)
docs.text:
The server is optional. It is activated by the presence of src/server/routes/. If this directory does not exist, the embedded server serves static assets only and QuickJS never starts.

src/
  server/
    routes/
      users.ts          → GET /api/users, POST /api/users
      users/
        [id].ts         → GET /api/users/:id

Each file exports GET, POST, PUT, DELETE functions. The CLI scans this directory at build time (esbuild bundles it into assets/server/bundle.js). Adding a file creates a route — no registration, no config.

Route handlers use the same @capsule/core package as client code. QuickJSBridge (Phase 2) is the bridge implementation that makes all 6 native APIs available from within server handlers.

HTTP = data, Bridge = events — route handlers return data/JSON/HTML. They never push events; events always come through the Bridge.

docs.title: 7. Two Bundles, One Atomic Deploy (Phase 2+)
docs.text:
capsule build android
  → Vite/ng build  →  assets/www/          (client bundle)
  → esbuild        →  assets/server/        (server bundle.js, if src/server/routes/ exists)

Both bundles always build and deploy together. Developer sees one version number and one deploy. codeSync deploys atomically — never client without server or vice versa.

Self-healing rollback: If the app crashes 3 times in 60 seconds after a deploy, the runtime automatically rolls back to the previous bundle. Silent recovery — developer sees a version number if they check, not a crash.

docs.title: 8. Core SDK vs. Community Integrations
docs.text:
@capsule/core is a monolithic SDK — every platform API ships together and is versioned as one unit.

@capsule/core   # camera, GPS, push, NFC, Bluetooth, haptics, biometrics,
                # filesystem, microphone, accelerometer, barcode, connectivity,
                # clipboard, share sheet, battery, device info, CodeSync — all built-in

No version matrix. No plugin compatibility issues. One version manages everything.

The rule for what goes in core:

If it is a platform OS API that ships with Android/iOS — it is in @capsule/core.

Community integrations are separate packages for capabilities that require a third-party SDK:

@capsule-community/google-maps   # requires Google Maps SDK (license + ~15 MB)
@capsule-community/stripe        # requires Stripe iOS/Android SDK
@capsule-community/braintree     # requires Braintree SDK
@capsule-community/facebook-auth # requires Facebook SDK

Tree-shaking: R8 (Android) and the iOS linker strip every core capability that is never imported.

docs.title: Project Folder Structure (developer side)
docs.text:
my-app/
  src/                       # pure web code, any framework
    index.html               # standard HTML5, no custom tags
    main.ts
    App.tsx / App.vue / App.svelte
  src/server/                # optional — activates embedded runtime (Phase 2+)
    routes/
      users.ts               # exports GET, POST, PUT, DELETE
      users/
        [id].ts              # dynamic route
  public/                    # static assets
  capsule-plugins/           # optional: source plugins (Kotlin/Swift/C/Lua)
    my-scanner/
      capsule-plugin.json
      android/MyScanner.kt
      ios/MyScanner.swift
      web/index.ts
  capsule.config.ts          # the ONLY native configuration
  capsule.lock               # ← COMMIT THIS: pins resolved shell + plugin versions
  package.json
  vite.config.ts

  # Generated/managed by CLI — gitignored, do not edit
  .capsule/
    android/                 # thin wrapper (generated from config + capsule.lock)
    ios/                     # thin wrapper (generated from config + capsule.lock)

docs.title: Build Pipeline
docs.text:
capsule build android --release

1. Vite/ng build → dist/                               (client bundle, ~1-3s)
2. esbuild → server/bundle.js  (if src/server/routes/ exists)
3. Copy dist/ → .capsule/android/assets/www/
4. Copy server/bundle.js → .capsule/android/assets/server/  (if applicable)
5. ./gradlew bundleRelease               (AAB for Play Store)
   ./gradlew assembleRelease             (APK for direct install)
6. Sign with keystore
7. Output: .capsule/android/app-release.aab  (or .apk)

Gradle build cache means after the first build, incremental rebuilds only recompile changed Java/Kotlin. Since the capsule shell changes rarely (only on capsule update), most builds skip native compilation entirely.

docs.title: Phased Roadmap
docs.text:
Canonical phase status lives in ../project/roadmap.md (re-sequenced 2026-06-15, capability-first). This table mirrors it — if they diverge, the roadmap wins; update there.

Phase Deliverable Goal 1 — Foundation ✅ CLI + Android capsule + Vite integration + hot reload + 6 native APIs + WebBridge Prove the concept works end-to-end on a real device 2 — Embedded Runtime ✅ Embedded HTTP server (NanoHTTPD, replaced by CivetWeb 2026-10) + QuickJS + CapsuleRuntime + file-based routes + atomic CodeSync On-device server-side route handlers; production HTTP serving 3 — Native APIs Expansion Camera, filesystem, push (FCM/APNs), network, biometrics, SQLite db, background jobs, … Complete OS API surface 4 — iOS CivetWeb (shared with Android) + QuickJS iOS + WKWebView — same config, same TS code Dual-platform, zero developer-facing changes 5 — Capsule UI capsule add ui registry + shared iOS/Material Tailwind preset — native-look layer (no native APIs); after iOS so presets target a real WKWebView shell Native look-and-feel on both platforms 6 — Server Code Push / OTA Cloud OTA network delivery + portal + canary/auto-rollback + multi-tenant + billing (+ AI/agents) The funding engine 7 — Migration On-Ramp capsule migrate ionic + @capsule/compat-capacitor + plugin importer Acquisition funnel 8 — Ecosystem GitHub org, publishing pipeline, CI/CD, npm, Docker, shell + template registry, docs site Open source growth 9 — DX VS Code extension, error overlays, device inspector, Fastlane signing Developer delight

See ../contributing/codesync-internals.md for the OTA system spec, ../contributing/docker.md for Docker strategy, lockfile.md for the lock file spec, and ../project/server-design/overview.md for the self-hosted portal.

docs.title: Technology Choices
docs.text: Concern Choice Reason CLI runtime Node.js + TypeScript Ecosystem, easy to distribute via npm Web bundler Vite Fastest HMR, works with any framework Server bundle esbuild Fast, tree-shakes TypeScript for QuickJS target Android capsule Kotlin Modern, concise, Google-preferred iOS capsule Swift Modern, Apple-preferred Embedded HTTP server (both platforms) CivetWeb (C, vendored) One server for Android + iOS; ready when start() returns; loopback-only — adr-004 amendment On-device JS runtime QuickJS ES2020, ~700KB, embeds cleanly via JNI Bridge protocol JSON-RPC 2.0 Typed, standard, supports events + error registry Plugin distribution npm + Maven/SPM Unified install experience Lock file format YAML Human-readable, diff-friendly Native version format npm semver (^1.0.0, >=2.0.0) Familiar, tooling exists

docs.title: Critical Differentiators vs Capacitor
docs.text:
Capacitor already solved Cordova's worst problems. Capsule goes further:

  1. Capsule as true binary dep — Capacitor still has android/ and ios/ dirs with editable source. Capsule generates minimal wrappers only.
  2. Monolithic core SDK — All platform OS APIs ship in @capsule/core. No plugin compatibility matrix.
  3. Embedded HTTP server — Production assets served from http://127.0.0.1:{port}/. No file:// limitations. Service workers work. CORS is clean.
  4. On-device TypeScript server — Route handlers written in TypeScript, same language as the client, same @capsule/core package. Runs on QuickJS on-device, Node.js in dev. Capacitor has no equivalent.
  5. Config-driven — One capsule.config.ts, CLI generates all native manifests.
  6. Built-in CodeSync — OTA updates are part of @capsule/core, opt-in per app. Atomic deploy with self-healing rollback.
  7. Surgical override — Individual core capability methods can be patched without forking or recompiling the shell.

docs.title: The Single Most Important Architectural Decision
docs.text:
Keep the native capsule as a compiled binary dependency from day one.

This is the architectural bet everything else rests on. If developers are allowed to customize native capsule code freely, Capsule becomes Cordova. If the boundary holds, SDK updates remain a one-liner forever — and that is the entire value proposition.

docs.title: Primers — the native stack for a web/C# developer
docs.text:
Onboarding explainers for the parts of Capsule that sit below the TypeScript surface. Written for a developer fluent in C# (OO) and TypeScript/web who is newer to the Android/native side. Each primer maps concepts to what you already know and links to the real Capsule files, so read them next to the code.

Suggested order:

  1. kotlin-for-csharp-devs.md — Kotlin idioms mapped from C#/TS (data class ≈ records, sealed class ≈ unions, suspend ≈ async/await, companion object ≈ static, fun interface ≈ delegates). The language the whole Android shell is written in.
  2. quickjs.md — the embedded JavaScript engine that runs your server-side routes; why it exists alongside the WebView's V8, and its hard constraints (globalThis, return-objects, no DOM/Node).
  3. civetweb.md — the in-app localhost HTTP server (the same C server on Android and iOS) that gives the WebView a real http:// origin and routes /api/* into QuickJS.
  4. jni-and-cpp.md — the JNI boundary (≈ P/Invoke) by which Kotlin reaches the C QuickJS engine; CMake/NDK build, the opaque native handle, the single-thread + 4 MB-stack rule.

These are living docs — extend them as the native surface grows (iOS/Swift will earn its own primer in Phase 4).

docs.title: CivetWeb in Capsule — the embedded web server
docs.text: Coming from web dev, you know HTTP servers as a process you deploy (Kestrel, Express, nginx). Capsule runs a tiny HTTP server inside the mobile app, bound to localhost, serving the app's own bundle to its own WebView. This primer explains why, and how Capsule uses CivetWeb specifically — on Android and iOS.

docs.title: Why a server inside the app at all?
docs.text:
The app's UI is a web app (HTML/JS/CSS) rendered in a WebView (an embedded Chromium on Android, WKWebView on iOS). A WebView can load content two ways:

  • file:// — works, but browsers treat file:// as a hostile origin: no proper CORS, flaky fetch, service-worker and module quirks, inconsistent relative-path resolution.
  • http://localhost/… — a real web origin, so everything behaves like production: fetch, history API, modules, caching all work normally.

So Capsule stands up a loopback HTTP server at http://127.0.0.1:{port}/ and points the WebView at it. The server serves the static front-end and exposes an /api/* surface that runs the app's server-side JavaScript in QuickJS. It's the same "web app + API" shape you know — just both halves live on-device, on localhost. Why a real server rather than a custom URL scheme: adr-004.

docs.title: What is CivetWeb?
docs.text:
CivetWeb is a small, embeddable HTTP server written in C (MIT). You start it with a list of options and give it callbacks; it owns the listening socket and a pool of worker threads. Because it is plain C, the same sources compile into both shells — Android through the NDK, iOS through SwiftPM. One server, identical behaviour on both platforms.

The sources are vendored once, at packages/native/civetweb/ (pinned release tag in VERSION, build flags explained in its README.md). Capsule compiles it with NO_FILES: CivetWeb never serves files itself. Every request goes to Capsule's own code.

Replaced NanoHTTPD (Android) on 2026-10-24 — see the adr-004 amendment for why.

docs.title: How Capsule wires it
docs.text:
Three layers, the same on both platforms:

socket ── CivetWeb (C) ── begin_request callback ── CivetwebServer ── RequestRouter ── /api/* → QuickJS
                                                    (Kotlin / Swift)   (pure logic)  └ else  → www/ assets
  • RequestRouter decides what each request gets back. It is pure logic — no HTTP library, no Android/iOS types — so it is unit-tested on its own.
  • Static branch: any path maps to a file under the app's www/ (your built front-end — what capsule build produces). / → index.html. A missing file is a 404 with the body Not found: <path>. Paths with .. segments are refused. Files under assets/server/ are never served (that's server-side code, not public).
  • API branch: /api/* goes to the QuickJS route handler (your src/server/routes/**). No matching route → 404 No handler for <path>; a throwing route → 500, never a crashed server. See quickjs.md.
  • CivetwebServer is the transport: it starts CivetWeb, turns each request into an HttpRequest, calls route(), and writes the HttpResponse back (adding Cache-Control: no-cache, because an OTA update swaps files behind the same URLs).
  • The glue between C and the host language:
  • Android: capsule_server_jni.c, built into libcapsule_server.so. Each CivetWeb worker thread is attached to the JVM once (in init_thread), so a request never pays for an attach. All JNI lookups happen up front in nativeStart — a CivetWeb thread can't see app classes through FindClass.
  • iOS: CivetwebServer.swift calls the C API directly (the CCivetweb target in the repo-root Package.swift).

Files: Android CivetwebServer.kt and RequestRouter.kt; iOS the same names under packages/capsule-ios/Sources/dev/capsule/runtime/.

docs.title: The one interesting seam: sync server ↔ async handler
docs.text:
CivetWeb calls begin_request synchronously, on one of its worker threads. But the QuickJS route handler is asynchronous (a Kotlin suspend function; an async closure in Swift), and the engine runs on its own pinned thread — see jni-and-cpp.md. The router bridges the two by blocking the worker until the handler finishes:

val response = runBlocking { handler(request.method, request.path, body, request.headers) }

runBlocking waits on CivetWeb's worker thread while the handler dispatches the actual JS execution onto the QuickJS thread. No deadlock, because QuickJS never runs on a server worker thread. (Swift does the same with a semaphore around a detached Task; CivetWeb's threads are not part of Swift's cooperative pool, so blocking one starves nothing.) C#/TS analogy: .GetAwaiter().GetResult() from a sync entry point, where the awaited work runs on a different scheduler.

docs.title: Lifecycle — start and stop
docs.text:
• start() returns only when the server accepts connections. CivetWeb's mg_start2 binds and listens before it returns, so a request made immediately afterwards succeeds — no probe, no retry. (NanoHTTPD returned before binding, which caused the startup race in 2026-10-embedded-server-startup.md.) If the port is taken, start() throws a typed "port in use" error.
  • stop() returns at once. Shutting CivetWeb down waits for its worker threads, and a worker can be inside an /api route that is itself waiting on the main thread — waiting on the main thread would deadlock. So the shutdown runs in the background, and the next start() on the same port waits for it.

The owning CapsuleRuntime starts the server before pointing the WebView at the port and stops it on teardown.

docs.title: Where the port comes from
docs.text: Each app gets a stable, app-specific port derived from its package name / bundle id (portForAppId), so two Capsule apps on one device don't collide. The server binds 127.0.0.1 only — nothing off the device can reach it. Dev mode skips the embedded server entirely — the WebView loads the Vite dev server on your host via adb reverse instead (that's why devServerUrl != null short-circuits the runtime in CapsuleActivity.loadApp()).

docs.title: Mental summary
docs.text:
• Capsule = a localhost web app + API, both running on-device, so the WebView gets a real http:// origin.
  • CivetWeb = one small C server compiled into both shells; it owns sockets and threads, Capsule answers every request.
  • RequestRouter routes /api/* → QuickJS and everything else → www/; it is plain, tested logic.
  • The sync-server → async-handler gap is bridged by blocking the worker, safe because the engine runs on a separate pinned thread.

Next: quickjs.md — what actually runs behind /api/*.

docs.title: JNI, C & C++ in Capsule — for a managed-language developer
docs.text: You've lived in C#/TS where memory is managed and there's no "native boundary." Capsule has one: the JavaScript engine (QuickJS) is written in C, compiled to a native .so library, and Kotlin talks to it through JNI. This primer explains just enough of that world to read and reason about Capsule's runtime. You will rarely edit the C; you need to understand the seam.

docs.title: The mental model
docs.text:
Kotlin (JVM bytecode)         ──JNI──▶   C (native .so)            QuickJS (C library)
 QuickJSEngineImpl                         quickjs_jni.c             quickjs.c, dtoa.c, …
 `external fun nativeCall(...)`  ───────▶  Java_..._nativeCall(...)  JS_Eval / JS_Call

Three layers, two boundaries: 1. Kotlin ↔ C — crossed via JNI (Java Native Interface). The Kotlin side declares external functions; the C side implements them with special JNI signatures. This is the "FFI" / P/Invoke analogue from C#. 2. C (our glue) ↔ QuickJS (the engine) — ordinary C function calls into the vendored QuickJS library.

C#/.NET analogy: JNI ≈ P/Invoke / DllImport. The .so ≈ a native DLL. The JVM ≈ the CLR. The big difference: across JNI there is no garbage collector and no bounds-checking — C owns its memory and a mistake is a crash (SIGSEGV), not an exception.

docs.title: Why C at all?
docs.text: QuickJS-ng is a small, embeddable JavaScript engine written in C (see quickjs.md for why we embed a JS engine). It's distributed as C source. To run it on Android we compile that C for each CPU architecture into a shared library (.so) and load it at runtime. There is no "managed" QuickJS; the engine is C.

docs.title: The build: CMake compiles the C into a .so
docs.text:
Android builds native code with CMake + the NDK (Native Development Kit — the C/C++ toolchain for Android). Capsule's CMakeLists.txt declares two libraries:

add_library(quickjs STATIC          # 1. the engine, as a static lib
    quickjs/quickjs.c quickjs/dtoa.c quickjs/libregexp.c quickjs/libunicode.c)

add_library(capsule_quickjs_jni SHARED   # 2. our JNI glue, as a loadable .so
    quickjs_jni.c)
target_link_libraries(capsule_quickjs_jni quickjs android …)
  • STATIC lib = compiled into the consumer (the JNI .so), not shipped separately (like a .lib/ static .a).
  • SHARED lib = the .so the app loads at runtime (like a DLL). Gradle builds one per ABI (arm64-v8a, x86_64 — see abiFilters in build.gradle.kts) and packs them into the AAR/APK.
  • The four .c files are the vendored QuickJS source (no package manager — see the upkeep doc; bumping = re-copying those files).

docs.title: The Kotlin side: external fun + System.loadLibrary
docs.text:
QuickJSEngineImpl.kt:

private external fun nativeCreate(): Long                       // returns an opaque pointer
private external fun nativeCall(handle: Long, fn: String, args: String): String
private external fun nativeDestroy(handle: Long)

companion object { init { System.loadLibrary("capsule_quickjs_jni") } }  // loads the .so once
  • external fun = "implemented in native code" (≈ C#'s [DllImport] static extern). No Kotlin body.
  • System.loadLibrary("capsule_quickjs_jni") loads libcapsule_quickjs_jni.so (Android adds the lib/.so). Done once in the companion object's init (≈ a static constructor).
  • The Long handle is a raw C pointer to the QuickJS runtime/context, smuggled through the JVM as a 64-bit integer. Kotlin treats it as opaque; only the C side dereferences it. (This is the classic "native handle" pattern — like an IntPtr/SafeHandle in C#.)

docs.title: The C side: JNI function naming + the type marshalling
docs.text:
For an external fun nativeCall declared in class dev.capsule.runtime.QuickJSEngineImpl, JNI looks for a C function named by a strict convention in quickjs_jni.c:

JNIEXPORT jstring JNICALL
Java_dev_capsule_runtime_QuickJSEngineImpl_nativeCall(
    JNIEnv *env, jobject thiz, jlong handle, jstring fn, jstring args) {
    // 1. marshal: JVM String → C UTF-8 char*
    const char *fn_c = (*env)->GetStringUTFChars(env, fn, NULL);
    // 2. call into QuickJS via the handle (cast jlong back to a pointer)
    // 3. marshal back: C string → jstring with (*env)->NewStringUTF(...)
    // 4. release the GetStringUTFChars buffer — no GC will do it for you
}

What to notice (the things that bite managed-language devs): - Name mangling: Java_<package_with_underscores>_<Class>_<method>. Rename the Kotlin package or method and the C symbol must change too, or you get UnsatisfiedLinkError at runtime (not compile). - JNIEnv* env is your handle to the JVM from C — every conversion (GetStringUTFChars, NewStringUTF) goes through it. - Manual memory: what you Get… you must Release…. There's no using/finalizer. Leaks and use-after-free are real here. - Errors don't auto-propagate: a C-side failure must be turned into a JVM exception deliberately; otherwise it silently corrupts or crashes. QuickJSEngineImpl wraps native RuntimeExceptions into typed QuickJSException.CallError/EvaluateError on the Kotlin side.

docs.title: The one subtlety worth internalising: the single-thread + big-stack rule
docs.text:
QuickJS is not thread-safe and records the stack base of the thread that created it. So Capsule pins all engine calls to one dedicated thread with a large stack:

Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { r ->
    // 4 MB stack — QuickJS records this thread's stack pointer as the JS stack base.
    Thread(null, r, "capsule-quickjs", 4 * 1024 * 1024).also { it.isDaemon = true }
}.asCoroutineDispatcher()
// nativeCreate() MUST run on this thread so the base address is correct:
private val handle: Long = runBlocking(dispatcher) { nativeCreate() }
  • One thread for the engine's whole life — create, evaluate, call, destroy all on it. Calling from another thread = undefined behaviour / crash.
  • 4 MB stack because deep JS recursion uses the native C stack; the JVM default would overflow.
  • withContext(dispatcher) (in evaluate/call) hops onto that thread; the rest of the app stays on normal coroutine dispatchers. This is how a synchronous, single-threaded C engine lives safely inside an async Kotlin app.

docs.title: What you actually need to remember
docs.text:
1. Kotlin ↔ C is JNI (≈ P/Invoke); the .so is built by CMake/NDK from vendored C.
  2. The Long handle is a raw C pointer treated as opaque on the JVM side.
  3. Across the boundary you lose the GC and exceptions — the C glue marshals strings and translates failures back into Kotlin exceptions.
  4. The engine is single-threaded with a 4 MB stack, pinned via a coroutine dispatcher.

The shell builds two JNI libraries from src/main/cpp/CMakeLists.txt: libcapsule_quickjs_jni.so (the engine, this primer) and libcapsule_server.so (the CivetWeb HTTP server and its glue, capsule_server_jni.c — see civetweb.md).

You'll almost never touch quickjs_jni.c. When you do, it's usually to expose one more external fun — add the Kotlin declaration, add the matching Java_… C function, rebuild the AAR. Next: quickjs.md for what runs inside the engine, and civetweb.md for how JS gets invoked over HTTP.

docs.title: Kotlin for C# / TypeScript developers
docs.text: A Capsule-specific primer. You know C# (OO) and TypeScript well; Kotlin sits between them and will feel familiar fast. Every concept below links to a real file in the Capsule Android shell so you can see it in context, not in the abstract. Read it next to the code.

docs.title: The 30-second orientation
docs.text:
Kotlin is a statically-typed JVM language (compiles to the same bytecode as Java). Mentally: C#'s type system + TypeScript's terseness + null-safety baked into the compiler. No semicolons, type-after-name (val x: Int), expressions over statements. If you can read a C# record and a TS union, you can read 90% of Capsule's Kotlin.

Concept C# TypeScript Kotlin Immutable local readonly var / const const val Mutable local var let var Nullable string? string \| null String? Class class class class Record/DTO record interface/type data class Static static member module-level companion object Interface interface interface interface Enum enum enum/union enum class async fn async Task<T> async (): Promise<T> suspend fun (): T Discriminated union (none, pre-OneOf) union + tag sealed class

docs.title: 1. val / var, type inference, no new
docs.text:
val port: Int = 5173      // immutable (prefer this), explicit type
val name = "capsule"      // inferred String
var count = 0             // mutable
val provider = AndroidNetworkProvider(this)   // no `new`

Like C#'s var/readonly and TS's const/let. val ≈ a readonly binding (the reference can't be reassigned). Construct objects by calling the class like a function — no new keyword.

docs.title: 2. Null-safety is in the compiler (the biggest mental shift)
docs.text:
C# bolted nullable-reference-types on as warnings; Kotlin enforces it. A String cannot be null; only String? can, and the compiler forces you to handle it.

var launchUrl: String? = null          // nullable
launchUrl.length                       // ❌ compile error — might be null
launchUrl?.length                      // safe call → Int? (null if launchUrl is null)
launchUrl ?: "default"                 // elvis: value-or-fallback (C# ??)
launchUrl!!.length                     // assert non-null (throws if wrong — avoid unless certain)

See it real: AppLifecycleController.kt — consumeLaunchUrl(): String? returns nullable; callers must handle the null. ?.let { } (below) is the idiomatic "do this only if non-null."

docs.title: 3. data class ≈ C# record — the wire models
docs.text:
@Serializable
data class PushToken(val value: String, val platform: String)

You get constructor, equals/hashCode, toString, and copy() for free — exactly like a C# record. The @Serializable annotation is from kotlinx.serialization (think System.Text.Json source-generators): it lets Json.encodeToJsonElement(token) produce the JSON the TS side expects. Real: PushProvider.kt (PushToken, PushMessage, NotificationChannel).

@SerialName("wifi") on an enum constant pins its JSON form — so ConnectionType.WIFI serializes as "wifi", matching the TS union. (See ChannelImportance / PermissionStatus in the same file.)

docs.title: 4. sealed class ≈ a closed type hierarchy / discriminated union
docs.text:
C# has no real discriminated union (pre-OneOf libraries); TS fakes it with tagged unions. Kotlin's sealed class is the real thing — a fixed, compiler-known set of subtypes.

sealed class BridgeError(val code: Int, val message: String) {
    object PermissionDenied  : BridgeError(2001, "PERMISSION_DENIED")
    object FileNotFound      : BridgeError(5001, "FILE_NOT_FOUND")
    object PushRegistrationFailed : BridgeError(6001, "PUSH_REGISTRATION_FAILED")
}

Real: BridgeError.kt. object X : BridgeError(...) is a singleton subtype (Kotlin's object = a one-instance type; think C# static-but-it's-a-value). A when over a sealed type is exhaustive — the compiler errors if you miss a case, like a switch on a closed union.

docs.title: 5. companion object ≈ C# static members
docs.text:
Kotlin has no static keyword. Per-class constants/factories live in a companion object:

interface PushProvider {
    fun register(/* … */)
    companion object {
        const val CAPABILITY = "push"
        const val CAPABILITY_VERSION = 1
    }
}
// usage: PushProvider.CAPABILITY   ← reads exactly like a C# static

Real: every provider interface (PushProvider, NetworkProvider) and the method-name constants in PushController.kt.

docs.title: 6. interface + fun interface ≈ interfaces and delegates
docs.text:
Plain interface is what you expect. A fun interface (single-abstract-method) is Kotlin's delegate/Func<>: you can pass a lambda where the interface is expected.

fun interface BridgeEventEmitter {
    fun emit(method: String, params: JsonElement)
}
// construct from a lambda — like assigning a method group to an Action<,> in C#:
val emitter = BridgeEventEmitter { method, params -> bridge.sendNotification(method, params) }

Real: BridgeEventEmitter.kt and its use in CapsuleActivity / the controllers. In tests it's a recording fake — same seam, no WebView.

docs.title: 7. suspend fun ≈ async/await (without the await)
docs.text:
suspend fun handle(params: JsonElement): JsonElement { … }

suspend ≈ C#'s async Task<T> / TS async (): Promise<T>, but there's no await keyword — you call a suspend function and it just suspends at that point. Coroutines run on a dispatcher (≈ a TaskScheduler / the JS event loop). Real: every BridgeHandler.handle is suspend; see BridgeHandler.kt.

Callback → suspend bridge (you'll meet this in push): when a native API hands you a result via a callback, suspendCancellableCoroutine turns it into a suspend value:

override suspend fun handle(params: JsonElement): JsonElement =
    suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont ->
        provider.register(
            onToken = { cont.resume(Json.encodeToJsonElement(it)) },
            onError = { cont.resumeWithException(CapsuleException(BridgeError.PushRegistrationFailed, it.message)) },
        )
    }

cont.resume(x) ≈ TaskCompletionSource.SetResult(x); resumeWithException ≈ SetException. Real: PushHandlers.kt.

docs.title: 8. when ≈ switch expression (but better)
docs.text:
val devUrl = capsuleConfig.devServerUrl
when {
    devUrl != null -> webView.loadUrl(devUrl)
    else           -> startEmbeddedRuntime()
}

It's an expression (returns a value), matches on types/ranges/conditions, and is exhaustive over sealed types/enums. Like C# 8+ switch expressions, used everywhere.

docs.title: 9. Extension functions ≈ C# extension methods
docs.text:
fun LocationData.toPosition() = GeolocationPosition(/* … */)   // adds a method to LocationData
session.headers.toMap()                                        // stdlib extension

Same idea as C# this-parameter extension methods, but terser and pervasive. Real: the toPosition() mapper in GeolocationHandler.kt.

docs.title: 10. Small syntax you'll see constantly
docs.text:
• String templates: "port $port at ${config.appId}" (≈ C# $"..." / TS template literals).
  • Trailing-lambda: runBlocking { … }, withContext(dispatcher) { … } — if the last arg is a lambda it goes outside the parens. Looks like a language keyword but it's just a function taking a lambda.
  • ?.let { } — "if non-null, run this block with it as the value": url?.let { appLifecycle.onNewUrl(it) }.
  • it — the implicit single lambda parameter (like a terse x =>).
  • Single-expression functions: fun current(): NetworkStatus = status (no braces/return).
  • Default + named args: PushMessage(id = "m1", title = "Hi") — no overloads needed (kills most builder/overload boilerplate you'd write in C#).

docs.title: Where to look next
docs.text:
• Read BridgeError.kt (sealed) and PushProvider.kt (data classes + enums + companion) — they exercise §3–§6 in 100 lines.
  • Then PushHandlers.kt for §7 (suspend + the callback bridge).
  • For how Kotlin reaches the C engine, see jni-and-cpp.md.

docs.title: QuickJS in Capsule — the on-device JavaScript engine
docs.text: You write JS/TS for browsers and Node, where the engine (V8) is invisible. Capsule embeds its own JS engine inside the native app and runs your server-side code in it. This primer explains what that engine is, why Capsule embeds one, and the few hard constraints it imposes.

docs.title: What is a "JavaScript engine"?
docs.text:
A JS engine parses and executes JavaScript. You already use two without thinking: V8 (Chrome, Node, the Android WebView) and JavaScriptCore (Safari/iOS). They're big, fast, and tied to their host. QuickJS-ng is a different animal: a small (~1 MB), embeddable, spec-compliant engine written in C that you can compile into your own app and call directly. (QuickJS-ng is the maintained community fork of Fabrice Bellard's original QuickJS.)

C#/.NET analogy: it's like embedding a scripting runtime (think a tiny self-contained ClearScript/Jint) inside your process and calling into it — except QuickJS is C, reached via JNI (see jni-and-cpp.md).

docs.title: Why does Capsule embed one? (There's already a WebView with V8…)
docs.text:
The WebView runs your front-end JS. But Capsule also runs your server-side code — the src/server/routes/** handlers and JSON-RPC route overrides — and that code must run:

  • Outside the WebView, so it isn't coupled to the page's lifecycle, DOM, or a reload;
  • In a controlled, swappable sandbox, because this is the code Server Code Push / OTA will hot-update (Phase 6). You can ship new bundle JS to QuickJS without touching the native shell.

So the architecture is: front-end JS in the WebView (V8); back-end JS in QuickJS. The localhost server (civetweb.md) routes /api/* from the WebView into QuickJS. That clean split — and an OTA-updatable JS layer that the native capabilities back — is the whole point.

docs.title: How Capsule drives it
docs.text:
The JS bundle (built by capsule build from your src/routes + src/server/routes, bundled with esbuild into assets/server/bundle.js) is loaded once, then invoked per request. The engine surface is tiny — QuickJSEngine.kt:

suspend fun evaluate(bundle: String)                       // load/run the bundle once (defines handlers)
suspend fun call(fn: String, args: String): String         // call a global fn, JSON in → JSON out

evaluate runs your bundle, which registers route handlers on globalThis. Each HTTP/RPC request becomes a call("handleHttpRequest", jsonArgs) (or dispatch) that returns a JSON string. The implementation (QuickJSEngineImpl.kt) crosses JNI into the C engine on its pinned single thread.

docs.title: The hard constraints (these are non-obvious and bite people)
docs.text:
These are distilled in the [[quickjs-constraints]] note; they matter whenever you touch the runtime or the bundle contract:

  1. globalThis is the only reliable store. QuickJS-ng's embedding here doesn't give you ES module semantics or a persistent module registry across calls the way Node does. Route handlers must register themselves onto globalThis (that's what the bundle's addRoute/addHttpRoute do), and the Kotlin side calls global functions by name (call("handleHttpRequest", …)). Don't assume import/module-scope state survives between calls — put shared state on globalThis.

  2. dispatch() must return an object, not a string. The C JNI glue serializes the return value; if JS already returns a JSON string, it gets double-encoded (string-of-a-string). Handlers return plain JS objects and let the boundary serialize once. (This is exactly why core/src/router.ts's dispatch() returns an object.)

  3. It's not V8. QuickJS-ng is spec-compliant and current (ES2023-ish) but it is not a browser and not Node: no DOM, no window, no Node built-ins (fs, http, Buffer), no V8-specific extensions, and performance is "small and fast for embedding," not "JIT-fast like V8." Your server routes must be self-contained JS. Native capabilities (filesystem, network, etc.) are reached by the app through the bridge, not by QuickJS calling Node APIs.

  4. Single-threaded, pinned thread, 4 MB stack. (Mechanics in jni-and-cpp.md § "single-thread + big-stack rule".) Don't try to call the engine concurrently — it's serialized through one dispatcher by design.

docs.title: Versioning / vendoring
docs.text: QuickJS-ng is vendored — its C source lives in the repo at packages/native/quickjs/, shared by both shells (the Android CMake compiles four files: quickjs.c, dtoa.c, libregexp.c, libunicode.c), pinned in its VERSION file (0.15.1). There's no package manager for it — "bumping" means pnpm update:quickjs <tag> and re-running the instrumented JNI tests. The upkeep routine tracks this, watching for GC / spec / dtoa fixes since the engine is pre-1.0 and reserves the right to change its ABI.

docs.title: Mental summary
docs.text:
• QuickJS-ng = a small embeddable JS engine (C) compiled into the app; it runs your server-side JS, separate from the WebView's V8 that runs the front-end.
  • The split exists so back-end JS is decoupled from the page and is the unit OTA hot-updates.
  • Hard rules: register on globalThis, return objects (not JSON strings) from dispatch, no DOM/Node, single pinned thread. The engine is vendored C, bumped by hand.

Related: civetweb.md (how requests reach QuickJS) · jni-and-cpp.md (how Kotlin reaches the C engine).

docs.title: Contributing to Capsule Framework
docs.text:
Thank you for considering a contribution! The full guide lives at the repository root so GitHub shows it next to every pull request:

  • CONTRIBUTING.md — setup, the test layers (TypeScript, Kotlin, Android instrumented, Swift in Docker, docs), and what a pull request needs.
  • Code of Conduct — Contributor Covenant 2.1.
  • Security policy — report vulnerabilities privately, never in a public issue.

docs.title: Reporting bugs
docs.text: Use the issue tracker. Provide a clear title, steps to reproduce, expected vs. actual behavior, the platform (Android / iOS / browser dev mode) and versions, and any relevant logs.

docs.title: Suggesting features
docs.text: Open an issue with the enhancement label: the problem it solves, how it would work, and any drawbacks. Check the roadmap first — it may already be planned.

docs.title: CI — GitHub Actions
docs.text: The framework's continuous build + test: .github/workflows/ci.yml (the docs site deploys from .github/workflows/docs.yml). The repo is public, so GitHub-hosted Linux and macOS runners are free — every layer that doesn't need a real device runs here, Android and iOS alike.

docs.title: What runs
docs.text:
Triggered on pushes to main, on every pull request, and manually (Run workflow).

Job Runner What it checks js ubuntu-latest pnpm install --frozen-lockfile → format:check → lint → build → typecheck → test → test:scripts → docs:check → generated-reference freshness (node scripts/gen/index.mjs --check); docs:lint runs as advisory (continue-on-error) android ubuntu-latest + JDK 17 + Android SDK/NDK ./gradlew assembleDebug testDebugUnitTest — the AAR builds (CivetWeb + QuickJS through CMake) and the pure-JVM unit tests pass; reports uploaded on failure android-instrumented ubuntu-latest, KVM, API-35 emulator ./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest — the instrumented suite (QuickJS, CivetwebServerTest, AndroidDbProviderTest, AndroidGeminiNanoProviderTest, …). Opt-in (see below); runs after android ios-linux swift:6.4-jammy container swift test — the same run contributors do locally in Docker ios-macos macos-latest swift test on macOS — adds the Apple-only suites (e.g. SqliteDbProviderTests over the system SQLite3)

The ndk version installed in CI is pinned in ci.yml (NDK_VERSION) and must match ndkVersion in packages/capsule-android/capsule/build.gradle.kts.

docs.title: The opt-in instrumented run
docs.text:
Emulator runs are slow, so android-instrumented only runs when asked:

  • Manually: Actions → CI → Run workflow → tick instrumented.
  • On a pull request: add the label instrumented.

Not covered anywhere in CI: camera capturePhoto / pickImage are interactive (system camera, photo picker) and stay a manual on-device pass, alongside the real-device e2e tier.

docs.title: Running the same checks locally
docs.text:
Command (repo root) Same as pnpm verify the js job (--keep-going reports every failure instead of stopping at the first) pnpm verify:android the android job (uses the JDK/SDK from your .env.local) pnpm verify:ios the ios-linux job (Docker, swift:6.4-jammy) pnpm with-env --cwd packages/capsule-android gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest android-instrumented (start an emulator first: pnpm dev:emulator start)

pnpm verify green is the definition of done for a change (CONTRIBUTING).

docs.title: Test-tier alignment
docs.text:
Mirrors the tier strategy that holds on both platforms (ios-bring-up.md):

Tier Android iOS unit vitest + Gradle testDebugUnitTest — every push swift test on Linux + macOS — every push integration connectedDebugAndroidTest on the emulator (opt-in) Simulator tests (with the WKWebView shell, Phase 4) e2e real device — manual real iPhone — manual

docs.title: CodeSync internals
docs.text:
How over-the-air (OTA) updates work under the hood: the bundle format, the publish flow, the self-hosted server, the wire protocol and the on-device client. For using CodeSync in an app, read ota-updates.md first.

OTA hub. The topic spans several docs; this one owns the mechanism. - Why the bundle can be replaced at all (embedded runtime) → 0001-embedded-runtime.md - App developer how-to → ota-updates.md - Cloud control plane (portal, database, workers) → server-design/overview.md, server-design/database.md (Phase 6) - Bundle storage (content-addressed, differential) → server-design/file-storage.md - Store release plus OTA, the two release layers → publishing.md - Bandwidth economics → infrastructure.md - Store policy, capability gating, liability → ota-policy-and-liability.md - OTA cloud as the funding engine → business-model.md - Status and sequencing (on-device done; delivery and cloud in Phase 6) → roadmap.md

docs.title: Status at a glance
docs.text:
CodeSync is the Capsule equivalent of Microsoft CodePush (retired) and Expo Updates. It is built in layers, and each layer below is tested on its own. The parts are not connected end to end yet (see Known gaps).

Layer Code State Config block packages/cli/src/config.ts (codeSync) Built. Only enabled, url, apiKey are read. Publish CLI packages/cli/src/commands/codesync.ts Built: capsule codesync publish [--channel] [--notes]. Self-hosted server packages/codesync-api/src/index.ts, api-spec.yaml Built: single-process, file-based, one shared API key. AGPL-3.0. Android client packages/capsule-android/capsule/src/main/kotlin/dev/capsule/codesync/, runtime/FileBundleStore.kt, runtime/CrashLoopGuard.kt Built and unit-tested on the JVM. iOS client packages/capsule-ios/Sources/dev/capsule/codesync/, runtime/ Client core built and tested on Linux (swift test); constructed in CapsuleViewController but not on the bridge yet (Phase 4). JS module packages/core/src/codesync.ts Built: checkForUpdate, getStatus, applyUpdate. Cloud control plane, dashboard, staged rollout CLI, targeting, differential updates, signing — Planned, see Planned: cloud control plane.

What can be updated: the whole web bundle (www/) and the QuickJS route bundle (server/bundle.js), always together as one ZIP. What cannot: the native shell, permissions, plugins. Those need a store release.

The update client ships in the Capsule AAR (and the Swift package) whether or not an app uses it. When the shell config has no codeSync, no codesync.* bridge handlers are registered, so the feature is absent from the bridge surface. It is not compiled out.

docs.title: Bundle ZIP format
docs.text:
bundle.zip
  www/                         ← client bundle (Vite / ng build output)
    index.html                 ← required: the shell rejects a bundle without it
    assets/…
  server/                      ← only when the app has src/server/routes/
    bundle.js                  ← esbuild output: the QuickJS route bundle
  capsule-bundle.json          ← bundle manifest

capsule-bundle.json, written by the CLI from capsule.config.ts:

{
  "version": "1.4.2",
  "buildNumber": 47,
  "createdAt": "2025-10-15T14:32:00Z",
  "capsuleSchemaVersion": 1
}

The manifest is for Capsule only; the stores never see it. capsuleSchemaVersion lets the format change later without breaking older clients. The device client today validates a bundle by the presence of www/index.html; it does not read the manifest yet.

The ZIP is written in-process with archiver (DEFLATE, level 9) by packages/cli/src/lib/zip.ts, so publishing behaves the same on Windows, macOS and Linux.

The whole dist/ folder is copied into www/. Planned, not built: stripping source maps (--source-maps to keep them) and a .capsuleignore file.

docs.title: Publish flow
docs.text:
capsule codesync publish (packages/cli/src/commands/codesync.ts):

  1. Requires codeSync.enabled, codeSync.url and codeSync.apiKey; exits with an error otherwise.
  2. Builds the web app: web.buildCommand when set, else pnpm exec vite build. Output is dist/.
  3. When src/server/routes/ exists, bundles the routes with esbuild into server/bundle.js. The bundle registers JSON-RPC overrides from src/routes/*.ts and HTTP routes from src/server/routes/**/*.ts, the same scheme capsule build uses.
  4. Assembles www/, server/ and capsule-bundle.json in a unique OS temp directory, which is removed in a finally block.
  5. Zips it and computes its SHA-256.
  6. POSTs multipart/form-data to <codeSync.url>/publish with bundle, version, buildNumber, channel (from --channel, default production) and optional notes, and an Authorization: Bearer <apiKey> header.

docs.title: Self-hosted server
docs.text:
@capsule/codesync-api (packages/codesync-api/) is the minimal self-hostable delivery server: Fastify 5 (multipart uploads via @fastify/multipart 10), one process, a JSON manifest on disk. The contract is api-spec.yaml (OpenAPI 3).

Endpoint Auth Does GET /health — Liveness: { status, timestamp }. GET /bundles/:version[?channel=] — Returns a stored bundle; latest resolves the channel's current version. Sends an ETag (SHA-256). GET /manifest[?channel=] — The current version per channel. GET /releases[?channel=] — Release history, newest first. POST /publish x-api-key Stores an uploaded bundle (multipart: bundle, version, buildNumber, channel, notes). 409 if the version exists. POST /rollback x-api-key Points a channel back at its previous release. POST /pause, POST /resume x-api-key Sets or clears a channel's paused flag. GET /devices x-api-key Stub, returns 204.
  • Auth: one shared key, CODESYNC_API_KEY, compared with the x-api-key header.
  • Storage: storage/ next to the package, or CODESYNC_STORAGE_DIR. It holds manifest.json and bundles/<version>.js (the uploaded file is stored under that name whatever it contains).
  • Limits: uploads up to 10 MB. Listens on 0.0.0.0:3000.
  • Tests: packages/codesync-api/tests/smoke.test.ts drives the routes with server.inject().

License. packages/codesync-api is AGPL-3.0; the rest of Capsule is Apache-2.0 (see the repository NOTICE). Anyone may run and modify the server. If you offer a modified version to others over a network, you must publish your changes under the same license.

docs.title: Device client
docs.text: The update check runs in the native layer, not in JS, so it still works when the web bundle is broken. Android is described here; the iOS client mirrors it type for type (CodeSyncManager.swift, CodeSyncModels.swift, Rollout.swift, FileBundleStore.swift).

docs.title: Opt-in
docs.text: CapsuleShellConfig.codeSync (CodeSyncConfig: url, appId, channel, nativeVersion). When it is set, CapsuleActivity builds a CodeSyncManager and registers the three codesync.* handlers (codesync/CodeSyncHandlers.kt). When it is null, neither exists.

docs.title: Update check endpoint
docs.text:
GET {url}/v1/check/{appId}/{channel}/{nativeVersion}

The URL carries everything that varies, so a CDN can cache one response for every device on the same app, channel and native version. Device identity is deliberately kept out of this request: custom headers such as a device id would make every request unique and destroy the cache hit rate.

Response (the shape CodeSyncModels.kt and CodeSyncModels.swift decode; this exact example is pinned by CodeSyncModelsTest):

{
  "latestBuildNumber": 47,
  "bundle": {
    "id": "6f1c2a7e-0b4d-4c1a-9e2f-3a5b6c7d8e9f",
    "version": "1.4.2",
    "buildNumber": 47,
    "rolloutPercent": 100,
    "url": "https://cdn.capsule.dev/bundles/6f1c2a7e.zip",
    "hash": "sha256:abc123def456",
    "sizeBytes": 284000,
    "mandatory": false
  }
}

rolloutPercent defaults to 100 and mandatory to false when absent. The sha256: prefix on hash is optional.

docs.title: Rollout decision
docs.text:
Gradual rollout is decided on the device, with no extra round trip (codesync/Rollout.kt): MurmurHash3 x86 32-bit over the UTF-8 bytes of the device id, seed 0, bucketed by the unsigned hash modulo 100. The device is in the rollout when bucket < rolloutPercent.

Any server-side implementation must compute the same bucket, i.e. murmurhash3js-revisited x86.hash32(bytes, 0). The repo has no TypeScript implementation yet; the vectors in Kotlin's RolloutTest and Swift's Murmur3Tests were generated with that library and pin the contract. The trap is the sign: Kotlin's Int is signed, and Math.abs(hash) % 100 puts roughly half of all ids in the wrong bucket. The device id is a random UUID created on first use and kept in SharedPreferences (PrefsCodeSyncStore).

docs.title: Download and install
docs.text:
When the device is in the rollout and bundle.buildNumber is higher than the installed build (CodeSyncManager.checkForUpdate):

  1. Download the ZIP from bundle.url.
  2. Compute its SHA-256 and compare it with bundle.hash. On mismatch, delete it and report an error.
  3. Unzip into filesDir/bundles/<bundle.id>/ (CodeSyncUnzipper).
  4. Reject the bundle if www/index.html is missing.
  5. Install it with BundleStore.install.

Every failure returns UpdateResult.Error and cleans up the staged directory; the manager never throws. After the check, the manager posts a fire-and-forget check-in (failures ignored):

POST {url}/v1/devices/checkin
{ "deviceId", "appId", "platform": "android", "nativeVersion", "bundleId", "channel" }

docs.title: Bundle store
docs.text:
FileBundleStore keeps two slots under filesDir/bundles/:

active/     ← the bundle to serve
previous/   ← the last known-good bundle, the rollback target

install() demotes a valid active/ to previous/, then moves the staged bundle to active/. Each File.renameTo is atomic, with a recursive-copy fallback across filesystems. A directory counts as a bundle only if it contains www/index.html, so a broken bundle is never promoted to the rollback slot. The interface uses String paths so the same contract exists on iOS.

docs.title: Crash-loop rollback
docs.text: CrashLoopGuard (runtime/CrashLoopGuard.kt) records a timestamp for each launch. The record is cleared when the WebView reports the page finished loading (CapsuleRuntime.notifyAppReady). At the start of each launch, CapsuleRuntime.start() checks: if 3 unconfirmed launches fall inside the last 60 s and a previous bundle exists, it calls BundleStore.rollback(), clears the guard and calls onRollback(). The guard's clock and log are injected, so it is tested on the plain JVM.

docs.title: Bridge surface
docs.text:
Method Returns codesync.checkForUpdate { status, update? }: runs a check, status is "download ready" when a bundle was installed codesync.getStatus { status }: the manager's last status codesync.applyUpdate { status }: "update applied" when an update is pending, else "idle"

Status strings must match the JS CodeSyncStatus union exactly, spaces included ("download ready"). @capsule/core's CodeSyncModule maps them: checkForUpdate() returns the update object only for "download ready".

docs.title: Known gaps
docs.text:
What still blocks an end-to-end update, found by reading the code on 2026-10-24. Each item names the code to change.

  1. No server speaks the device protocol. Devices call GET /v1/check/… and POST /v1/devices/checkin; @capsule/codesync-api serves /manifest and /bundles/:version instead. One side has to adopt the other's shape.
  2. CLI and server disagree on auth. capsule codesync publish sends Authorization: Bearer <key>; the server reads x-api-key. Publishing to the bundled server gets 401.
  3. The server ignores the bundle checksum. codesync publish sends the ZIP (bundle, file name bundle.zip) plus a sha256 field, but codesync-api neither verifies nor stores it, so the manifest it serves carries no hash for the device's integrity gate.
  4. The OTA route bundle exposes the wrong global. codesync.ts aliases capsuleRouter.handleHttpRoute; build.ts uses capsuleRouter.handleHttpRequest. HTTP routes in an OTA bundle would have no handleHttpRequest. Routes are also bundled only when src/server/routes/ exists, which drops JSON-RPC overrides in src/routes/ when there are no HTTP routes.
  5. The server stores the ZIP as bundles/<version>.js and serves it as application/javascript. That is left over from an earlier JS-only design; api-spec.yaml still describes a gzipped JS bundle.
  6. Generated apps never enable OTA. The MainActivity that capsule sync writes sets only devServerUrl. The codeSync block in capsule.config.ts is not passed into CapsuleShellConfig.
  7. An installed bundle is not served. The embedded server reads static files from the APK (AssetManagerStaticAssets), and QuickJSBridgeImpl loads server/bundle.js from the APK too, not from BundleStore.activeDir(). A crash-loop rollback therefore swaps directories that nothing serves.
  8. One crash can trigger a rollback. CapsuleActivity and CapsuleRuntime.start() both call recordLaunchAttempt(), so each launch adds two records and the 3-in-60-s threshold is reached after the first crashing launch.
  9. applyUpdateOnNextResume loads file://<path>/index.html — not www/index.html, and not through the loopback server.
  10. Config fields with no effect: codeSync.channel, strategy, checkOnForeground, mandatory. publish takes the channel from --channel only.
  11. iOS constructs its CodeSyncManager but does not register bridge handlers yet (Phase 4).

docs.title: Planned: cloud control plane (design)
docs.text: Everything below is design, not built. It describes the managed, multi-tenant service (Phase 6) that the self-hosted server is a small subset of. Where it and the built code differ, the built sections above win.

docs.title: Prior Art Analysis
docs.text:
Project Status Key Lesson Microsoft CodePush (microsoft/code-push) Archived 2023, merged into App Center then killed Proved the model. Don't depend on it. Expo Updates (expo/expo — packages/expo-updates) Active, open source Best-in-class architecture. Study the differential update approach. Shorebird (shorebirdtech/shorebird) Active, commercial Dart/Flutter-specific but excellent rollout/rollback UX hot-updater (gronxb/hot-updater) Active GitHub project Self-hosted, React Native, clean architecture reference AppFlow (Ionic) Commercial SaaS Reference for enterprise feature set

Recommendation: Model the protocol and update flow after Expo Updates (open source, battle-tested at scale) but implement self-hosted from day one. Do not depend on third-party SaaS.

docs.title: Database Schema
docs.text:
Designed for millions of devices with proper partitioning strategy.

-- ============================================================
-- USERS (dashboard accounts / API key owners)
-- ============================================================
CREATE TABLE users (
  id           UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  email        TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- ============================================================
-- APPS
-- ============================================================
CREATE TABLE apps (
  id           UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  app_id       TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,        -- 'com.yourcompany.app'
  name         TEXT NOT NULL,
  owner_id     UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- ============================================================
-- CHANNELS
-- Deployment targets: production, staging, beta, etc.
-- ============================================================
CREATE TABLE channels (
  id           UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  app_id       UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES apps(id),
  name         TEXT NOT NULL,              -- 'production', 'staging'
  UNIQUE(app_id, name)
);

-- ============================================================
-- BUNDLES
-- One row per published web bundle
-- ============================================================
CREATE TABLE bundles (
  id                UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  app_id            UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES apps(id),
  channel_id        UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES channels(id),
  version           TEXT NOT NULL,          -- semver: '1.4.2'
  build_number      BIGINT NOT NULL,        -- monotonic, used for ordering
  storage_key       TEXT NOT NULL,          -- S3/R2 object key
  storage_url       TEXT NOT NULL,          -- CDN URL
  size_bytes        BIGINT NOT NULL,
  hash_sha256       TEXT NOT NULL,          -- integrity verification
  min_native_version TEXT,                  -- npm semver range e.g. '>=1.4.0' (see ../reference/lockfile.md)
  max_native_version TEXT,                  -- npm semver range e.g. '<2.0.0' (optional upper bound)
  metadata          JSONB DEFAULT '{}',
  status            TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active',
                    -- active | paused | rolled_back | archived
  rollout_percent   SMALLINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 100,  -- 0-100
  created_at        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  created_by        UUID REFERENCES users(id),

  CONSTRAINT build_number_monotonic UNIQUE (app_id, channel_id, build_number)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_bundles_channel_status ON bundles(channel_id, status, build_number DESC);

-- ============================================================
-- DEVICES
-- One row per installed app instance
-- Partitioned by app_id for scale
-- ============================================================
CREATE TABLE devices (
  id                  UUID NOT NULL DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  app_id              UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES apps(id),
  device_id           TEXT NOT NULL,           -- UUID generated on first launch, stored in keychain/keystore
  platform            TEXT NOT NULL,           -- 'android' | 'ios'
  platform_version    TEXT NOT NULL,           -- '14', '17.2', etc.
  native_version      TEXT NOT NULL,           -- capsule shell version: '1.4.0'
  app_version         TEXT NOT NULL,           -- store app version: '2.1.0'
  bundle_id           UUID REFERENCES bundles(id),   -- currently running bundle
  channel             TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'production',
  last_seen_at        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  first_seen_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  timezone            TEXT,
  locale              TEXT,
  device_model        TEXT,                    -- 'Pixel 8', 'iPhone 15'
  metadata            JSONB DEFAULT '{}',

  PRIMARY KEY (app_id, device_id)             -- compound PK for partitioning
) PARTITION BY HASH (app_id);                 -- hash-partition by app

-- Create 16 partitions (adjust as scale grows)
CREATE TABLE devices_p0  PARTITION OF devices FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 16, REMAINDER 0);
CREATE TABLE devices_p1  PARTITION OF devices FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 16, REMAINDER 1);
-- ... p2 through p15

CREATE INDEX idx_devices_last_seen   ON devices(app_id, last_seen_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_devices_channel     ON devices(app_id, channel);
CREATE INDEX idx_devices_bundle      ON devices(bundle_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_devices_platform_v  ON devices(app_id, platform, platform_version);

-- ============================================================
-- DEVICE EVENTS (timeseries — partition by month)
-- Records update lifecycle: checked / downloaded / applied / error
-- ============================================================
CREATE TABLE device_events (
  id          BIGSERIAL,
  app_id      UUID NOT NULL,
  device_id   TEXT NOT NULL,
  bundle_id   UUID REFERENCES bundles(id),
  event       TEXT NOT NULL,
              -- 'check' | 'download_start' | 'download_complete'
              -- | 'apply' | 'rollback' | 'error'
  error_code  TEXT,
  metadata    JSONB DEFAULT '{}',
  occurred_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),

  PRIMARY KEY (id, occurred_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (occurred_at);           -- monthly partitions

-- Auto-partition creation via pg_partman (recommended)
-- Retain 12 months of granular events, then aggregate

-- ============================================================
-- AGGREGATED METRICS (pre-computed, avoid querying device_events at scale)
-- ============================================================
CREATE TABLE bundle_stats (
  bundle_id       UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES bundles(id),
  hour            TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,        -- truncated to hour
  checks          INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  downloads       INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  installs        INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  errors          INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  active_devices  INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,

  PRIMARY KEY (bundle_id, hour)
);

docs.title: Backend API
docs.text: Stack: Node.js + TypeScript + Fastify (or Hono for edge). Stateless — scales horizontally behind a load balancer.

docs.title: Check endpoint at scale
docs.text:
GET /v1/check

Called by every device on app foreground (potentially millions of req/min).

Two-request design — separates the CDN-cacheable check from the device-specific parts:

Request 1 — Bundle check (CDN-cacheable GET): URL encodes the cache key so CDN can serve the same response to all devices sharing the same app/channel/native-version: 

GET /v1/check/{appId}/{channel}/{nativeVersion}

# Example:
GET /v1/check/com.yourcompany.app/production/1.4.0

The response is the check response the device client already decodes. CDN-cached with a 30 s TTL, it is identical for every device on the same app, channel and native version; each device then applies the rollout decision locally (Rollout decision).

Request 2 — Device check-in (background, fire-and-forget POST): This is where device identity, platform version, and current bundle are reported. Runs async, never blocks the UX. See Device Check-in section below.

Caching strategy: - CDN caches by URL path: {appId}/{channel}/{nativeVersion} — same response served to all matching devices - Redis key (origin cache): check:{app_id}:{channel}:{native_version} — TTL 30s - On bundle publish: invalidate affected Redis keys → CDN TTL expires naturally within 30s

docs.title: Device Check-in (background, fire-and-forget)
docs.text:
POST /v1/devices/checkin

{
  "deviceId": "uuid",
  "appId": "com.yourcompany.app",
  "platform": "android",
  "platformVersion": "14",
  "nativeVersion": "1.4.0",
  "bundleId": "uuid",
  "channel": "production",
  "deviceModel": "Pixel 8",
  "metadata": {
    "user_tier": "enterprise",
    "experiment_group": "checkout-v2"
  },
  "locale": "en-US",
  "timezone": "America/New_York"
}

Upsert into devices table. Response: 202 Accepted. Use a write queue (BullMQ / Redis queue) to absorb spikes and batch writes.

docs.title: Bundle Upload
docs.text:
POST /v1/bundles/upload   (multipart/form-data)
Authorization: Bearer <api-key>

Fields: - bundle — ZIP file of the built dist/ - appId - channel - version — {appVersion}+{bundlePatch} format (e.g. 1.0.0+3). Bundle counter resets to 1 when appVersion changes. - minNativeVersion (optional) — npm semver range e.g. >=1.4.0 - rolloutPercent (default: 100) - filter (optional) — JSONB filter expression targeting device metadata: "metadata.user_tier = 'enterprise'" - scheduledAt (optional) — ISO 8601 timestamp; bundle is ready but delivery begins at this time

Processing pipeline: 1. Validate API key → app ownership 2. Receive ZIP → stream to temp storage 3. Compute SHA-256 hash 4. Upload to S3/R2 (storage key: bundles/{app_id}/{build_number}.zip) 5. Insert into bundles table 6. Invalidate Redis cache for affected channel 7. Return bundle record

docs.title: Rollout Control
docs.text:
PATCH /v1/bundles/:bundleId
{
  "rolloutPercent": 10,    // gradual rollout: start at 10%
  "status": "paused"       // emergency stop
}

Gradual rollout: The update check endpoint uses rolloutPercent with a deterministic hash of device_id to assign devices consistently to a cohort. Same device always gets the same answer for a given percent.

// npm install murmurhash3js-revisited  (or any consistent hash — must match client)
import { x86 } from 'murmurhash3js-revisited'

function isInRollout(deviceId: string, percent: number): boolean {
  if (percent >= 100) return true
  if (percent <= 0) return false
  const hash = x86.hash32(deviceId) % 100   // deterministic: same device always same bucket
  return hash < percent
}

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
POST /v1/bundles/:bundleId/rollback

Sets status = 'rolled_back' on the bundle. The previous active bundle for that channel becomes active. All devices receive the previous bundle on next check.

docs.title: Frontend Dashboard
docs.text: Stack: React + TanStack Query + Recharts. Single-page app served by the backend.
