docs.title: How it handles millions of devices
docs.text:
The hot path is the update check endpoint. This must handle spikes (everyone opens the app at 9am).

Layer Solution Check endpoint Stateless, horizontally scaled behind load balancer Redis cache Active bundle per channel cached 30s — 99% of requests never hit the DB Database Read replicas for all read queries; primary only for writes Device writes Write queue (BullMQ) — absorbs spikes, batches upserts Bundle downloads Served from CDN (CloudFront/Cloudflare R2) — backend not involved Metrics Pre-aggregated into bundle_stats hourly — dashboard never queries device_events directly Partitioning devices table hash-partitioned by app_id; device_events range-partitioned by month

Capacity rough math: - 10M devices, check every foreground = ~50M checks/day = ~580 req/sec average - Peak (morning rush, 10x): ~5,800 req/sec - With 30s Redis cache: cache hit rate ~95%+, effective DB load < 300 req/sec - 3 backend instances handle this comfortably

Device storage: 10M devices × ~1KB per row = ~10GB. Trivial for PostgreSQL with proper partitioning.

Events storage: 50M events/day × 30 days = 1.5B rows/month. Partition by month, drop after 12 months, aggregate into bundle_stats.

docs.title: Version Numbering Convention
docs.text:
Bundle versions follow {appVersion}+{bundlePatch} — semver build metadata:

Store release: 1.0.0   → CodeSync bundles: 1.0.0+1, 1.0.0+2, 1.0.0+3 ...
Store release: 1.1.0   → CodeSync bundles: 1.1.0+1, 1.1.0+2 ...

capsule codesync publish auto-increments the bundle counter within the current appVersion and resets it to +1 when appVersion changes. CLI and dashboard always display as two separate columns (VERSION + BUNDLE) — the + notation is never surfaced directly.

docs.title: Device Metadata API
docs.text:
The shell automatically sends standard metadata at every check-in: os_version, locale, timezone, device_model, app_version, bundle_version.

For custom business metadata, the app registers it via the bridge:

import { codesync } from '@capsule/core'

// Call after authentication — when business context is known
codesync.setDeviceMetadata({
  user_tier: user.subscriptionPlan,   // 'free' | 'pro' | 'enterprise'
  experiment_group: abTest.group,     // 'control' | 'checkout-v2'
  store_id: user.assignedStore        // for retail/franchise use cases
})

Metadata is stored in devices.metadata JSONB, merged with standard metadata. No PII — use opaque identifiers, not email or name.

Targeting at publish time: 

# Geographic (automatic metadata — no app code needed)
capsule codesync publish --filter "metadata.locale LIKE 'pt-%'"

# Business segment (custom metadata)
capsule codesync publish --channel staging --filter "metadata.user_tier = 'enterprise'"

# Named group (saved filter expression in the dashboard)
capsule codesync publish --group "brazil-enterprise"

docs.title: Channel Promotion
docs.text:
Channels are the approval mechanism. capsule codesync promote is the approval gesture.

# Publish to staging (developers can do this)
capsule codesync publish --channel staging

# After QA sign-off — promote to production (Releaser role required)
capsule codesync promote --from staging --to production --rollout 5

# Increase rollout after monitoring
capsule codesync rollout 25
capsule codesync rollout 100

Role-based access in the portal: Developer role can publish to non-production channels. Releaser role required to promote to production. The audit log records who ran each promote.

docs.title: Planned CLI commands
docs.text:
Only capsule codesync publish --channel --notes exists today (Publish flow). The rest of this list is the target surface.

# Publish a new bundle
capsule codesync publish
capsule codesync publish --channel staging
capsule codesync publish --channel production --rollout 10
capsule codesync publish --filter "metadata.user_tier = 'enterprise'"   # metadata targeting
capsule codesync publish --group "beta-testers"                          # named group
capsule codesync publish --at "2026-06-01T09:00:00Z"                    # scheduled release
capsule codesync publish --min-native-version ">=1.4.0"                 # native version gate

# Promote between channels (approval gesture)
capsule codesync promote --from staging --to production
capsule codesync promote --from staging --to production --rollout 5

# Manage releases
capsule codesync releases                    # list releases
capsule codesync rollback                    # rollback latest on current channel
capsule codesync rollback --bundle v1.4.1    # rollback to specific version
capsule codesync pause                       # emergency stop
capsule codesync rollout 50                  # increase to 50%
capsule codesync rollout 100                 # full rollout

# Device info
capsule codesync devices                     # fleet summary
capsule codesync devices --platform android  # filtered

docs.text:
# docker-compose.yml for CodeSync service
services:

docs.title: API Key Setup
docs.text:
CodeSync publish operations require an API key tied to your app registration in the Capsule portal (see ../project/server-design/overview.md).

How to get an API key: 1. Sign up at the Capsule portal (self-hosted or cloud) 2. Create an organization and register your app with its appId 3. Generate an API key under Settings → API Keys 4. Add it to your environment:

# .env.local (never commit this file)
CODESYNC_API_KEY=csk_live_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx

# Or in CI secrets:
# CODESYNC_API_KEY → GitHub/GitLab/Azure secret

// capsule.config.ts
codeSync: {
  url:    process.env.CODESYNC_URL,
  apiKey: process.env.CODESYNC_API_KEY,   // ← portal-generated key
  channel: 'production'
}

The API key is only used by the CLI for publishing — it is never embedded in the app binary. The app reads from the check endpoint (public, CDN-cached) and the check-in endpoint (unauthenticated, rate-limited by IP).

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
Built today: SHA-256 verification before install, and an API key that only the publish side uses. Everything else in this list is planned.

  • Bundle integrity: SHA-256 hash verified by the native client before applying. Reject and report if mismatch.
  • HTTPS only: All check and download endpoints require TLS. Native client pins the cert (configurable).
  • API keys: Publish endpoint requires API key (never embedded in app). Generated in the Capsule portal. Dashboard uses JWT auth (see ../project/server-design/overview.md).
  • Bundle signing (future): Sign bundles with a private key; native client verifies with embedded public key. Prevents MITM even with compromised CDN.
  • No arbitrary code at capsule layer: CodeSync can only update the web bundle (www/) and the server bundle (server/bundle.js). It cannot update native code, permissions, or the capsule shell. This is enforced by the native runtime loading only from the designated bundle directory.
  • min_native_version: Uses npm semver ranges (e.g. >=1.4.0). Evaluated client-side using an embedded semver library that matches npm's semver package behavior exactly.

docs.title: Phased Delivery
docs.text: Phase Deliverable CS-1 Backend API (check, upload, checkin) + PostgreSQL schema + S3 storage CS-2 Android client runtime (check, download, apply) CS-3 CLI commands (publish, rollback, rollout) CS-4 Dashboard (releases, fleet view, funnel) CS-5 iOS client runtime + gradual rollout + mandatory updates CS-6 Differential updates — file-level content-addressed storage. CodeSync is a service pack / hotfix channel: a typical fix changes 1–3 Vite output chunks. Server stores files by content hash; devices download only what changed. Since Vite outputs content-hashed filenames, unchanged chunks are never retransferred. Expected reduction: 80–95% of full bundle size for a typical hotfix. No binary diff algorithm needed.

docs.title: Appendix: iOS shell build with xtool
docs.text:
This section is about building the iOS shell, not OTA. It is kept here until it moves to ios-bring-up.md; the steps are unverified on real hardware.

The iOS capsule shell can now be built entirely on Linux/WSL/Windows using the xtool cross‑platform Xcode replacement. This eliminates the need for a macOS machine during development and CI.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. Install xtool – follow the official guide: https://xtool.sh/documentation/xtooldocs/installation-linux (Linux/WSL) or the Windows equivalent.
  2. Authenticate with Apple Developer Services – required for code signing and SDK access: 
    xtool auth login   # opens a browser flow or prompts for credentials + 2FA
xtool auth status  # should show you are logged in
  3. The iOS capsule package is a SwiftPM project – manifest at the capsule repo root, Package.swift (sources stay in packages/capsule-ios/; deps: swift-crypto for bundle SHA-256, ZIPFoundation for extraction — both Apple + Linux; the embedded server builds from the vendored packages/native/civetweb as the CCivetweb target; XKit stays optional until a device-management feature needs it). The CodeSync client core is implemented and unit-tested on Linux (swift test in a swift:6.4-jammy container, 89 tests); see packages/capsule-ios/README.md. Wire-contract note: the rollout hash is MurmurHash3 x86 32-bit over the UTF-8 bytes of the device id (murmurhash3js-revisited x86.hash32(bytes, 0)), bucketed by the unsigned hash modulo 100 — the Swift/Kotlin/TS implementations are pinned to the same shared vectors.

docs.title: Build Steps
docs.text:
From the root of the capsule repo (where Package.swift is):

# 1. Resolve dependencies and fetch the Darwin Swift SDK
xtool sdk install iphoneos   # installs the iOS device SDK
xtool sdk install iphonesimulator # installs the iOS simulator SDK

# 2. Build the XCFramework for device and simulator
xtool build -c release --scheme Capsule \
    -destination 'generic/platform=iOS' \
    --archive-path ./build/ios-arm64.xcarchive \
    SKIP_INSTALL=NO BUILD_LIBRARIES_FOR_DISTRIBUTION=YES

xtool build -c release --scheme Capsule \
    -destination 'generic/platform=iOS Simulator' \
    --archive-path ./build/ios-simulator.xcarchive \
    SKIP_INSTALL=NO BUILD_LIBRARIES_FOR_DISTRIBUTION=YES

# 3. Create the universal XCFramework
xtool create-xcframework \
    -framework ./build/ios-arm64.xcarchive/Products/Library/Frameworks/Capsule.framework \
    -framework ./build/ios-simulator.xcarchive/Products/Library/Frameworks/Capsule.framework \
    -output ./build/Capsule.xcframework

docs.title: Using the Built Framework
docs.text:
The resulting ./build/Capsule.xcframework can be consumed by the Capsule CLI exactly as before. Set the environment variable to point to your locally built override:

export CAPSULE_SHELL_OVERRIDE_PATH=$(pwd)/build/Capsule.xcframework

Then run the usual CLI commands (capsule dev ios, capsule build ios, etc.) – they will pick up the overridden shell.

docs.title: Testing the Swift Side (Optional)
docs.text:
Add Swift unit tests under packages/capsule-ios/Tests/ and run them from the repo root with:

xtool test   # builds and runs tests on the host using the iOS Simulator SDK

or, with no Apple tooling at all, swift test in Docker — see packages/capsule-ios/README.md.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The build process uses xtool build, which is a thin wrapper around xcodebuild that automatically selects the correct toolchain and SDKs provided by xtool.
  • All code‑signing steps (if you intend to distribute the app) are handled by xtool codesign under the hood; you can also invoke it manually for ad‑hoc signing.
  • For CI pipelines, simply install xtool, run xtool auth login (store the session token securely), and execute the build steps above.

This approach keeps the iOS capsule shell lightweight, enables rapid iteration on non‑macOS workstations, and aligns the build process with the existing Android Gradle‑based workflow.

docs.title: Capsule — Command Reference
docs.text: Every command runs from the capsule repo root and works the same on Windows, macOS and Linux: machine-specific paths live in a git-ignored .env.local, and the contributor scripts in scripts/ (exposed as pnpm dev:* / pnpm update:*) resolve the right executables per OS. The example apps live in examples/ (override with CAPSULE_EXAMPLES_DIR in .env.local).

docs.title: 0. Session startup (always run first)
docs.text:
cp .env.example .env.local      # first time on a machine — then set JAVA_HOME, ANDROID_HOME, …
pnpm dev:env                    # show the effective JDK / SDK / AAR paths + adb version
adb devices                     # expect your device or emulator

What .env.local fixes:

  • JAVA_HOME — pinned per machine; it wins over a stale value a version manager left in the shell.
  • CAPSULE_SHELL_OVERRIDE_PATH — the local AAR the CLI builds apps against until the Maven AAR is published. Defaults to packages/capsule-android/capsule/build/outputs/aar/capsule-release.aar.

Every key and its default is documented in .env.example. Two ways to use it:

pnpm with-env <command> [args]                  # one command with the env applied (simplest)
eval "$(pnpm -s dev:env --sh)"                  # bash/zsh: apply to the current shell
pnpm -s dev:env --ps | Out-String | Invoke-Expression   # PowerShell: apply to the current session

docs.title: 1. TypeScript — @capsule/core
docs.text:
pnpm --filter @capsule/core run build           # compile TS → dist/ (after any change in packages/core/src/)
pnpm --filter @capsule/core run test            # Vitest
pnpm --filter @capsule/core run test -- --watch # watch mode

docs.title: Lint + format
docs.text:
pnpm run lint          # ESLint across all packages
pnpm run format        # Prettier --write  "packages/*/src/**/*.ts"  (rewrites in place)
pnpm run format:check  # Prettier --check — fails if anything is unformatted (CI / pre-commit gate)

Run pnpm format before every commit. Prettier config (.prettierrc): no semicolons, single quotes, ES5 trailing commas, width 100, 2-space indent. The format script only globs the capsule monorepo's packages/*/src/**/*.ts — .tsx and the examples/templates repos are not covered by it. See §9 Before committing.

docs.title: 2. Android — Kotlin AAR
docs.text:
pnpm with-env --cwd <dir> gradlew … runs the Gradle wrapper in <dir> (gradlew.bat on Windows) with JAVA_HOME applied.

pnpm with-env --cwd packages/capsule-android gradlew assembleRelease     # build the AAR
pnpm with-env --cwd packages/capsule-android gradlew testDebugUnitTest   # Kotlin JVM unit tests
pnpm with-env --cwd packages/capsule-android gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest   # device/emulator tests

AAR output: packages/capsule-android/capsule/build/outputs/aar/capsule-release.aar. Rebuild it any time Kotlin or native source in packages/capsule-android/ (or packages/native/) changes.

docs.title: Emulator
docs.text:
pnpm dev:emulator start          # launch the AVD detached, wait for a FULL boot (boot_completed + pm)
pnpm dev:emulator start --fresh  # cold boot + wipe — recovers a wedged snapshot
pnpm dev:emulator status         # readiness signals
pnpm dev:emulator stop           # graceful shutdown (keeps the snapshot)

Other flags: --no-wait, --headless, --gpu host (default is software rendering, swiftshader_indirect: host-GPU mode hangs at boot on GPUs without working Vulkan/OpenGL), --avd <name> (default AVD_NAME, CapsuleTest).

Create the AVD (one time):

pnpm with-env avdmanager create avd -n CapsuleTest -k "system-images;android-36;google_apis_playstore;x86_64" -d "Nexus 5"

(with-env finds avdmanager, adb and emulator under ANDROID_HOME. Set ANDROID_AVD_HOME in .env.local first if your AVDs live off the default disk.)

docs.title: 3. CLI — @capsule/cli
docs.text:
pnpm --filter @capsule/cli run build
pnpm --filter @capsule/cli run test       # Vitest (scoped to src/**/*.test.ts)
pnpm capsule <command>                    # run the built CLI from the repo root

The CLI is not globally linked. From inside an example app, call the built entry point: node ../../packages/cli/dist/index.js <command>.

docs.title: First-time setup
docs.text: pnpm dev:examples install --filter react-ts   # or: cd examples/react-ts && pnpm install

docs.title: Build Android APK + install on device
docs.text:
Release build — embedded server (no dev server needed):

# from the capsule repo root
pnpm with-env --cwd examples/react-ts node ../../packages/cli/dist/index.js build android --release
pnpm with-env --cwd examples/react-ts node ../../packages/cli/dist/index.js run android --release

(Or apply the env to your shell once — §0 — then, inside the example dir, call node ../../packages/cli/dist/index.js … directly. The rest of this section does that.)

build android --release runs assembleRelease → BuildConfig.DEBUG = false → devServerUrl = null → the app uses the embedded server (CivetWeb) + bundled assets. Use this to test the full embedded runtime (QuickJSBridge, routes.js, etc.).

Debug build — dev server (requires capsule dev android after install):

node ../../packages/cli/dist/index.js build android
node ../../packages/cli/dist/index.js run android

build android runs assembleDebug → BuildConfig.DEBUG = true → devServerUrl = http://localhost:5173/ → the app tries to reach Vite. Follow with capsule dev android or you get ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED.

docs.title: Start dev server on device (do this after every install)
docs.text:
node ../../packages/cli/dist/index.js dev android

This does two things automatically: 1. adb reverse tcp:<devPort> tcp:<devPort> — tunnels the device's localhost to your machine 2. Starts the Vite dev server on the configured port

Use capsule dev android, not pnpm run dev. pnpm run dev alone starts Vite but skips the adb reverse step, so the device's WebView cannot reach your machine (ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED).

After capsule dev android is running, any file change in src/ hot-reloads on the device — no reinstall needed. When src/server/routes/ exists, it also starts the server-bundle sidecar and forwards that port too.

docs.title: All examples at once
docs.text:
pnpm dev:examples install              # every app under examples/
pnpm dev:examples build --release      # needs the CLI built (pnpm build)
pnpm dev:examples test                 # `pnpm test` per app; apps without a test script are skipped
pnpm dev:examples all --release        # install → build → test, with a pass/fail/skip summary
pnpm dev:examples build --filter react # only dirs whose name contains "react"

docs.title: 5. Full rebuild from scratch
docs.text:
When switching branches or after significant Kotlin + TS changes, in this order:

pnpm with-env --cwd packages/capsule-android gradlew assembleRelease   # 1. AAR
pnpm build                                                            # 2. core + CLI (+ all packages) via Turbo
pnpm dev:examples build --release --filter react-ts                   # 3. example app (embedded server)

Then install it with capsule run android --release from the example dir (§4).

docs.title: 6. Device management (adb)
docs.text:
adb devices                        # list connected devices
adb logcat -s CapsuleActivity      # Capsule-specific logs
adb logcat "*:E"                   # errors only
adb uninstall dev.capsule.myapp    # uninstall the app
adb shell pm list packages capsule # confirm install

docs.title: rspack — defineConfig is not a function (rspack ≥ 1.7)
docs.text:
defineConfig was removed from @rspack/core in 1.7.x. Export the config object directly:

// ❌ broken in 1.7+
const { defineConfig, HtmlRspackPlugin } = require('@rspack/core')
module.exports = defineConfig({ ... })

// ✅ correct
const { HtmlRspackPlugin } = require('@rspack/core')
module.exports = { ... }

docs.title: rspack — Module not found: Can't resolve './app-element'
docs.text:
rspack does not resolve .ts extensions by default. Add resolve.extensions:

module.exports = {
  resolve: {
    extensions: ['.ts', '.js'],
  },
  ...
}

docs.title: rspack + Lit — class field shadowing reactive properties
docs.text:
When using Lit web components, native class fields (the SWC default) overwrite Lit's reactive property accessors, causing @property() decorators to silently stop working. Set useDefineForClassFields: false in the SWC transform:

module: {
  rules: [{
    test: /\.ts$/,
    loader: 'builtin:swc-loader',
    options: {
      jsc: {
        parser: { syntax: 'typescript', decorators: true },
        transform: { legacyDecorator: true, useDefineForClassFields: false },
        target: 'es2020',
      },
    },
  }],
},

Symptom: Uncaught Error: The following properties on element <x> will not trigger updates as expected because they are set using class fields.

docs.title: 8. Turbo, docs and repo tooling
docs.text:
pnpm run build          # build all packages via Turbo
pnpm run test           # test all packages via Turbo
pnpm run lint           # lint all packages via Turbo
pnpm docs:check         # mkdocs nav + map-level links
pnpm docs:lint          # deep docs consistency: all links, phase numbering, principles mirror, INDEX coverage
pnpm test:scripts       # node --test for the contributor scripts' pure logic
pnpm update:quickjs [ref]    # re-vendor quickjs-ng (packages/capsule-android/.../cpp/quickjs)
pnpm update:civetweb [tag]   # re-vendor CivetWeb (packages/native/civetweb) — release tags only

docs.title: 9. Before committing (pre-commit checklist)
docs.text:
Apply Prettier before staging any commit — an unformatted file is the most common avoidable diff-noise and review nit. The capsule monorepo is the Prettier source of truth.

pnpm run format
pnpm run format:check          # must print "All matched files use Prettier code style!"
pnpm run lint
pnpm run test                  # Turbo: @capsule/core + @capsule/cli vitest (+ other packages)
pnpm with-env --cwd packages/capsule-android gradlew testDebugUnitTest   # Kotlin JVM unit tests
pnpm docs:check                # after doc edits

Then commit per-repo (English Conventional Commits), one repo at a time — capsule / examples / templates each have their own history.

Scope caveats for pnpm format: - It only matches packages/*/src/**/*.ts in the capsule repo. It does not touch .tsx files, nor the examples and templates repos. Format those with a direct invocation when they change, e.g. from the example dir: npx prettier --write "src/**/*.{ts,tsx}". - Device/instrumented tiers (connectedDebugAndroidTest, run android --release) are not part of the routine pre-commit gate — run them when native/Kotlin code changes (stale-AAR rule).

docs.title: Capsule Framework — Docker Strategy
docs.text: Docker as the backbone for framework development, app building, and CI/CD. No local SDK installs required.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. Develop the framework itself inside Docker — consistent environment across contributors
  2. Build Android APKs/AABs inside Docker — no Android Studio or SDK on developer machines
  3. Build iOS IPAs — addressed honestly (Docker cannot, macOS required — see iOS section)
  4. Publish Docker images so app developers using Capsule can build without any native toolchain

docs.title: Image Family
docs.text:
ghcr.io/capsule/
  ├── dev                  # framework development (Node + Android SDK + all tools)
  ├── build-android        # production Android builds (leaner, no dev tools)
  ├── build-web            # web-only builds and tests (Node only, smallest)
  ├── codesync-api         # CodeSync Fastify backend (Node + Postgres + Redis client)
  └── codesync-dashboard   # CodeSync React dashboard (nginx static, multi-stage build)

docs.title: Image 1 — capsule/dev
docs.text: Used by Capsule framework contributors. Everything needed to develop and test the framework.

docs.title: Dockerfile
docs.text:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:22-bookworm-slim AS base

# ── System dependencies ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    curl \
    git \
    unzip \
    zip \
    openjdk-17-jdk-headless \
    wget \
    ca-certificates \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# ── Android SDK ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ENV ANDROID_HOME=/opt/android-sdk
ENV PATH="${ANDROID_HOME}/cmdline-tools/latest/bin:${ANDROID_HOME}/platform-tools:${PATH}"

RUN mkdir -p ${ANDROID_HOME}/cmdline-tools && \
    wget -q https://dl.google.com/android/repository/commandlinetools-linux-11076708_latest.zip \
         -O /tmp/cmdline-tools.zip && \
    unzip -q /tmp/cmdline-tools.zip -d /tmp/cmdline-tools && \
    mv /tmp/cmdline-tools/cmdline-tools ${ANDROID_HOME}/cmdline-tools/latest && \
    rm /tmp/cmdline-tools.zip

# Accept licenses non-interactively
RUN yes | sdkmanager --licenses > /dev/null 2>&1

# Install SDK components (pin exact versions for reproducibility)
RUN sdkmanager \
    "platform-tools" \
    "platforms;android-36" \
    "build-tools;35.0.0" \
    "extras;android;m2repository" \
    "extras;google;m2repository"

# ── Gradle distribution ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Pre-download the Gradle distribution so first capsule build doesn't fetch it.
# Each app project brings its own gradlew wrapper — we don't install Gradle globally.
# The distribution is pre-cached at GRADLE_USER_HOME so gradlew finds it immediately.
ENV GRADLE_USER_HOME=/root/.gradle
RUN mkdir -p ${GRADLE_USER_HOME}/wrapper/dists/gradle-8.14.6-bin && \
    wget -q https://services.gradle.org/distributions/gradle-8.14.6-bin.zip \
         -O ${GRADLE_USER_HOME}/wrapper/dists/gradle-8.14.6-bin/gradle-8.14.6-bin.zip

# NOTE: We do NOT attempt to pre-warm the Android Gradle Plugin (AGP) here.
# AGP warmup requires a valid Android project with settings.gradle — a stub project
# silently fails (|| true) and wastes image build time. AGP deps are instead cached
# via the named `gradle-cache` Docker volume, which persists across runs.

# ── Node.js tooling ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
RUN npm install -g pnpm@9 turbo@2

# ── Working directory ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
WORKDIR /workspace

CMD ["bash"]

docs.title: Image 2 — capsule/build-android
docs.text:
Leaner image for CI and app developers. No dev tools, just what's needed to run capsule build android.

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jdk-jammy AS base

# Android build requires JDK (not JRE) — Gradle's annotation processors and
# some AGP tasks invoke javac directly. JRE is insufficient.
# Minimal Android SDK — only what Gradle needs to build
ENV ANDROID_HOME=/opt/android-sdk
ENV PATH="${ANDROID_HOME}/cmdline-tools/latest/bin:${ANDROID_HOME}/platform-tools:${PATH}"

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    curl wget unzip ca-certificates \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Install Node (slim install via NodeSource)
RUN curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_22.x | bash - && \
    apt-get install -y nodejs && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Android cmdline-tools + SDK components (same as dev image)
RUN mkdir -p ${ANDROID_HOME}/cmdline-tools && \
    wget -q https://dl.google.com/android/repository/commandlinetools-linux-11076708_latest.zip \
         -O /tmp/cmdline-tools.zip && \
    unzip -q /tmp/cmdline-tools.zip -d /tmp/cmdline-tools && \
    mv /tmp/cmdline-tools/cmdline-tools ${ANDROID_HOME}/cmdline-tools/latest && \
    rm /tmp/cmdline-tools.zip && \
    yes | sdkmanager --licenses > /dev/null 2>&1 && \
    sdkmanager "platform-tools" "platforms;android-36" "build-tools;35.0.0"

# Pre-cache Gradle distribution (same version as dev image — must stay in sync)
ENV GRADLE_USER_HOME=/root/.gradle
RUN mkdir -p ${GRADLE_USER_HOME}/wrapper/dists/gradle-8.14.6-bin && \
    wget -q https://services.gradle.org/distributions/gradle-8.14.6-bin.zip \
         -O ${GRADLE_USER_HOME}/wrapper/dists/gradle-8.14.6-bin/gradle-8.14.6-bin.zip

# Capsule CLI (installed globally so it's available as a command)
RUN npm install -g @capsule/cli

WORKDIR /app

ENTRYPOINT ["capsule"]
CMD ["build", "android"]

Usage by app developer (zero local setup):

docker run --rm \
  -v $(pwd):/app \
  -v capsule-gradle-cache:/root/.gradle \
  -e CAPSULE_KEYSTORE_PASS=$CAPSULE_KEYSTORE_PASS \
  ghcr.io/capsule/build-android:latest \
  build android --release

# Output: /app/.capsule/android/app-release.apk

The named volume capsule-gradle-cache persists the Gradle cache across runs — subsequent builds are as fast as local.

docs.title: Image 3 — capsule/build-web
docs.text:
Smallest image. For web-only builds and tests.

FROM node:22-alpine
RUN npm install -g pnpm@9 @capsule/cli
WORKDIR /app
CMD ["sh", "-c", "vite build"]

docs.title: Image 4 — capsule/codesync-api
docs.text:
The CodeSync backend service. Runs the Fastify API, connects to Postgres + Redis + S3.

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:22-alpine AS base

WORKDIR /app

# ── Dependencies ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
COPY package.json pnpm-lock.yaml ./
RUN npm install -g pnpm@9 && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --prod

# ── Application source ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
COPY dist/ ./dist/
COPY migrations/ ./migrations/

# ── Runtime config ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ENV NODE_ENV=production
ENV PORT=3000

EXPOSE 3000

# Run migrations then start the server
# Migrations are idempotent — safe to run on every container start
CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]

Build context: packages/codesync-api/

The image is kept minimal — no build tools, no devDependencies. The dist/ is compiled in CI and copied in. This is the standard Node.js production image pattern.

docs.title: Image 5 — capsule/codesync-dashboard
docs.text:
The React dashboard served via nginx. A static site — no Node.js at runtime.

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

# ── Build stage ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FROM node:22-alpine AS builder

WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json pnpm-lock.yaml ./
RUN npm install -g pnpm@9 && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

COPY . .
RUN pnpm build   # outputs to /app/dist

# ── Serve stage ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FROM nginx:1.27-alpine AS final

# Custom nginx config: SPA routing (all paths → index.html) + gzip
COPY docker/nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf

COPY --from=builder /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html

EXPOSE 80
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]

docker/nginx.conf (SPA routing + compression):

server {
    listen 80;
    root /usr/share/nginx/html;
    index index.html;

    gzip on;
    gzip_types text/plain text/css application/json application/javascript text/xml application/xml;
    gzip_min_length 1024;

    # SPA: serve index.html for all routes; browser handles routing
    location / {
        try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;
    }

    # Cache hashed assets aggressively (Vite names them with content hash)
    location ~* \.(js|css|png|jpg|jpeg|gif|svg|woff2?)$ {
        expires 1y;
        add_header Cache-Control "public, immutable";
    }
}

Build context: packages/codesync-dashboard/

docs.title: Framework Development with Docker Compose
docs.text:
For contributors working on the Capsule framework itself.

# docker-compose.yml (framework repo root)
services:

  # Main dev environment — framework source mounted in
  dev:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: docker/dev.Dockerfile
    volumes:
      - .:/workspace                          # framework source
      - node_modules:/workspace/node_modules  # isolated node_modules
      - gradle-cache:/root/.gradle            # Gradle cache persisted
      - android-sdk:/opt/android-sdk          # SDK persisted (don't re-download)
    ports:
      - "5173:5173"   # Vite dev server (for testing web layer)
    environment:
      - ANDROID_HOME=/opt/android-sdk
    stdin_open: true
    tty: true

  # Run the CLI under test against a sample app
  test-app:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: docker/dev.Dockerfile
    volumes:
      - ./examples/react-ts:/app              # sample app
      - .:/capsule-framework                  # framework source (symlinked via pnpm workspace)
      - gradle-cache:/root/.gradle
    working_dir: /app
    command: capsule dev
    ports:
      - "5174:5173"

  # CodeSync stack (for testing the full update pipeline locally)
  codesync-api:
    build:
      context: packages/codesync-api
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://capsule:capsule@postgres:5432/capsule
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
      STORAGE_ENDPOINT: http://minio:9000
      STORAGE_BUCKET: capsule-bundles
      STORAGE_ACCESS_KEY: minioadmin
      STORAGE_SECRET_KEY: minioadmin
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_started

  codesync-dashboard:
    build:
      context: packages/codesync-dashboard
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    ports:
      - "8080:80"   # dashboard at http://localhost:8080
    depends_on:
      - codesync-api

  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: capsule
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: capsule
      POSTGRES_DB: capsule
    volumes:
      - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
      - ./packages/codesync-api/migrations:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U capsule"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    volumes:
      - redis-data:/data

  minio:
    image: minio/minio:RELEASE.2024-11-07T00-52-20Z   # pin — never use latest for data stores
    command: server /data --console-address ":9001"
    environment:
      MINIO_ROOT_USER: minioadmin
      MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD: minioadmin
    volumes:
      - minio-data:/data
    ports:
      - "9000:9000"
      - "9001:9001"   # MinIO web console

volumes:
  node_modules:
  gradle-cache:
  android-sdk:
  postgres-data:
  redis-data:
  minio-data:

Developer workflow:

# First time
docker compose build dev
docker compose run --rm dev pnpm install

# Daily work — open a shell in the dev container
docker compose run --rm dev bash

# Inside container:
pnpm build           # build all framework packages
pnpm test            # run tests
capsule build android  # test a build against sample app

# Start full stack (CodeSync + DB + storage)
docker compose up codesync-api postgres redis minio

docs.title: iOS — Honest Assessment
docs.text:
Docker cannot build iOS IPAs. This is a hard platform constraint, not a tooling gap.

Constraint Detail Xcode runs only on macOS Apple does not license macOS to run in containers or VMs on non-Apple hardware xcrun, xcodebuild, simctl macOS-only binaries, no Linux port Code signing Requires access to the macOS Keychain or a hardware Secure Enclave

docs.title: What's possible
docs.text: Approach Works? Notes Docker on Linux for iOS No Xcode cannot run on Linux Docker on macOS (Docker Desktop) Partial Container runs Linux; host macOS still needed for actual Xcode commands macOS GitHub Actions runner Yes runs-on: macos-15 — standard, free minutes for public repos Xcode Cloud Yes Apple's own CI — tightly integrated, good for App Store delivery Self-hosted macOS runner (Mac mini / Mac Studio) Yes Full control, fast, can be Dockerless Fastlane on macOS runner Yes Automates signing, building, uploading — same result as manual

docs.title: Recommended CI split
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/release.yml

jobs:
  build-android:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest         # Docker image, fully controlled
    container:
      image: ghcr.io/capsule/build-android:latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: capsule build android --release
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: android-release
          path: .capsule/android/app-release.apk

  build-ios:
    runs-on: macos-15              # Apple's constraint — must be macOS
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
      - run: npm install -g @capsule/cli
      - run: capsule build ios --release
        env:
          MATCH_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.MATCH_PASSWORD }}
          APP_STORE_CONNECT_KEY: ${{ secrets.ASC_KEY }}

The Android job is fully reproducible via the Docker image. The iOS job is macOS-native but equally automated via Fastlane (see ../project/known-issues.md Issue 4).

docs.title: Image Versioning & Publishing
docs.text:
Images are tagged to match the Capsule CLI version:

ghcr.io/capsule/build-android:1.4.0   # pinned
ghcr.io/capsule/build-android:1.4     # minor-pinned
ghcr.io/capsule/build-android:latest  # rolling

The Android SDK version baked into each image is documented in the image label:

LABEL org.capsule.android-sdk-version="35"
LABEL org.capsule.build-tools-version="35.0.0"
LABEL org.capsule.gradle-version="8.10"
LABEL org.capsule.node-version="22"

Published automatically on every Capsule CLI release via GitHub Actions:

- name: Build and push Docker images
  uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
  with:
    context: .
    file: docker/build-android.Dockerfile
    push: true
    tags: |
      ghcr.io/capsule/build-android:${{ env.VERSION }}
      ghcr.io/capsule/build-android:latest
    cache-from: type=gha
    cache-to: type=gha,mode=max    # GitHub Actions layer cache

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Need Solution iOS? Framework development capsule/dev + docker compose Partial (native compile needs macOS) App developer builds Android capsule/build-android image N/A App developer builds iOS macOS runner (GitHub Actions / Mac mini) Yes, but not Docker CI/CD Android Docker image in any Linux CI Full CI/CD iOS macos-15 GitHub Actions runner + Fastlane Full (macOS only) Full local stack (CodeSync) docker compose up Yes

docs.title: Capsule Framework — Development Environment
docs.text:
Three audiences, three sections.

  • Building an app with Capsule? Start at Part 1 — Getting Started (App Developer).
  • Setting up the creator machine to build the framework itself? Go to Part 2 — Framework Creator Setup (Windows 11).
  • Contributing to the Capsule framework? Jump to Part 3 — Framework Contributors.

docs.title: Platform Requirements
docs.text: Work OS requirement App development (CLI + web layer) Windows, macOS, or Linux Android builds and emulator Windows, macOS, or Linux iOS builds macOS only — Apple constraint Docker-based CI builds Windows (WSL2), macOS, or Linux

docs.title: Part 1 — Getting Started (App Developer)
docs.text: Everything you need to go from zero to a running Capsule app on an Android device or emulator.

docs.title: 1.1 Install prerequisites
docs.text:
Node.js 22 (LTS)

# macOS / Linux — using nvm
curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.39.7/install.sh | bash
source ~/.bashrc   # or ~/.zshrc
nvm install 22 && nvm use 22 && nvm alias default 22

node --version    # v22.x.x

# Windows — nvm-windows
# Download from github.com/coreybutler/nvm-windows/releases
nvm install 22
nvm use 22

pnpm (or npm — both work for app development)

npm install -g pnpm@9

docs.title: 1.2 Install the Capsule CLI
docs.text:
Note — App developers only. This step assumes @capsule/cli has been published to npm. If you are building the framework itself, skip Parts 1–4 entirely and go to Part 3 — Framework Contributors.

npm install -g @capsule/cli

capsule --version    # 1.x.x

docs.title: 1.3 Android prerequisites
docs.text:
You need a JDK and the Android SDK command-line tools. No Android Studio required.

JDK 17

# macOS — SDKMAN
curl -s "https://get.sdkman.io" | bash
source "$HOME/.sdkman/bin/sdkman-init.sh"
sdk install java 17.0.11-tem
java -version    # openjdk 17.x.x

# Linux (Debian/Ubuntu)
sudo apt-get install -y openjdk-17-jdk-headless

# Windows — download Eclipse Temurin 17 from adoptium.net, set JAVA_HOME

Android SDK command-line tools

# macOS / Linux
mkdir -p ~/android-sdk/cmdline-tools
wget https://dl.google.com/android/repository/commandlinetools-linux-11076708_latest.zip \
     -O /tmp/cmdline-tools.zip
unzip /tmp/cmdline-tools.zip -d /tmp/cmdline-unzip
mv /tmp/cmdline-unzip/cmdline-tools ~/android-sdk/cmdline-tools/latest

echo 'export ANDROID_HOME=$HOME/android-sdk' >> ~/.bashrc
echo 'export PATH=$ANDROID_HOME/cmdline-tools/latest/bin:$ANDROID_HOME/platform-tools:$PATH' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc

# Accept licenses and install required components
yes | sdkmanager --licenses
sdkmanager "platform-tools" "platforms;android-36" "build-tools;35.0.0" "ndk;27.3.13750724" "cmake;3.22.1"

Android Emulator (skip if testing on a physical device)

sdkmanager "emulator" "system-images;android-36;google_apis;x86_64"  # Intel/AMD
# Apple Silicon: use system-images;android-36;google_apis_playstore;arm64-v8a

avdmanager create avd \
    --name "Pixel_8_API36" \
    --device "pixel_8" \
    --package "system-images;android-36;google_apis;x86_64"

emulator -avd Pixel_8_API36 -no-audio -no-boot-anim &

docs.title: 1.4 iOS prerequisites (macOS only)
docs.text:
# Install Xcode 15+ from the Mac App Store, then:
sudo xcodebuild -license accept
xcodebuild -version    # Xcode 15.x or 16.x

docs.title: 2.1 Scaffold
docs.text:
# Interactive (prompts for template, app ID, etc.)
capsule init my-app

# Or non-interactive with flags
capsule init my-app --template react-ts --app-id com.yourcompany.myapp

# Available templates: react-ts | vue-ts | svelte-ts | vanilla-ts
# Community template: --template github:org/template-name

cd my-app
pnpm install

What gets generated:

my-app/
  src/
    index.html
    main.ts
    App.tsx              # or .vue / .svelte depending on template
  public/
  capsule.config.ts      # the ONLY native configuration file
  capsule.lock           # commit this — pins resolved shell versions
  package.json
  vite.config.ts

docs.title: 2.2 Add a platform
docs.text:
# Android (works on Windows, macOS, Linux)
capsule add android

# iOS (macOS only)
capsule add ios

This generates the thin .capsule/android/ or .capsule/ios/ wrapper from capsule.lock. The wrapper is gitignored — never edit it directly.

docs.title: 2.3 Configure your app
docs.text:
Open capsule.config.ts — this is the only file you touch for native configuration:

import { defineConfig } from '@capsule/cli'

export default defineConfig({
  appId:   'com.yourcompany.myapp',   // reverse-domain, must match store listing
  appName: 'My App',

  version: {
    name:        '1.0.0',
    buildNumber: 1
  },

  android: {
    minSdk:    26,
    targetSdk: 35,
    permissions: ['CAMERA']           // only if your app uses camera
  }
})

See ../concepts/principles.md for the full defineConfig reference.

docs.title: 3.1 Start the dev server
docs.text:
capsule dev

What this does: - Starts a Vite dev server at http://localhost:5173 - Runs adb reverse tcp:5173 tcp:5173 so the emulator/device loads from your machine - Watches for file changes → hot module replacement in <50ms

# Physical device on the same WiFi
capsule dev --qr            # prints QR code — scan with device

# Physical device on corporate WiFi / different network
capsule dev --tunnel --qr   # HTTPS tunnel, no network config needed

# Custom port
capsule dev --port 3000

Open the emulator — the app loads and hot-reloads as you edit files in src/.

docs.title: 3.2 Using platform APIs
docs.text:
Import from @capsule/core — no separate packages to install:

import { camera, geolocation, haptics, db, preferences, browser } from '@capsule/core'

// Camera
const photo = await camera.capture({ quality: 0.9 })

// Collection API — zero SQL, auto-schema
const items = db.collection<{ id: string; name: string }>('items')
const item = await items.add({ name: 'hello' })
const all  = await items.getAll()
const found = await items.get(item.id)
await items.update(item.id, { name: 'world' })
await items.remove(item.id)

// Raw SQL tagged template (values always parameterized — injection-safe)
const recent = await db.sql<{ id: string; name: string }[]>`
  SELECT * FROM items WHERE name LIKE ${'%world%'} LIMIT 10
`

// Encrypted named database (developer supplies key)
const key = await biometrics.getKey('db-key')
const secureDb = await database.open('secure', { key })
const secrets = secureDb.collection<{ id: string; token: string }>('secrets')
await secureDb.close()

// Key-value storage (SharedPreferences / UserDefaults)
await preferences.set({ key: 'theme', value: 'dark' })
const { value } = await preferences.get({ key: 'theme' })

// In-app browser (Chrome Custom Tabs / SFSafariViewController)
// Best for OAuth, payment pages, external links
const unsub = browser.onNavigationChange(({ url }) => {
  if (url.startsWith('myapp://callback')) { browser.close(); unsub() }
})
await browser.open({ url: 'https://accounts.google.com/...' })

// GPS, haptics, push, NFC, Bluetooth, biometrics — all in @capsule/core
const position = await geolocation.getCurrentPosition()
await haptics.impact('medium')

Unused capabilities are tree-shaken from the release build. Full API reference: core-api.md.

docs.title: 3.3 Build
docs.text:
# Debug build
capsule build android

# Signed release APK
capsule build android --release

# Signed AAB (required for Play Store)
capsule build android --release --format aab

# iOS (macOS only)
capsule build ios --release

Output: .capsule/android/app-release.aab (or .apk)

docs.title: 3.4 Run on device / emulator
docs.text:
# Deploy to the running emulator or connected USB device
capsule run android

# Target a specific device
capsule run android --device <id>    # get IDs from: adb devices

# iOS
capsule run ios

docs.title: 3.5 Publish to stores
docs.text:
# Android — Play Store
capsule publish android --track internal      # internal testing
capsule publish android --track production    # production

# iOS — App Store Connect
capsule publish ios --track testflight
capsule publish ios --track production

See publishing.md for signing setup and full publish options.

docs.title: CLI cheat sheet
docs.text:
capsule init <name>                      # scaffold new app
capsule add android | ios                # add platform
capsule sync                             # regenerate .capsule/ wrappers
capsule dev                              # start dev server + hot reload
capsule build android [--release]        # build APK/AAB
capsule build ios [--release]            # build IPA (macOS only)
capsule run android | ios                # deploy to device/emulator
capsule publish android | ios            # upload to store
capsule version bump patch|minor|major   # manage version numbers
capsule codesync publish                 # push OTA update (CodeSync)
capsule update                           # update capsule shell version
capsule doctor                           # diagnose environment issues

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
capsule doctor          # verify environment — always run this first
capsule sync            # regenerate wrappers if something looks wrong
adb devices             # confirm emulator/device is visible

docs.title: Part 2 — Framework Creator Setup (Windows 11)
docs.text:
Audience: The creator of Capsule — setting up a Windows 11 Pro machine to build the framework from scratch.

This is not the app-developer getting-started guide. This is the environment needed to build, test, and publish the Capsule framework itself.

docs.title: What You Need to Build
docs.text: Target Tools Required @capsule/cli (Node/TypeScript) Node ≥ 22.12, pnpm, TypeScript @capsule/core (TypeScript) Node 22, pnpm, TypeScript Android shell (Kotlin AAR) JDK 17, Android SDK, Gradle CodeSync backend (Node/Fastify) Node 22, Docker, PostgreSQL, Redis CodeSync dashboard (React) Node 22 Docker images Docker Desktop Publishing / CI/CD GitHub account, GHCR, GitHub Actions

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Phase 1 — Local MVP
  Windows 11 Pro
    └── WSL2 (Ubuntu 22.04)          ← primary dev environment
          ├── Node.js 22 (nvm)
          ├── pnpm 9 + Turbo 2
          ├── JDK 17 (Temurin)
          ├── Android SDK (API 36)
          └── Docker CLI (via Docker Desktop socket)
    └── Docker Desktop 4.30+         ← runs on Windows, socket shared to WSL2
    └── VS Code                      ← IDE, WSL2 + Dev Containers extension
    └── Git (local config only)
    └── Windows Terminal
    └── ADB (platform-tools)        ← Windows side
    └── Android Emulator             ← Windows host (KVM not available in WSL2)

Phase 8 — Go Online / Ecosystem  (after local MVP works)
  └── GitHub CLI (gh)               ← Windows + WSL2
  └── GitHub org + repos
  └── GHCR (container registry)
  └── GitHub Actions CI/CD

docs.title: 1.1 Windows Terminal
docs.text: Download from Microsoft Store or: winget install Microsoft.WindowsTerminal

docs.title: 1.2 WSL2 + Ubuntu 22.04
docs.text:
# Run as Administrator in PowerShell
wsl --install -d Ubuntu-22.04
# Restart when prompted

After restart, Ubuntu will finish setup. Create your UNIX username + password.

# Verify
wsl --list --verbose
# Should show Ubuntu-22.04  Running  2

docs.title: 1.3 Set Ubuntu 22.04 as default
docs.text: wsl --set-default Ubuntu-22.04

docs.title: 1.4 Update Ubuntu
docs.text:
# Inside WSL2 Ubuntu terminal
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get upgrade -y
sudo apt-get install -y curl wget git unzip zip ca-certificates build-essential

docs.title: 2.1 Node.js 22 via nvm (WSL2)
docs.text:
# Install nvm
curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.39.7/install.sh | bash

# Reload shell
source ~/.bashrc

# Install and use Node 22
nvm install 22
nvm use 22
nvm alias default 22

node --version   # v22.x.x
npm --version    # 10.x.x

docs.title: 2.2 pnpm 9 + Turbo 2
docs.text:
npm install -g pnpm@9 turbo@2

pnpm --version   # 9.x.x
turbo --version  # 2.x.x

docs.title: 2.3 Node.js on Windows (for tools that run on the host)
docs.text:
# Download nvm-windows from github.com/coreybutler/nvm-windows/releases
# Install, then:
nvm install 22
nvm use 22
npm install -g pnpm@9

docs.title: Step 3 — JDK 17 (WSL2)
docs.text:
# Install Eclipse Temurin 17 (the same JDK used in the Docker images)
sudo apt-get install -y wget apt-transport-https gnupg

wget -qO - https://packages.adoptium.net/artifactory/api/gpg/key/public \
  | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/adoptium.gpg

echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/adoptium.gpg] \
  https://packages.adoptium.net/artifactory/deb $(. /etc/os-release && echo "$VERSION_CODENAME") main" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/adoptium.list

sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y temurin-17-jdk

java -version
# openjdk version "17.0.x" ... Temurin

# Set JAVA_HOME
echo 'export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/temurin-17-jdk-amd64' >> ~/.bashrc
echo 'export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc

docs.title: Step 4 — Android SDK (WSL2)
docs.text:
# Create SDK directory
mkdir -p ~/android-sdk/cmdline-tools

# Download command-line tools
wget -q https://dl.google.com/android/repository/commandlinetools-linux-11076708_latest.zip \
     -O /tmp/cmdline-tools.zip
unzip -q /tmp/cmdline-tools.zip -d /tmp/cmdline-unzip
mv /tmp/cmdline-unzip/cmdline-tools ~/android-sdk/cmdline-tools/latest
rm /tmp/cmdline-tools.zip

# Set environment variables
echo 'export ANDROID_HOME=$HOME/android-sdk' >> ~/.bashrc
echo 'export PATH=$ANDROID_HOME/cmdline-tools/latest/bin:$ANDROID_HOME/platform-tools:$PATH' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc

# Accept licenses and install required SDK components
yes | sdkmanager --licenses > /dev/null 2>&1
sdkmanager \
    "platform-tools" \
    "platforms;android-36" \
    "build-tools;35.0.0" \
    "ndk;27.3.13750724" \
    "cmake;3.22.1" \
    "extras;android;m2repository" \
    "extras;google;m2repository"

# Verify
sdkmanager --list_installed

docs.title: Step 5 — Android Emulator (Windows host)
docs.text: The Android Emulator must run on the Windows host (not inside WSL2 — KVM is not available on Windows WSL2).

docs.title: 5.1 Install Android Studio (Windows)
docs.text:
Download from developer.android.com/studio (Ladybug 2024.2 or later).

During setup:

  • SDK location: C:\Users\<you>\AppData\Local\Android\Sdk
  • Install Android 16 (API 36) system image

docs.title: 5.2 Or — SDK Manager on Windows (no Android Studio)
docs.text:
# Download cmdline-tools for Windows
# From developer.android.com/tools/releases/cmdline-tools
# Extract to C:\android-sdk\cmdline-tools\latest\

# Add to PATH (System Environment Variables):
# C:\android-sdk\cmdline-tools\latest\bin
# C:\android-sdk\platform-tools

sdkmanager "platform-tools" "platforms;android-36" "build-tools;35.0.0" "ndk;27.3.13750724" "cmake;3.22.1"
sdkmanager "emulator" "system-images;android-36;google_apis;x86_64"

avdmanager create avd `
    --name "Pixel_8_API36" `
    --device "pixel_8" `
    --package "system-images;android-36;google_apis;x86_64"

# Launch emulator
emulator -avd Pixel_8_API36 -no-audio -no-boot-anim

docs.title: 5.3 ADB on Windows + WSL2 bridge
docs.text:
ADB runs on Windows host. WSL2 talks to it via host.docker.internal.

# Windows: ensure adb is in PATH
adb version    # Android Debug Bridge version 1.x.x
adb devices    # lists connected emulators/devices

# WSL2: point to host ADB server
echo 'export ANDROID_ADB_SERVER_ADDRESS=host.docker.internal' >> ~/.bashrc
echo 'export ANDROID_ADB_SERVER_PORT=5037' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc

adb devices   # connects to the host ADB server automatically

docs.title: 6.1 Install Docker Desktop
docs.text:
Download from docker.com/products/docker-desktop.

Settings to enable:

  • General → Use the WSL 2 based engine ✅
  • Resources → WSL Integration → Ubuntu-22.04 ✅
# Verify from WSL2
docker --version
docker compose version

docs.title: 7.1 Install VS Code
docs.text: winget install Microsoft.VisualStudioCode

docs.title: 7.2 Essential extensions
docs.text:
Install from Extensions panel (Ctrl+Shift+X):

dbaeumer.vscode-eslint             ESLint
esbenp.prettier-vscode             Prettier
ms-vscode.vscode-typescript-next   Latest TS language server
fwcd.kotlin                        Kotlin syntax + completion
ms-azuretools.vscode-docker        Docker explorer
ms-vscode-remote.remote-wsl        WSL2 integration
ms-vscode-remote.remote-containers Dev Containers
eamodio.gitlens                    Git lens
streetsidesoftware.code-spell-checker  Spell check

docs.title: 7.3 Open the project in WSL2
docs.text:
# From WSL2 terminal, inside your project folder:
code .
# VS Code opens with the WSL2 remote — file system is Linux, tools are Linux

docs.title: Step 8 — Kotlin IDE
docs.text:
For Kotlin/AAR work:

  • Android Studio (free, specialized) — download from developer.android.com/studio
  • IntelliJ IDEA (free Community edition) — download from jetbrains.com/idea

Set the project JDK to Temurin 17.

docs.title: Step 9 — Git (local config)
docs.text:
# Windows
winget install Git.Git
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

# WSL2
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

docs.title: Step 10 — Local Environment Variables
docs.text:
Create ~/.capsule-dev.env (never commit):

# ~/.capsule-dev.env
export CAPSULE_KEYSTORE_PATH=/path/to/debug.jks
export CAPSULE_KEYSTORE_PASS=debug
export CAPSULE_KEY_ALIAS=debug
export CAPSULE_KEY_PASS=debug

Add to ~/.bashrc:

[ -f ~/.capsule-dev.env ] && source ~/.capsule-dev.env

docs.title: Step 11 — Verify Local Setup
docs.text:
# From WSL2
node --version          # v22.x.x
pnpm --version          # 9.x.x
turbo --version         # 2.x.x
java -version           # openjdk 17 Temurin
sdkmanager --version    # 12.0 or later
adb version             # connects to host ADB
docker --version        # 27.x.x
docker compose version  # 2.x.x

# From Windows PowerShell
adb devices             # emulator-5554   device  (if emulator running)
docker --version        # Docker version 27.x.x

docs.title: Local Checklist
docs.text:
[ ] WSL2 Ubuntu 22.04 installed and updated
[ ] Node 22 in WSL2 (nvm install 22)
[ ] pnpm 9 + Turbo 2 in WSL2
[ ] JDK 17 Temurin in WSL2 (java -version)
[ ] Android SDK API 36 + Build Tools 35.0.0 + NDK 27.3 + NDK 27.3 in WSL2
[ ] ANDROID_HOME set in WSL2 ~/.bashrc
[ ] Android Emulator (Pixel 8 API 36) running on Windows host
[ ] adb devices shows the emulator from Windows and WSL2
[ ] Docker Desktop 4.30+ installed, WSL2 integration enabled
[ ] VS Code with WSL2 + Dev Containers extensions
[ ] Git configured (name + email) on Windows + WSL2
[ ] All verify commands in Step 11 pass

Once this checklist is complete — build the local MVP before continuing to Phase 8 (Go Online / Ecosystem).

docs.title: Phase 8 — Go Online (Ecosystem)
docs.text: Do this after the local MVP is running end-to-end.

docs.title: Step 12 — GitHub CLI + Authentication
docs.text:
# Windows
winget install GitHub.cli
gh auth login
# Choose: GitHub.com → HTTPS → Authenticate with browser

# WSL2
curl -fsSL https://cli.github.com/packages/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg \
  | sudo dd of=/usr/share/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg
echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg] https://cli.github.com/packages stable main" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/github-cli.list > /dev/null

docs.title: Part 3 — Framework Contributors
docs.text:
This section is for contributors building Capsule itself — the CLI, the Kotlin AAR, the Swift XCFramework, the CodeSync backend. Skip if you are building an app with Capsule.

Two setup paths available:

Path A — Full Local Install          Path B — Docker-First (Dev Container)
────────────────────────────────     ────────────────────────────────────────
Install Node, JDK, Android SDK,      Install only Docker Desktop + ADB.
pnpm, etc. directly on your host.    Everything else runs inside a container.

Pros: fastest iteration, direct      Pros: zero host environment setup,
  IDE integration, no overhead         identical to CI, onboard in minutes
Cons: version juggling, "works on    Cons: first build slower, emulator
  my machine" risk                     still needs host ADB bridge

TL;DR: Use Path B if you want the cleanest setup with the fewest host installs. Use Path A if you need direct Android Studio access or work heavily on the Kotlin/Swift shells.

docs.title: 5.0 Bootstrap — Starting from Zero (before the GitHub repo exists)
docs.text:
This is where you actually start. Section 5.2 assumes a published GitHub repo to clone. If you are bootstrapping the monorepo from scratch (Phase 1), follow this instead.

Prerequisites first — complete section 1.1 (Node.js 22 + pnpm) and section 1.3 (JDK 17 + Android SDK) before continuing.

Create the monorepo:

mkdir capsule && cd capsule

# Workspace root
pnpm init

# Dev toolchain
pnpm add -D -w turbo@2 typescript @types/node eslint prettier
pnpm add -D -w @changesets/cli
pnpm changeset init

# Package directories
mkdir -p packages/cli/src
mkdir -p packages/core/src
mkdir -p packages/capsule-android
mkdir -p examples   # demo apps — their own pnpm workspace (examples/pnpm-workspace.yaml)

Create pnpm-workspace.yaml:

packages:
  - 'packages/*'
# examples/ is its own pnpm workspace (examples/pnpm-workspace.yaml) — not listed here

Create turbo.json:

{
  "$schema": "https://turbo.build/schema.json",
  "pipeline": {
    "build": { "dependsOn": ["^build"], "outputs": ["dist/**"] },
    "test":  { "dependsOn": ["build"] },
    "lint":  {}
  }
}

Create tsconfig.base.json:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "Node16",
    "moduleResolution": "Node16",
    "strict": true,
    "declaration": true,
    "declarationMap": true,
    "sourceMap": true
  }
}

Use the local CLI during development (not the global npm install):

# Build the CLI package first
cd packages/cli && pnpm build && cd ../..

# Run it directly — no global install needed
node packages/cli/dist/index.js --version

# Or add a root-level convenience script in package.json:
# "scripts": { "capsule": "node packages/cli/dist/index.js" }
# Then: pnpm capsule --version

For test-app development, use CAPSULE_SHELL_OVERRIDE_PATH to bypass the shell registry (which doesn't exist yet in Phase 1):

export CAPSULE_SHELL_OVERRIDE_PATH=/path/to/capsule-debug.aar
node ../../packages/cli/dist/index.js build android

Once the monorepo is running locally, continue with Phase 1 in cli.md. Section 5.2 below applies once you have a GitHub remote.

docs.title: 5.2 Repository setup
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/alex-vinny/capsule_framework
cd capsule_framework
pnpm install
pnpm build         # Turbo resolves build order automatically
cp .env.example .env.local   # per-machine paths (JAVA_HOME, ANDROID_HOME, …) — git-ignored
pnpm dev:env                 # check what the contributor scripts will use

Contributor scripts (scripts/, Node only — the same on Windows, macOS and Linux; they read .env.local, documented key by key in .env.example):

Script What it does pnpm dev:env Show the effective JDK / SDK / AAR paths; --sh / --ps emit them for your shell pnpm with-env [--cwd dir] <cmd> Run one command with that env (gradlew, adb, emulator, avdmanager resolved per OS) pnpm dev:emulator start\|stop\|status Contributor AVD, waits for a full boot (--fresh, --no-wait, --headless, --gpu, --avd) pnpm dev:examples install\|build\|test\|all Batch over the example apps in examples/ (--release, --filter) pnpm update:quickjs [ref] / pnpm update:civetweb [tag] Re-vendor the native sources pnpm docs:check / pnpm docs:lint Docs gates (nav + map links / deep consistency)

Full command reference: commands.md.

Monorepo structure:

capsule/
  packages/
    cli/                    ← @capsule/cli
    core/                   ← @capsule/core (JS bridge runtime)
    capsule-android/        ← Kotlin AAR (Android shell)
    capsule-ios/            ← Swift XCFramework (iOS shell)
    codesync-api/           ← Node.js/Fastify backend
    codesync-dashboard/     ← React dashboard
  examples/               ← demo apps (own nested pnpm workspace; apps link packages/core)
    react-ts/  vue-from-template/  …
  docker/
  pnpm-workspace.yaml
  turbo.json

Build order (Turbo handles this via turbo.json):

1. @capsule/core       — JS bridge runtime
2. @capsule/cli        — imports core for types
3. codesync-api        — standalone Node.js service
4. codesync-dashboard  — standalone React app

Install host ADB only:

# Linux

.devcontainer/devcontainer.json:

{

ADB bridge — container to host emulator:

# docker-compose.yml — dev service additions
services:
  dev:
    extra_hosts:
      - "host.docker.internal:host-gateway"   # Linux needs explicit; Mac/Win get it automatically
    environment:
      - ANDROID_ADB_SERVER_ADDRESS=host.docker.internal

# Inside container terminal:
adb connect host.docker.internal:5555
adb devices     # emulator-5555   device

capsule dev     # Vite runs on container:5173, forwarded to host:5173
                # CLI runs adb reverse tcp:5173 tcp:5173 automatically

Linux — emulator inside container (KVM):

services:
  dev:
    devices:
      - /dev/kvm:/dev/kvm

emulator -avd Pixel_8_API36 -no-window -no-audio &
adb wait-for-device && adb devices

Opening the Dev Container:

git clone https://github.com/alex-vinny/capsule_framework
code capsule_framework
# VS Code prompts: "Reopen in Container" → click it
# (or: Ctrl+Shift+P → Dev Containers: Reopen in Container)
# First time: ~5–10 min to pull/build (cached after)

docs.title: 5.7 Path A vs Path B
docs.text: Scenario Recommended New contributor, first setup Path B — fastest to working state Heavy Kotlin/AAR work (Android Studio) Path A — better IDE integration Windows developer Path B — avoids Windows toolchain pain macOS, iOS shell development Either — Xcode is always on host Linux developer Path B — emulator in container with KVM CI environment Path B model — exactly what CI uses

docs.title: 5.8 buildNumber auto-commit in CI
docs.text:
capsule publish android|ios auto-increments version.buildNumber in capsule.config.ts after a successful upload and commits the bump. In CI, push it back:

# .github/workflows/release.yml
- run: capsule publish android --track internal
  env:
    PLAY_STORE_JSON_KEY_DATA: ${{ secrets.PLAY_STORE_JSON_KEY_DATA }}

- run: |
    git config user.name  "capsule-bot"
    git config user.email "bot@capsule.dev"
    git push origin HEAD:${{ github.ref_name }}

The commit message includes [skip ci] to prevent a loop.

docs.title: iOS Bring-Up — Without Buying a Mac (Yet)
docs.text: How to make real iOS progress before owning Apple hardware, and how it sequences against monetization. Decided in the 2026-06-15 strategy session. Architecture target: CivetWeb (the same embedded server Android runs — adr-004 amendment, 2026-10-24) + QuickJS compiled for iOS + WKWebView shell, same capsule.config.ts, same TS route handlers — see ../decisions/0001-embedded-runtime.md.

docs.title: Where iOS sits
docs.text: Phase 4 — after native-API expansion (Phase 3), before the Server Code Push / OTA cloud (Phase 6). Capsule is a personal project, so capability comes first: finish the native APIs on Android, then bring up iOS so the platform is cross-platform before the OTA cloud — which is gated on iOS, since almost nobody pays for an Android-only OTA service (../project/business/business-model.md). This still pulls iOS forward from its old Phase 6 slot. See roadmap.md.

docs.title: You do not need a physical device to make progress
docs.text:
The iOS Simulator covers the non-device-dependent layers — exactly the unit + integration tiers of the 3-tier test strategy. Only the e2e tier (real iPhone, performance, App Store submission, signing) truly needs a Mac mini, and that's the part deferred until the OTA business funds the hardware.

Capability macOS VM (recent macOS, VirtualBox/VMware) GitHub Actions macOS Compile Swift + QuickJS-for-iOS ✅ ✅ iOS Simulator tests (WKWebView, scheme handler, logic) ✅ (slow on x86 host) ✅ Interactive native debugging ✅ (the VM's only real edge) ❌ batch: push → wait → read logs Real device / signing / submission ❌ ❌ Legal / stable ❌ EULA-gray, fragile ✅ real Apple HW, sanctioned

docs.title: Hard stops
docs.text:
• macOS Lion (2011) is useless — can't run modern Xcode, can't target current iOS, can't submit. If you VM at all, use a recent macOS (Sonoma/Sequoia).
  • Virtualizing macOS on non-Apple hardware violates Apple's EULA. Acceptable for throwaway personal bring-up; never bake it into CI or anything customer-facing.

docs.title: Free macOS CI — GitHub Actions on the public repo
docs.text:
The repo is public, so GitHub-hosted macOS runners are free and unmetered — no minute quota, no multiplier, no grant to request. The ios-macos job in .github/workflows/ci.yml runs swift test on macos-latest on every push and pull request, next to the Linux container run (ios-linux); see ci.md. Locally, pnpm verify:ios runs the Linux half in Docker — no Mac needed.

History: while the repo was private, Azure Pipelines was the planned macOS CI because it billed macOS minutes 1:1 instead of GitHub's 10× multiplier. Going public (2026-10-24) removed the reason.

docs.title: Contract readiness — assessed 2026-06-26
docs.text:
An audit of the Android contracts (every runtime + provider interface, the protocol/event layer, the shared controllers, the platform-edge wiring, and the native QuickJS C/JNI layer) against the question "how far are these from being iOS-portable?"

Verdict: the contracts are essentially iOS-ready — no interface needs redesign to support iOS. The "interface + provider + Fake" discipline placed the cross-platform seam at the provider/controller boundary, not at the Android plumbing underneath. Of all the contract files (i.e. excluding the Android*/Fused*/server implementations), only three leak android.*/androidx.* into a signature — and all three are genuine platform-edge glue (CapsuleBridge → WebView/JavascriptInterface; activity/ActivityResultBroker + activity/SuspendingActivityLauncher → Activity-result helpers). Every interface is clean.

Porting cost falls into four tiers:

  1. Transliterate 1:1 to Swift protocols (zero redesign). All runtime interfaces (CapsuleServer, QuickJSEngine, QuickJSBridge+HttpRouteResponse, AppNavigator, SplashController, BundleStore, CrashLog, Clock, QuickJSException), all provider interfaces (CameraProvider, FilesystemProvider, NetworkProvider, LocationProvider, PushProvider, PermissionManager + their data classes/enums), and the protocol layer (BridgeEventEmitter, CapabilityRegistry, BridgeError, JsonRpcModels, BridgeHandler). They use only Kotlin primitives, suspend (→ Swift async), callbacks (→ closures/delegates), and a couple of JVM types. Each interface's KDoc already names its iOS impl.
  2. Pure-JVM shared logic — re-coded in Swift, but trivial and test-locked. NetworkStatusController, PushController, AppLifecycleController, CapabilityRegistry, CrashLoopGuard logic. These own zero Android types (in a KMP setup they'd be literally shared). Each has a pure-JVM unit suite pinning exact behaviour (de-dup, consume-once launch URL/notification, "3 crashes in 60s"). Low risk.
  3. Platform-edge — rewritten per platform (the point of the seam, not a gap). CapsuleBridge → WKScriptMessageHandler; every Android*/Fused* provider → Swift; the embedded server → already done: CivetwebServer.swift over the same CivetWeb C sources (2026-10-24); navigator/splash → WKWebView; PrefsCrashLog → UserDefaults; FileBundleStore → FileManager (logic portable, IO swapped); CapsuleActivity (309-line composition root) → AppDelegate/SceneDelegate. ActivityResultBroker/SuspendingActivityLauncher have no iOS analog needed — iOS uses delegate callbacks.
  4. Native engine — the pleasant surprise. QuickJS-ng is vendored as plain C (quickjs.c, libregexp.c, libunicode.c, dtoa.c) and compiles for iOS unchanged. Only quickjs_jni.c (120 lines) is Android-specific; its core __capsule_call JSON round-trip helper is embedded JS, fully portable. iOS replaces just the JNI glue with a C/Swift bridge. Carry-over correctness constraint: the single-thread dispatcher + 4 MB stack-base requirement in QuickJSEngineImpl must be replicated in the Swift port (QuickJS records the JS stack base from the creating thread).

Portability backbone + the one real risk. There is no Kotlin-Multiplatform, so contracts are hand-transliterated to Swift, not literally shared → contract-drift risk. What de-risks it: every Kotlin data class explicitly mirrors @capsule/core's TS types, and the wire JSON is the true contract (locked by kotlinx @SerialName on Android; matched on iOS by Codable + CodingKeys). So @capsule/core is the shared source of truth that keeps both shells honest — the cross-check that protects the hand-port.

One interface nit to fix before the port: BundleStore exposes java.io.File (activeDir(): File?, install(staged: File)) and FilesystemProvider's KDoc references java.io.File plumbing. A neutral path/URI type would make BundleStore a literal shared contract. Minor — every other interface is already platform-neutral.

docs.title: Recommended path
docs.text:
1. Now (no Mac): write the Swift/QuickJS port interface-first, in parallel with the proven Android architecture — most of this is just code that doesn't need to compile on macOS yet. Mirror the Android interface set (cross-platform seams confirmed by the 2026-06-26 readiness audit above):
Android iOS equivalent Tier runtime + provider + protocol interfaces (CapsuleServer, QuickJSEngine, QuickJSBridge, *Provider, BridgeEventEmitter, BridgeError, …) same contracts as Swift protocols 1 — transliterate 1:1 AppLifecycleController / NetworkStatusController / PushController / CapabilityRegistry / CrashLoopGuard logic re-coded in Swift, behaviour pinned by the JVM unit suites 2 — shared logic CivetwebServer (CapsuleServer) + RequestRouter CivetwebServer.swift + RequestRouter.swift over the same CivetWeb C sources — ✅ built, 17 tests green on Linux 3 — platform edge (done) QuickJSEngineImpl (JNI) same vendored QuickJS C + Swift/C bridge (keep the single-thread + 4 MB stack-base rule) 3/4 — re-glue only CapsuleBridge (@JavascriptInterface) WKScriptMessageHandler 3 — platform edge WebViewNavigator / WebViewSplashController WKWebView equivalents 3 — platform edge CivetwebServer → http://127.0.0.1:{port}/ CivetwebServer.swift → same http://127.0.0.1:{port}/ (embedded server, symmetric — adr-004) · ~~WKURLSchemeHandler~~ rejected 3 — platform edge FileBundleStore / PrefsCrashLog same interfaces; iOS impls (FileManager / UserDefaults) 3 — platform edge CapsuleActivity (composition root) AppDelegate / SceneDelegate 3 — platform edge activity/ActivityResultBroker, SuspendingActivityLauncher no analog — iOS uses delegate callbacks — drop

Why the iOS shell serves the bundle from an embedded loopback HTTP server — not WKURLSchemeHandler, and not https://localhost (full rationale: adr-004): - Embedded server, not a scheme handler. WKURLSchemeHandler is lighter, but it can't serve WebSockets, is a thinner HTTP emulation (streaming/range/POST-body sharp edges), and makes the platforms asymmetric (Android must run a real server — its WebView intercept API can't read POST bodies). A real CapsuleServer (CivetWeb, the same C server as Android) on iOS keeps /api semantics identical to Android and unlocks the HTTP fidelity tiers. Scheme handler is recorded as considered and rejected in adr-004 #2. - http loopback, not https. TLS on loopback needs a cert the WebView trusts; no public CA issues one for 127.0.0.1/localhost, and a self-signed cert means per-device trust-anchor provisioning (fragile). Plain http on loopback is already a stable, app-controlled, secure-context origin — so localStorage / IndexedDB / service workers / CORS behave correctly. https buys nothing and costs a cert burden. (iOS needs the one-line NSAllowsLocalNetworking ATS exception for cleartext loopback; that's it.) - Background-socket discipline: re-bind the server on sceneWillEnterForeground; long-lived connections reconnect on foreground (standard mobile-web behaviour). See adr-004 realism notes.

  1. Build + Simulator tests: GitHub Actions macOS (free on the public repo — see above). Optional recent-macOS VM as an interactive scratchpad for native debugging, accepting it's gray/throwaway.
  2. Real-device e2e + signing + App Store: defer to the Mac mini (~$599), bought when OTA revenue funds it. Until then, capsule publish ios (Fastlane path in publishing.md) is designed but unexercised on real submission.

docs.title: Test-strategy alignment
docs.text:
This keeps iOS honest with the existing 3-tier strategy that must hold on both platforms:

  • Unit + integration: run in CI/Simulator now (no device).
  • e2e: real iPhone, deferred to hardware.

docs.title: Android ↔ iOS Parity — Languages & Tooling
docs.text:
The cross-platform map of Capsule's languages and tooling, layer by layer. Use it to see, at a glance, what is shared (the contract / the JS brain), what is re-coded (pure logic), and what is per-platform plumbing (the edge). Companion to the iOS bring-up plan (ios-bring-up.md) and the contract-readiness audit there.

Web serving is decided — embedded loopback HTTP server on both platforms — the same CivetWeb C sources (packages/native/civetweb, adr-004 amendment 2026-10-24); WKURLSchemeHandler and https://localhost were considered and rejected. See adr-004 for the rationale and the HTTP fidelity tiers (request/response + streaming now; WebSockets/SSE deferred-by-design).

Where iOS has a real choice, the chosen option is bold; rejected/alternative options are noted.

docs.title: Languages

docs.title: Capsule Framework — Community Integration Authoring Guide
docs.text:
For authors building third-party SDK wrappers or custom integrations. Core platform capabilities (camera, GPS, push, NFC, Bluetooth, haptics, biometrics, filesystem, etc.) are already part of @capsule/core — you do not need to build plugins for OS APIs that ship with the platform.

Use this guide when wrapping: Google Maps, Stripe, Braintree, Firebase, Facebook Auth, or any SDK that requires a third-party dependency. For bridge internals and language feasibility see plugins.md.

docs.title: Quick Start — Your First Integration in 5 Minutes
docs.text:
# Scaffold a new community integration
capsule plugin create google-maps

# Result:
# capsule-plugins/
#   google-maps/
#     capsule-plugin.json
#     android/GoogleMapsIntegration.kt
#     ios/GoogleMapsIntegration.swift
#     web/index.ts

Declare it in capsule.config.ts: 

plugins: ['./capsule-plugins/google-maps']

Run capsule build android — your integration compiles alongside the app. Done.

docs.title: File Structure
docs.text:
capsule-plugins/
  barcode/
    capsule-plugin.json      ← required: metadata, permissions, dependencies, platform declarations
    proguard.rules           ← optional: R8 keep rules (merged by CLI into proguard-rules.pro)
    android/
      BarcodeScanner.kt      ← Kotlin implementation (or .java)
    ios/
      BarcodeScanner.swift   ← Swift implementation
    web/
      index.ts               ← TypeScript bridge (web-facing API)
      index.d.ts             ← auto-generated types (from `capsule generate types`)

All files are optional per platform. A web-only plugin needs only web/index.ts. An Android-only plugin needs only android/ + web/index.ts.

docs.title: Plugin minSdk Conflict Behavior
docs.text:
When a source plugin's capsule-plugin.json declares a higher minSdk than the app's capsule.config.ts:

App:    android.minSdk: 26
Plugin: android.minSdk: 30

CLI behavior at capsule sync / capsule build:

⚠ Warning: Plugin "barcode" requires minSdk 30 (Android 11).
  The app targets minSdk 26 (Android 8.0).
  Devices on Android 8.0–10.x will not load this plugin.
  Plugin methods will return error 3001 (PLUGIN_UNAVAILABLE) on unsupported devices.

  Options:
  → Raise app minSdk to 30:  set android.minSdk: 30 in capsule.config.ts
  → Accept the limitation:   the plugin loads silently only on Android 11+

The plugin is not removed and the build does not fail — it compiles and ships with the app. On devices below the plugin's minSdk, the Capsule bridge returns a typed error:

// Web layer should handle this
try {
  const result = await barcode.scan()
} catch (e) {
  if (e.code === 3001) {
    // Plugin unavailable on this device/OS version
    showFallbackUI()
  }
}

When a plugin genuinely cannot support older Android (the warning is accurate): - Uses CameraX 1.3+ (requires API 28) - Uses BiometricPrompt (API 28) - Uses Foreground Service types (API 29) - Uses exact AlarmManager scheduling (API 31) - Uses Bluetooth LE with new permission model (API 31) - Uses UsbManager new APIs (API 31)

In these cases, raise the app's minSdk or document the device requirement clearly.
