Tier 3 — cloud inference through the Capsule OTA cloud (billing meter) + confidence-based fallback. 7. Agent layer — @capsule/core/agent (defineAgent, tool registry mapping bridge methods → tool schemas, thin loop), tool-permission model, MCP tool protocol decision. 8. OTA-updatable agent logic — agent definitions ride Server Code Push; canary + auto-rollback (already built in Step 7) protect a bad agent push.

Phase 8+ — ecosystem. Agent tool packs, model registry, fine-tune/RAG hooks (Cactus offers RAG on Flutter today).

docs.title: Testing — how, and can we actually test it?
docs.text:
Yes — fully, off-device, through the existing 4-tier harness (testing.md). The trick is the same one the whole codebase already uses: the model is a provider behind the bridge, so a FakeAiProvider / scripted FakeLlm makes everything deterministic. An agent is deterministic given a scripted sequence of model responses (the standard way agents are tested).

Tier What it asserts for AI/agents Determinism 1 — Route/contract + units (Vitest, node) Tool-registry wiring (every tool maps to a real bridge method — the 404 class); agent routing/branch logic as pure functions; prompt assembly Pure functions + FakeAiProvider returning scripted tool-calls 2 — Component (Vitest, jsdom) UI renders against @capsule/core's FakeBridge with a canned ai.generate result; streaming token plumbing; loading/error states FakeBridge canned completion 3 — QuickJS fidelity (Vitest + quickjs-emscripten) The agent loop runs in real QuickJS — defineAgent orchestration, tool dispatch, multi-turn loop — with inference stubbed to a scripted provider. Confirms the loop uses no Node/DOM globals Scripted provider; loop is JSON+bridge only — Integration (gated) Real model behavior — structure, not content: valid tool-call JSON, terminates within N turns, latency budget. Gated on CAPSULE_AI_* env (mirrors CAPSULE_API_BASE), skipped in hermetic CI Non-deterministic → assert shape/contract 4 — On-device smoke (Espresso-Web) Native provider attaches; ai.availability() returns sane tier; a short generation returns non-empty. On-device model perf/quality is non-deterministic — assert structure + a latency ceiling, never exact text Device-only; structural assertions

Provider-level Kotlin/Swift tests mirror existing handlers: FakeAiProvider (like FakeCameraProvider/ FakeLocationProvider) → AiHandler unit tests, pure JVM. What we cannot make deterministic is real model output quality — so we never assert exact strings against a live model; we assert contracts (valid JSON tool-calls, termination, token/latency budgets) and pin a model+seed where the engine allows.

Net: the layered harness already covers AI/agents; only the live-model integration tier needs a key, and only Tier-4 perf/quality needs a device — exactly like every other native API.

docs.title: Open questions / gates (close before committing Tier 2+)
docs.text:
• Cactus license (confirm the LICENSE file: Apache/MIT?) and .cact format longevity — keep a llama.cpp/GGUF escape hatch so we're never single-vendor-locked.
  • MCP vs. custom tool protocol for the agent tool surface.
  • Tool-permission UX — per-tool grants + sensitive-action confirmation.
  • Model distribution — bundle vs. on-first-run download; size budget; storage location contract (must sit outside the OTA bundle dirs, see D-series).
  • Default tier policy — when does hybrid escalate on-device → cloud (confidence? task class? config?).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A multi-phase initiative, but it compounds the existing roadmap rather than competing with it: every Phase-3 native API becomes an agent tool, and the agent layer makes the Phase-5 OTA cloud a stronger funding engine (cloud inference = a metered, billable surface).
  • New compatibility surface: the ai capability + tool schemas must be versioned and frozen like the bridge protocol (see adr-001 "contract to freeze").
  • Pulls a real native dependency (Cactus/llama.cpp) into the shell — opt-in + tree-shaken so apps that don't use AI pay zero size (Q16 discipline).
  • Positions Capsule's pitch as "build a cross-platform app and give it an on-device/hybrid agent whose tools are the device itself, updatable over the air" — sharper and more defensible than "we have an LLM API like Ionic."

docs.title: ADR-004 — Web-Serving Transport & HTTP Fidelity
docs.text: Status: Decided Date: 2026-06-26 Amends: adr-001 decision #4 ("No WebSockets, no SSE … deliberately minimal").

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR-001 already decided the production web-serving mechanism: an embedded loopback HTTP server — NanoHTTPD on Android, GCDWebServer (or equivalent) on iOS — fronting the QuickJS route runtime. That is Capsule's primary differentiator vs Ionic/Capacitor: your /api server routes run on-device, in QuickJS, and are OTA-updatable.

Two things drifted from that decision and need correcting:

  1. WKURLSchemeHandler crept in as the iOS serving mechanism (in ios-bring-up.md, capsule-vs-ionic-capacitor.md, and the nanohttpd primer). A custom scheme handler is the Capacitor approach and is lighter, but it cannot serve WebSockets, it is a thinner emulation of HTTP (streaming, range requests, POST-body handling are all sharp edges), and it makes the two platforms architecturally asymmetric — Android runs a real server (it is forced to: Android's shouldInterceptRequest/WebViewAssetLoader cannot read POST bodies), iOS would not. That asymmetry is exactly what we do not want.

  2. ADR-001 said "no WebSockets, no SSE, ever — deliberately minimal." The product intent has since sharpened: Capsule should give developers a full web experience — realistic, and it must work properly. Full HTTP fidelity (including, eventually, WebSockets and SSE) is in scope; it is deferred and designed, not permanently excluded.

docs.title: 1. Embedded loopback HTTP server on both platforms
docs.text:
Production serving is a real HTTP server bound to http://127.0.0.1:{port}/ (deterministic port from appId, per ADR-001 #7), on both platforms:

  • Android: CivetwebServer — CivetWeb (C) through JNI. Shipped; replaced the original NanoHttpdServer on 2026-10-24.
  • iOS: CivetwebServer — the same CivetWeb sources through a SwiftPM C target. Built and tested; wired into the shell with the Phase-4 bring-up.

The library choice is in the 2026-10-24 amendment below (originally NanoHTTPD on Android and GCDWebServer-or-equivalent on iOS).

This keeps the architectures symmetric: identical /api semantics on both platforms, one mental model, "write once, behaves identically." The shared abstraction already exists — see decision #4.

docs.title: 2. WKURLSchemeHandler is rejected as the primary iOS mechanism
docs.text: It is recorded here as considered and rejected, so it does not drift back in. Reasons: no WebSocket support; thinner HTTP fidelity (streaming/range/POST-body sharp edges); and it breaks cross-platform symmetry. (It remains a theoretical fallback only if the embedded server proves unviable on iOS — not expected.)

docs.title: 3. https://localhost is rejected on both platforms
docs.text: TLS on loopback needs a certificate the WebView trusts. No public CA issues certs for 127.0.0.1/localhost; a self-signed cert makes the WebView throw TLS errors unless you ship and install a trusted anchor (per-device provisioning, fragile, ongoing maintenance). Plain http on loopback already gives a stable, app-controlled, secure-context origin — so localStorage / IndexedDB / service workers / CORS all behave correctly. https buys nothing over loopback http and costs a cert-trust burden. (On iOS, cleartext loopback http needs the NSAllowsLocalNetworking ATS exception — declared once in Info.plist.)

docs.title: 4. The cross-platform abstraction is already built — keep it, finish one seam
docs.text:
The symmetric, unit-testable layer ADR-001 #13/#14 mandated already exists:

  • CapsuleServer interface + FakeCapsuleServer (neverStarts / startsAfter / crashesAfter) already unit-test the orchestration on the JVM.
  • CapsuleRuntime (start → splash → bind → navigate; crash-loop; rollback) is platform-neutral and never names the server library.
  • The routing brain is shared JS: both servers are thin socket-to-QuickJS pumps that marshal an HTTP request to a neutral shape (HttpRouteResponse / @capsule/core's CapsuleHttpRequest) and call QuickJSBridge.handleHttpRequest. The actual /api/* dispatch is @capsule/core JS running inside QuickJS — already identical on both platforms.

One refactor to finish the dream: the socket→QuickJS seam is currently an inline apiHandler lambda in the wiring. Promote it to a named HttpApiRouter interface so it is an explicit, fake-able contract on both platforms.

Done (2026-10-24), as RequestRouter (Kotlin and Swift, rule for rule). It owns every routing decision — /api/* → the injected QuickJS handler, everything else → a StaticAssets source, / → index.html, .. rejected, the 404/500 bodies — and has no HTTP-library or platform dependency, so it is unit-tested on its own (RequestRouterTest on the JVM, RequestRouterTests in Swift). The CivetwebServer transports only move bytes between the socket and route().

docs.title: 5. HTTP fidelity is tiered — request/response + streaming now; WebSockets/SSE deferred-by-design
docs.text:
This amends ADR-001 #4. HTTP is no longer "deliberately minimal forever":

Tier Capability Status Now Static asset serving + request/response /api/* routes (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE) + streaming responses (chunked) In scope for Phase 4 parity Future WebSockets (ws://localhost) for on-device real-time Designed, not excluded — roadmap Future Server-Sent Events (SSE) + range requests (media seeking) Designed, not excluded — roadmap

WebSockets/SSE are not free with a server. A socket gives the transport, but @capsule/core's route model is request/response (handleHttpRequest → one response). A WebSocket is a long-lived bidirectional stream — there is no onOpen/onMessage/onClose route type yet. Delivering it is a new core API design (on both platforms), plus the single-threaded QuickJS engine must pump frames. So WebSockets/SSE are scheduled as explicit future roadmap features, designed deliberately — not promised in the first iOS cut.

This does not change ADR-001's channel split (Bridge = native events/push; HTTP = request/response data). WebSockets/SSE here are web-standard real-time inside the on-device server — for "any web app just works" fidelity — distinct from Capsule's native-event Bridge.

docs.title: Realism constraints (it "must work properly")
docs.text:
1. iOS background-socket teardown. iOS closes the listening socket when the app suspends. Foregrounded — when the user is actually using the app — it is flawless. The discipline: re-bind the server on sceneWillEnterForeground (before the WebView is interactive); long-lived connections (WS/SSE, when they land) reconnect on foreground — exactly how real mobile web apps already handle backgrounding. Realistic, and matches web semantics.
  2. Single-threaded engine. Concurrent /api calls serialize through QuickJS. Fine for a local app; revisit only if a real workload bottlenecks.
  3. POST-body certainty. A real server reads request bodies natively — sidestepping the WKURLSchemeHandler httpBody-dropping sharp edge entirely (a bonus of decision #1).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The iOS shell ships a CapsuleServer impl (CivetWeb, see the amendment), not a scheme handler.
  • CapsuleRuntime, FakeCapsuleServer, and the QuickJS route brain are reused unchanged on iOS; only the thin server adapter is per-platform (see platform-parity.md).
  • The HttpApiRouter seam refactor (decision #4) is done — RequestRouter.
  • WebSockets and SSE become roadmap items with a core-API-design dependency (roadmap.md).
  • Three docs that drifted to WKURLSchemeHandler are corrected to point here.

Full Android ↔ iOS language/tooling parity (with this decision baked in): platform-parity.md.

docs.title: Amendment 2026-10-24: CivetWeb on both platforms
docs.text:
Decision. Both shells embed CivetWeb (C, MIT), replacing NanoHTTPD on Android and the planned GCDWebServer on iOS. One copy of the sources is vendored at packages/native/civetweb/ (pinned release tag in its VERSION file) and compiled by both builds — Android's CMake into libcapsule_server.so, iOS's repo-root Package.swift as the CCivetweb target — with the same defines.

Why:

  1. One server, two platforms. Decision #1's symmetry stops being "two libraries that should behave alike" and becomes the same C code answering the same requests. RequestRouter (decision #4) is ported rule for rule, so routing is identical too.
  2. Readiness by construction. mg_start2 returns only after the listening socket is bound and listening. The startup race NanoHTTPD 2.3.1 caused (2026-10-embedded-server-startup.md) cannot occur, so the readiness probe and bind-retry loop were deleted rather than ported.
  3. The deferred WebSocket tier (decision #5) is in the same library. CivetWeb implements WebSockets (USE_WEBSOCKET, off for now); when the core-API design for WS routes lands, the transport needs no second library.
  4. Loopback only. The server binds 127.0.0.1:{port}, not every interface — nothing off the device can reach it (NanoHTTPD bound all interfaces).
  5. Maintenance. NanoHTTPD's last stable release is 2.3.1 (2016); GCDWebServer's repository is archived (2023). CivetWeb is still developed upstream (commits in 2026); its newest release tag, v1.16, is what is vendored.

Build configuration (packages/native/civetweb/README.md): NO_SSL (decision #3), NO_CGI, NO_FILES (CivetWeb never serves files — Capsule answers every request in begin_request; assets come from the APK / app bundle), NO_CACHING. NO_FILESYSTEMS is deliberately not set — it would require custom error- and access-log hooks. Only release tags are vendored: an upstream master snapshot (2026-04) did not compile. Updating: node scripts/update-civetweb.mjs <tag>.

Behaviour both platforms now guarantee:

  • start() returns once the port accepts connections; a request made immediately after succeeds.
  • stop() returns at once and releases the port on a background thread (mg_stop joins workers, and a worker can be inside an /api route that waits on the main thread). The next start() on the same port waits for that shutdown instead of failing with "in use".
  • Every response carries Cache-Control: no-cache, because an OTA update swaps files behind the same URLs.
  • A bind failure surfaces as a typed error (Android ServerStartupException "Port N is already in use…", iOS ServerStartupError.portInUse).

docs.title: Capsule Framework — Decisions
docs.text: This document consolidates all design decisions for the Capsule Framework: API design decisions (Q-series, from spec review) and implementation decisions (D-series, ordered by urgency before each phase).

docs.title: Part 1 — API & Design Decisions
docs.text: Gaps, uncertainties, and unresolved design questions to be answered before or during implementation. Add answers inline as they are decided.

docs.title: Q1 — SDK Update: What If the Capsule Team Falls Behind?
docs.text:
Context: The "shell as binary dep" model means developers can't bump targetSdk themselves — they wait for a new shell release from the Capsule team.

Risk: Google mandates a new targetSdk by a hard deadline (e.g., August each year for Play Store). If the Capsule team hasn't shipped a compatible shell by then, apps can't be updated on the Play Store.

Questions: - What is the Capsule team's SLA for releasing a new shell when Google/Apple change requirements? - Is there a documented emergency path for developers to manually override targetSdk without waiting for a shell release? - Should capsule.config.ts expose a android.gradleOverrides: {} escape hatch for exactly this scenario?

Answer: Decided — closed.

Four-layer approach:

Layer 1 — Proactive tracking (prevents the crisis). Capsule team follows Google Developer Preview 1 (January) and Apple WWDC (June) from day one. Work starts on beta SDKs immediately, not after GA release. Since the shell is open source (Q15), community contributors can also submit SDK-update PRs.

Layer 2 — SLA commitment. Capsule team ships a compatible shell within 6 weeks of the first stable SDK release. Google's stable API 36 → Capsule ships compatible shell → developers have 3–4 months before the Play Store deadline. This SLA is published in the docs and tracked via a public GitHub milestone.

Layer 3 — capsule doctor deadline awareness. CLI warns proactively: 

⚠ Upcoming deadline: Google requires targetSdk 36 by Aug 31, 2026.
  Your shell targets 35. Watch for capsule update --shell in the next weeks.
  Status: https://github.com/capsule-framework/capsule/milestones/sdk-36

Layer 4 — android.gradleOverrides escape hatch (break-glass only). If the Capsule team misses the deadline, developers are not stuck: 

android: {
  gradleOverrides: {
    targetSdk: 36,          // emergency override — bypasses managed shell
    compileSdk: 36,
  }
}
CLI warns loudly: "gradleOverrides bypasses the managed shell. Some capsule features may break. Remove this after running capsule update." The override is injected into the generated build.gradle and is not guaranteed stable across shell versions — it is intentionally a last resort, not a feature.

docs.title: Q2 — Plugin Gradle Dependencies
docs.text:
Context: capsule-plugin.json currently only declares permissions, minSdk, and infoPlist keys. It has no way to declare arbitrary Maven dependencies a plugin needs (e.g., com.google.zxing:core:3.5.0).

Questions: - How does a source plugin declare its own Gradle dependencies? - Should capsule-plugin.json gain a dependencies.android[] array of Maven coordinates? - How are version conflicts between plugin dependencies resolved (Gradle's resolution strategy)?

Example of what's missing: 

{
  "name": "barcode",
  "android": {
    "dependencies": [
      "com.google.zxing:core:3.5.0",
      "androidx.camera:camera-core:1.3.0"
    ]
  }
}

Answer: Decided — closed.

capsule-plugin.json gains android.dependencies[] and ios.podDependencies[]. Plugin author declares Maven coordinates — no Gradle syntax required:

{
  "android": {
    "dependencies": ["com.google.zxing:core:3.5.0", "androidx.camera:camera-core:1.3.0"]
  },
  "ios": {
    "podDependencies": [{ "name": "ZXingObjC", "version": "~> 3.6" }]
  }
}

At capsule sync, the CLI: 1. Collects all dependencies from installed plugins and core overrides (capsule override) 2. Groups by groupId:artifactId, applies "highest compatible version wins" (mirrors Gradle default) 3. Hard-errors only when versions are in different majors — names exactly which plugins conflict 4. Injects the resolved set into the generated build.gradle

Conflict detection runs before Gradle — actionable CLI error, not a cryptic build failure: 

✗ Dependency conflict: com.squareup.okhttp3:okhttp
  @capsule-community/stripe requires 4.9.0
  @capsule-community/maps requires 4.11.0
  Resolved to 4.11.0 (highest compatible — patch-level only, safe).

Rejected alternatives: - build.gradle.fragment file per plugin — Plugin author writes raw Gradle syntax. Breaks the no-Gradle-knowledge rule; fragile across AGP versions. - Semantic version aliases ("needs-camerax") — CLI maintains an alias-to-version mapping. Too rigid for community plugins, high Capsule team maintenance burden. - Delegate to android.gradleOverrides — Developer resolves conflicts manually. Last resort, not a first-class solution.

docs.title: Q3 — ProGuard / R8 Rules for Source Plugins
docs.text:
Context: ../guide/plugins.md mentions ProGuard as a gotcha for plugins that use reflection, but doesn't specify how a developer adds -keep rules to the generated proguard-rules.pro.

Questions: - Can a source plugin ship a proguard.rules file that gets merged by the CLI into the generated project? - For binary plugins (AAR), do they bundle their own consumer ProGuard rules (standard AAR feature)? - Is R8 enabled by default in Capsule release builds?

Answer: Decided — closed.

AAR plugins (binary integrations): Standard AAR format embeds consumer ProGuard rules. AGP applies them automatically when the AAR is consumed. No CLI action needed.

Source plugins and core overrides: Three-layer approach:

Layer 1 — Safe default (zero config): CLI adds a blanket -keep class <plugin.package>.** { *; } for every source plugin and override package. R8 still optimizes the rest of the app; plugin/override classes are preserved.

Layer 2 — Explicit rules (opt-in optimization): Plugin ships a proguard.rules file at the plugin root. CLI merges it verbatim into the generated proguard-rules.pro, overriding the blanket keep. Plugin authors who understand R8 use this to enable full optimization.

Layer 3 — @CapsuleKeep annotations (Phase 2): Annotation on Kotlin classes generates ProGuard rules at capsule sync time — plugin author never writes ProGuard syntax. Aligns with the existing bridge annotation pattern for TypeScript type generation.

R8: Enabled by default on release builds. Blanket keep ensures correctness; explicit proguard.rules unlocks maximum optimization for authors who want it.

Rejected alternatives: - Disable R8 entirely for plugin/override packages — Penalizes app binary size with no benefit to authors who write clean code. - Require all authors to write ProGuard rules — High barrier, common source of production reflection crashes.

docs.title: Q4 — Gradle / AGP Build Error UX
docs.text:
Context: When ./gradlew fails inside capsule build android, the developer sees raw Gradle output — which is often cryptic and unrelated to anything in capsule.config.ts.

Questions: - Should the CLI intercept common Gradle error patterns and translate them to actionable Capsule messages? - Example: minSdk < 21 error → "Set android.minSdk to at least 21 in capsule.config.ts" - What is the intended workflow when a Gradle error has no fix at the Capsule config level?

Answer: Decided — closed.

Layer 1 — Pre-flight validation (before Gradle runs): capsule build validates config state first. Most common errors are caught here with direct capsule.config.ts field references: - minSdk conflict between app config and plugin/override requirements - Missing signing config for --release builds - Missing google-services.json path - Unsatisfied requiresShell ranges on installed plugins

Layer 2 — Error pattern registry (for what slips through): CLI maintains a community-contributed JSON registry of { pattern, capsuleMessage, fix, docsUrl } entries. Gradle stderr is scanned on non-zero exit. Match → human-readable message. No match → raw Gradle output (last 30 lines) + capsule doctor suggestion:

✗ Build failed: minSdk conflict
  Plugin "@capsule-community/biometrics" requires android.minSdk ≥ 28.
  Your app declares android.minSdk: 24.
  Fix: raise android.minSdk to 28 in capsule.config.ts (drops Android 7.x support)
  Docs: https://capsule.dev/docs/errors/minsdk-conflict

The pattern registry lives as a JSON file in the CLI repo — community PRs add patterns. After real-world usage the registry covers the 80% of common failures. Unknown errors: raw Gradle output + capsule doctor --verbose + GitHub issue link.

Rejected alternatives: - Gradle build scan (--scan) — Uploads data to Gradle infrastructure by default. Privacy concern disproportionate to the benefit. - Full structured Gradle output parsing — Fragile across Gradle/AGP version combinations, high ongoing maintenance.

docs.title: Q5 — capsule init Framework Selection
docs.text:
Context: The CLI has a capsule init command but the docs don't specify whether it prompts for a web framework (React, Vue, Svelte, etc.) or just scaffolds a bare Vite project.

Questions: - Does capsule init offer a framework selection menu (React / Vue / Svelte / Vanilla)? - Is Angular supported? Angular has its own build pipeline (not Vite-native) — does Capsule support it or explicitly not? - Who configures vite.config.ts with the correct framework plugin — the developer manually, or the CLI scaffolds it?

Answer: Decided — closed.

capsule init uses a --template flag backed by a template registry — same mental model as npm create vite@latest:

capsule init my-app --template react-ts
capsule init my-app --template vue-ts
capsule init my-app --template svelte-ts
capsule init my-app --template vanilla-ts
capsule init my-app --template github:myorg/my-capsule-template  # community / org template

Without --template: interactive prompt listing official templates with "Custom (GitHub URL)" at the bottom.

Official templates live in capsule-framework/templates repo. Each includes a pre-configured vite.config.ts, capsule.config.ts, package.json, and framework-specific entry point. The CLI uses degit to clone the template — no git history, clean working directory.

Angular: Not in official templates. Angular's build pipeline diverges enough to require disproportionate ongoing maintenance. Documented explicitly as unsupported with a note on the Vite-based Angular path. Community template via github: URL is the route for Angular users.

Rejected alternatives: - Interactive menu built into CLI core — Framework-specific Vite plugin setup logic lives in CLI, breaks whenever a framework updates its Vite plugin. - Delegate to create-vite first, then add Capsule — Two sequential interactive sessions on first use. Awkward UX for new developers. - Bare scaffold, developer adds framework manually — Every developer performs 3–5 manual steps before writing a line of app code. Poor first impression.

docs.title: Q6 — Mobile CSS Reset / Layout Library
docs.text:
Context: There is no mention of a CSS baseline for mobile layout (safe area insets, tap highlight removal, font normalization, etc.). Ionic provides this as @ionic/core/css. Capsule has no equivalent.

Questions: - Should Capsule ship a @capsule/mobile-css package with a minimal mobile reset? - Minimum contents would include: - env(safe-area-inset-*) variables - -webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent - touch-action: manipulation on interactive elements - overscroll-behavior: none where appropriate - Viewport height fix for mobile browsers (100dvh) - Should this be bundled automatically, or opt-in via capsule.config.ts? - Should capsule init prompt "Include Capsule mobile CSS reset? (Y/n)"?

Answer: Decided — closed.

Two automatic layers — zero developer configuration:

Layer 1 — Shell injects CSS custom properties (native layer, always on): The shell writes accurate device-specific values to :root at startup and on orientation change: 

:root {
  --sai-top: 44px;     /* safe-area-inset-top — notch / Dynamic Island */
  --sai-bottom: 34px;  /* safe-area-inset-bottom — home indicator */
  --sai-left: 0px;
  --sai-right: 0px;
}
Values come from the native shell, not from env(safe-area-inset-*) CSS which is unreliable inside WebView.

Layer 2 — CLI injects a minimal mobile reset into the built index.html (~150 bytes, opt-out): 

*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
html, body { height: 100%; margin: 0; overscroll-behavior: none; }
body { -webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent; touch-action: manipulation; }
Opt-out: web.mobileReset: false in capsule.config.ts. No prompt during capsule init.

@capsule/mobile-css may exist as an optional package for utility classes (safe area helpers, styled scroll containers) but is never required and never prompted.

Rejected alternatives: - Opt-in package (import '@capsule/mobile-css') — Developers forget it on every new project. The framework should be correct by default. - CSS variables only — Doesn't fix tap highlights, touch behavior, or overscroll. Every developer still writes the same 3 lines manually. - Full mobile UI component library (Ionic-style) — Out of scope for the framework layer. Capsule is infrastructure, not a design system.

docs.title: Q7 — Minimum Plugin Set to Ship with Framework
docs.text:
Context: Phase 3 of the roadmap lists camera, filesystem, push, geolocation, and haptics. But some of these are available via standard Web APIs without a plugin.

Questions: - What is the exact minimum plugin set for a real-world production app? - Which capabilities are handled by Web APIs (no plugin needed) vs. require native plugins? - Geolocation: navigator.geolocation works in WebView — plugin needed? - Camera: navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia works — is @capsule/camera for native camera UX only? - Push: definitely needs native plugin (APNs/FCM registration) - Should there be a "starter bundle" (@capsule/essentials) that installs the common set in one command?

Answer: Decided — closed. All platform OS APIs are built into @capsule/core. There is no "minimum plugin set" because there are no plugins for platform capabilities. Camera, GPS, push, NFC, Bluetooth, haptics, biometrics, filesystem, microphone, barcode, connectivity, clipboard, share sheet, battery, and device info all ship with the framework and are tree-shaken if unused. @capsule/essentials is not needed — @capsule/core is already the essentials. See the architectural decision in Q16.

docs.title: Q8 — Plugin LTS / Long-Term Support Policy
docs.text:
Context: One of the stated goals is to avoid "plugin hell." But this depends on the Capsule team committing to a support timeline for major versions.

Questions: - How long is a major version of @capsule/core supported after the next major is released? - What is the migration path when @capsule/core bumps a major version? Is there a codemod? - What happens to community (@capsule-community/*) plugins when @capsule/core bumps? Is there a grace period before they are delisted? - Is there a compatibility matrix published (core version × shell version × plugin version)?

Answer: Decided — closed.

The monolithic core model eliminates the cross-plugin compatibility matrix: there is only one version (core/shell) that everything is tied to. Community integrations still declare a requiresShell semver range. The capsule override mechanism (Q20) further reduces LTS urgency — bugs in core capabilities can be patched surgically without waiting for a new shell release.

LTS policy: 24-month security window after next major.

Major version bumps are rare by design — they happen only when: - The bridge protocol changes incompatibly - A core API must be renamed for platform reasons - A minimum supported Android/iOS version is dropped

Published policy: the previous major receives security patches for 24 months after the next major ships. This is the Node.js LTS model — well understood by enterprise teams.

capsule migrate command is required before any major version ships: 

capsule migrate --from v1 --to v2
# Automated codemods: renamed imports, config field changes, deprecated API replacements
# Produces a diff — developer reviews and commits
Migration guides alone are not sufficient. Automated tooling is the bar.

Community integrations (@capsule-community/*) declare their own support policy via capsule-plugin.json. CLI warns at install if a plugin's requiresShell range excludes the current shell version.

Rejected alternatives: - Two-version support window (Apple-style) — Potentially aggressive if majors ship on a fast cadence in early years. - No formal EOL — community takes over — Unpredictable for enterprises doing multi-year planning. The 24-month window is explicit and contractual.

docs.title: Q9 — CodeSync: Manual Approval Gate / Pilot Targeting
docs.text:
Context: CodeSync supports percentage-based rollout and channels, but has no concept of a named device list or explicit approval step before promoting a rollout.

Questions: - Can a release be put in "pending approval" state — staged but not delivered to any device until someone approves in the dashboard? - Can a specific set of named devices (by device_id or device model) be targeted for a pilot before opening to a percentage rollout? - Can devices be grouped by region, locale, or custom metadata tags? - Should the dashboard support a "promote to production" workflow with a required approver?

Answer: Decided — closed.

Channels are the approval mechanism — no new state machine needed. "Approval" is the act of running capsule codesync promote. Role-based access determines who can promote to production.

Deployment flow: 

developer publishes → staging channel → QA validates → Releaser promotes → production


# Publish to staging, targeting only QA devices
capsule codesync publish --channel staging --filter "metadata.group = 'qa'"

# After QA sign-off — promotion IS the approval gesture
capsule codesync promote --from staging --to production --rollout 5

Role-based access (capsule portal roles): Developer can publish to any non-production channel. Releaser role required to run promote --to production. This satisfies enterprise compliance without adding a separate approval state to the bundle lifecycle.

Pilot targeting via device metadata filters: 

# Target named pilot group before opening to percentage rollout
capsule codesync publish --channel staging --filter "metadata.group = 'pilot'"
# After pilot validation:
capsule codesync promote --from staging --to production --rollout 5

Scheduled releases: 

capsule codesync publish --channel production --at "2026-06-01T09:00:00Z"
# Bundle is ready and signed; delivery begins at the specified time
Useful for coordinated marketing launches across timezones.

Dashboard named groups: Saved filter expressions ("Brazil Enterprise", "Beta Testers"). capsule codesync publish --group "beta-testers" is shorthand for the saved filter. Groups are stored server-side, not in capsule.config.ts.

Rejected alternatives: - Formal draft → staged → approved state machine — Same outcome achievable with channels + RBAC. Extra states add implementation complexity with no behavioral difference. - Named device lists (manual dashboard tagging) — Only scales to small fleets. Metadata filters compose with channels and rollout %, making them strictly more powerful.

docs.title: Q10 — CodeSync Version Numbering Convention
docs.text:
Context: The relationship between the store app version (1.0.0) and the CodeSync bundle version is not explicitly defined as a convention.

Questions: - Is the CodeSync bundle version always tied to the store version name, or is it independent? - Proposed convention: {appVersion}.{bundlePatch} — e.g., store version 1.0.0, CodeSync bundles 1.0.0+1, 1.0.0+2, etc. - How is this displayed in the dashboard — does it show 1.0.0 (bundle #3) or something else? - How does capsule codesync releases output version info in a way that maps clearly to store releases?

Answer: Decided — closed.

Canonical format: {appVersion}+{bundlePatch} — semver build metadata. 1.0.0+3 means the 3rd CodeSync patch on the 1.0.0 store release. The bundle counter resets to 1 when appVersion changes.

Internal API and capsule-bundle.json use the canonical form. CLI and dashboard never surface the + notation directly — they display as two separate dimensions:

VERSION    BUNDLE  CHANNEL     ROLLOUT  STATUS       PUBLISHED
1.0.0      +3      production  100%     active       2026-05-21 14:30
1.0.0      +2      production  —        rolled-back  2026-05-19 09:12
1.0.0      +1      production  100%     superseded   2026-05-15 16:45
0.9.1      +7      production  100%     superseded   2026-04-30 10:00

capsule codesync publish auto-increments the bundle counter within the current appVersion and validates that appVersion in capsule.config.ts matches what's in capsule.lock.

Rejected alternatives: - Independent monotonic counter — Loses the "which store version was this built from" traceability in CLI output. Requires a dashboard lookup to understand context. - {appVersion}-bundle.{N} (pre-release notation) — Pre-release semver implies instability. Semantically wrong for production bundles. - Timestamp-based (1.0.0-20260521.1) — Verbose in logs, doesn't survive timezone differences in CI pipelines.

docs.title: Q11 — GTM / Analytics: Native Navigation Events
docs.text:
Context: GTM works as a standard web script with no plugin needed. However, Android's hardware back button is handled at the native layer and may not fire browser history events.

Questions: - Does the Capsule shell synthesize popstate or History API events when the Android back button is pressed? - If not, GTM's History Change trigger won't track navigation in multi-page Capsule apps — who is responsible for bridging this? - Should there be a @capsule/navigation bridge plugin that emits JS navigation events for GTM/analytics? - For single-page apps using React Router / Vue Router, this is a non-issue — should the docs clarify this?

Answer: Decided — closed. capsule.navigation is part of @capsule/core (not a plugin). Robust default behavior, fully overridable.

Default shell behavior (automatic, no developer code needed): 1. Android hardware back button intercepted by shell 2. Shell calls window.history.back() if history.length > 1 → this fires a native popstate event → GTM's History Change trigger fires automatically 3. If no history to go back to, shell dispatches a capsule:backbutton custom event on window → developer can handle "exit app?" confirmation

Developer override API (@capsule/core): 

import { navigation } from '@capsule/core'

// Override back button completely
navigation.onBackButton((event) => {
  if (event.canGoBack) {
    // custom logic before going back
    showExitConfirmation().then(confirmed => {
      if (confirmed) navigation.goBack()
    })
  } else {
    // no history — custom exit flow
    showExitConfirmation()
  }
})

// Listen without overriding (additive)
window.addEventListener('capsule:backbutton', (e) => {
  analytics.track('back_button_pressed', { canGoBack: e.detail.canGoBack })
})

For SPA frameworks (React Router, Vue Router): The popstate event fires normally — their routers already handle it. No action needed.

For GTM: The popstate event that fires from window.history.back() is the standard History Change trigger. Works automatically with zero GTM configuration.

docs.title: Q12 — iOS: capsule dev --qr Without macOS
docs.text:
Context: The QR code dev flow is documented for both platforms, but iOS builds always require macOS + Xcode.

Questions: - If a developer is on Windows/Linux, can they use capsule dev --qr for Android while a teammate handles the iOS side? - Is there a cloud macOS option (GitHub Actions macOS runner, Mac-in-Cloud) documented for teams without Apple hardware? - Should capsule dev clearly detect the platform and warn "iOS dev requires macOS" before attempting?

Answer: Decided — closed.

iOS requires macOS. This is Apple policy, not a Capsule limitation. The framework does not attempt to work around it.

DX handling: - capsule add ios on Windows/Linux → clear warning at setup time (not at build time, when the developer has already invested time) - capsule dev on Windows/Linux → starts Android-only mode silently; prints one note: iOS dev requires macOS — running Android only - capsule build ios on Windows/Linux → hard error with docs link

For cross-platform teams (Windows/Linux primary development): Develop and test on Android (95%+ of app code is platform-agnostic). Run iOS builds in CI on GitHub Actions macOS runners. Document this workflow explicitly in the docs as "The Windows/Linux team setup."

Phase 6 roadmap — capsule build ios --cloud: First-party or partnered Mac-in-Cloud integration. Configures via capsule portal with an API key. Handles production builds only (not dev hot reload — that round-trip is too slow for iteration). Removes the macOS dependency for release builds.

Rejected alternatives: - Remote relay (capsule dev --ios-relay <ip>) — macOS machine on the network serves as the iOS build/deploy relay. Complex networking, niche setup, hard to support and document. - WebKit emulation on Windows — Apple's rendering stack is not portable. Not realistic. - Hide the constraint — Worse than being explicit. Developers discover it mid-project rather than at setup time.

docs.title: Q13 — capsule eject for Closed-Source Plugins
docs.text:
Context: capsule eject requires a sourceRepo field in capsule-plugin.json. Closed-source plugins cannot be ejected.

Questions: - Should closed-source plugins be explicitly prohibited from the @capsule-community/* tier? - If a commercial plugin (e.g., a paid SDK wrapper) has no sourceRepo, what is the developer's recourse when it breaks? - Should the CLI warn at install time if a plugin has no sourceRepo?

Answer: Decided — closed.

@capsule-community/* scope requires open source. sourceRepo is a required field to publish under the community scope. Without it, capsule plugin publish rejects: 

✗ Community-scoped plugins must have a sourceRepo in capsule-plugin.json.
  For closed-source plugins, publish under your own npm scope
  and declare trust: 'unverified' in capsule.config.ts.

For closed-source or commercial plugins: They live outside @capsule-community/*, are trust: 'unverified' by default, and the developer must explicitly acknowledge the risk: 

plugins: [
  { path: 'vendor-sdk-plugin', trust: 'unverified' }  // required for non-community-scoped plugins
]

CLI warning at install for unverified plugins: 

⚠ Plugin "vendor-sdk" has no sourceRepo. capsule override and capsule eject are not available.
  If this plugin breaks or is abandoned, you cannot fork or patch it.
  Ensure you have a vendor support contract before shipping this to production.

The trust: 'unverified' declaration is deliberate friction — not a blocker, but an acknowledgment. This is the same model as Android's "Unknown sources" toggle.

Escape hatch context: For plugins that do have source (even if not in @capsule-community/*), capsule override covers surgical bug fixes and capsule eject covers full forks. For genuinely closed-source plugins, neither is available — the developer's only recourse is the vendor.

Rejected alternatives: - Allow closed-source in @capsule-community/* with a "license": "commercial" flag — Weakens the trust tier signal. The community scope should be a reliable indicator of open, auditable code. - Source escrow requirement for commercial plugins — Hard to enforce, complex verification process, disproportionate overhead for the community registry.

docs.title: Q14 — Capsule Server: Device Grouping by Custom Metadata
docs.text:
Context: The devices table has a metadata JSONB column, but the dashboard and API don't document how custom metadata is set or queried.

Questions: - Can the native client send custom metadata at check-in time (e.g., { "region": "br-south", "tier": "enterprise" })? - Can CodeSync channel targeting use metadata filters (e.g., "deliver to all devices where metadata.region = 'br-south'")? - If not, how do you do region-based or customer-segment-based rollouts?

Answer: Decided — closed.

Two-layer metadata model — automatic standard metadata + developer-registered business metadata:

Layer 1 — Shell sends standard metadata at every check-in (zero config): 

{
  "os_version": "Android 14",
  "locale": "pt-BR",
  "timezone": "America/Sao_Paulo",
  "device_model": "Pixel 8",
  "app_version": "1.0.0",
  "bundle_version": "1.0.0+3"
}
Handles geographic targeting (locale), OS version targeting, and device model targeting with no app code.

Layer 2 — App registers business metadata via bridge API: 

import { codesync } from '@capsule/core'

// Called after authentication — when business context is known
codesync.setDeviceMetadata({
  user_tier: user.subscriptionPlan,  // 'free' | 'pro' | 'enterprise'
  experiment_group: abTest.group,    // 'control' | 'checkout-v2'
  store_id: user.assignedStore       // for retail chains
})
Stored in devices.metadata JSONB. Merged with standard metadata. No PII — docs explicitly warn against storing email/name; use opaque identifiers.

Channel targeting uses filter expressions on any metadata key: 

# Geographic (automatic metadata — no app code needed)
capsule codesync publish --channel staging --filter "metadata.locale LIKE 'pt-%'"

# Business segment (custom metadata)
capsule codesync publish --channel staging --filter "metadata.user_tier = 'enterprise'"

# Composable
capsule codesync publish --channel staging \
  --filter "metadata.user_tier = 'enterprise' AND metadata.locale LIKE 'pt-%'"

Dashboard named groups are saved filter expressions — capsule codesync publish --group "brazil-enterprise" is shorthand. Groups are stored server-side.

Rejected alternatives: - Server-side device tagging via dashboard — Only practical for fleets under ~100 devices. No scale. - Named device lists (by explicit device IDs) — Not composable. Doesn't work for dynamic populations (new devices, new users).

docs.title: Q15 — Who Maintains the Capsule Shell Long-Term?
docs.text:
Context: The entire framework depends on the Capsule team continuously publishing new shell versions (AAR for Android, XCFramework for iOS) as Google and Apple evolve their platforms.

Questions: - Is the shell open source? Can the community contribute patches or fork it? - If the project is abandoned, is there a documented path for an organization to take over shell maintenance? - Should the shell source be published even if the CLI and portal remain proprietary?

Answer: Decided — closed. Open source from day one. Shell (Kotlin/Swift), CLI, and bridge runtime are all public repositories under the capsule-framework GitHub org. The portal/cloud infrastructure may have a proprietary tier, but the core toolchain is MIT or Apache 2.0. Any developer or organization can fork and continue maintenance. Community SDK-update PRs are explicitly welcome.

docs.title: Q16 — Architectural Decision: Monolithic Core SDK
docs.text:
Context: After design review, a fundamental architectural shift was made from a plugin-based model (where even platform OS APIs were separate packages) to a monolithic core SDK model.

Decision: Adopted.

Rule: - If a capability uses an OS API that ships with Android/iOS → it is part of @capsule/core - If a capability requires a third-party SDK dependency → it is a community integration (@capsule-community/* or local capsule-plugins/)

Core capabilities (always in @capsule/core, tree-shaken if unused): Camera, GPS/Geolocation, Push Notifications, NFC, Bluetooth LE, Haptics, Biometrics, Filesystem, Microphone/Audio, Barcode/QR, Connectivity, Clipboard, Share Sheet, Battery, Device Info, Screen Orientation, Accelerometer/Gyroscope, Preferences (key-value), Database (SQLite), Browser (in-app browser), InlineWebView

Community integrations (separate packages, require third-party SDK): Google Maps, Stripe, Braintree, Firebase, Facebook Auth, Segment, Twilio, etc.

CodeSync: Built into @capsule/core. Activated via codeSync.enabled: true in capsule.config.ts. Compiled out when disabled.

Rationale: Eliminates plugin compatibility matrix, reduces DX friction (no installs for OS APIs), enables one-version-manages-everything upgrade model. Tree-shaking ensures app size is not penalized for unused capabilities.

docs.title: Q17 — Shell Host Strategy: Expo/RN vs Custom Native Binary
docs.text:
Context: Two options were evaluated: (A) build the native shell as a custom Kotlin/Swift binary maintained by the Capsule team; (B) use Expo/React Native as the shell host, delegating Gradle/AGP/Xcode maintenance to the Expo team.

Decision: Decided — closed. Custom Kotlin/Swift binary (Option A).

Rationale: Expo dependency would introduce a large runtime (~12–15 MB), force React-only JS engine, and trade Gradle maintenance pain for Expo major-version migration pain. The open source model (Q15) and community SDK-update SLA (Q1) mitigate the maintenance risk that originally motivated Option B. Full control over the shell means the bridge protocol, WebView configuration, and lifecycle behavior are owned entirely by the project.

docs.title: Q18 — WASM Components for Community Integrations
docs.text:
Context: Community integrations currently support two modes: binary (AAR/XCFramework via npm) and source (Kotlin/Swift compiled alongside app). WASM components were evaluated as a third mode enabling OTA-updatable logic integrations without native code.

Decision: Decided — adopt as third mode.

WASM components work for pure-logic capabilities (barcode decoding, PDF, image processing, crypto, compression). They cannot directly call platform APIs — those still require native code. The split: - Logic integrations → WASM component, OTA-updatable via CodeSync, single .wasm binary for both platforms - Platform API integrations → native Kotlin/Swift, store update required

Toolchain responsibilities (@capsule/cli): 

capsule plugin create my-barcode --wasm   # scaffold Rust/C/TS WASM component
capsule plugin build --wasm               # compile to .wasm via wasm-pack / wasi-sdk
capsule plugin publish ./path             # packages .wasm into npm tarball (same flow)

Resolved via D2: WAMR is not embedded in the shell. It ships as the @capsule/wasm first-party plugin. Apps that need WASM capabilities install @capsule/wasm; apps that don't pay zero binary size overhead. The shell strictly contains native OS capabilities only — see D2.

Language support: Rust (best), C/C++, TypeScript via jco. Other languages are community-supported.

docs.title: Q19 — Push Notifications: Firebase SDK Ownership
docs.text:
Context: Q16's rule states "third-party SDK dependency → community integration." Push notifications on Android require FCM, which is implemented via com.google.firebase:firebase-messaging. This creates a conflict: push feels like a core OS capability, but its Android implementation requires a Google-owned third-party SDK.

Decision: Decided — Firebase FCM included in @capsule/core. Capsule team owns the dependency version.

Rationale: FCM is the only practical Android push mechanism. Every major framework (Expo, Capacitor, React Native) includes it. Google will not abandon its own push infrastructure. The risk of including it is manageable; the cost of not including it is mandatory developer boilerplate.

Q16 exception rule: Firebase FCM is a pragmatic exception because it is effectively Android's OS-level push infrastructure despite being distributed as a separate SDK.

iOS: APNs is a pure platform API — no third-party SDK, no exception needed.

Developer configuration in capsule.config.ts: 

android: {
  push: {
    // Path to google-services.json downloaded from Firebase Console
    // CLI injects this into the generated Android project
    googleServicesFile: process.env.GOOGLE_SERVICES_JSON  // e.g. './google-services.json'
  }
}

The google-services.json is app-specific (contains project ID, API key, app ID). It cannot be bundled in the shell — the app developer generates it from the Firebase Console and provides the path. The CLI copies it to .capsule/android/app/google-services.json during capsule sync.

Version conflict risk: Apps that also use Firebase for Firestore/Analytics may encounter Gradle dependency conflicts. Gradle resolves these via "highest compatible version wins," but the Capsule team commits to supporting a range of Firebase BOM versions to reduce friction. If a conflict occurs, android.gradleOverrides is the escape hatch.

docs.title: Q20 — Core Capability Override System
docs.text:
Context: @capsule/core is monolithic — all platform capabilities are compiled into the shell binary. If a bug exists in a core capability (e.g., camera.capture), developers have no path to fix it without: (a) waiting for a Capsule team patch, (b) compiling the entire shell from source, or (c) a full capsule eject-style fork.

Decision: Decided — closed. Runtime dispatch registry with surgical override support.

Shell internals (inside the compiled AAR/XCFramework — fixed at build time): 

object CapsuleBridgeRegistry {
    private val overrides = mutableMapOf<String, CapsuleHandler>()
    private val builtins  = mapOf(
        "camera.capture"           to CapsuleCameraHandler(),
        "camera.getPermission"     to CapsuleCameraPermissionHandler(),
        "gps.getCurrentPosition"   to CapsuleGpsHandler(),
        // ... all core capabilities pre-registered
    )

    fun registerOverride(method: String, handler: CapsuleHandler) {
        overrides[method] = handler   // called at app startup, before any JS runs
    }

    fun dispatch(method: String, params: JsonObject): JsonObject {
        return (overrides[method] ?: builtins[method])
            ?.handle(params) ?: throw CapsuleError(1002, "METHOD_NOT_FOUND")
    }
}

The registry is mutable at runtime. Built-ins are the defaults. Overrides win when present. This is a first-class design requirement — not retrofitted.

Developer workflow:

// capsule.config.ts
plugins: [
  { path: './capsule-plugins/camera-fix', overrides: 'camera' }
]

// capsule-plugins/camera-fix/android/CameraFix.kt
@CapsulePlugin("camera-fix")
class CameraFix(bridge: CapsuleBridge) : CapsuleCoreOverride(bridge) {

    @BridgeMethod("capture")
    suspend fun capture(params: JsonObject): JsonObject {
        // only this method is intercepted — others fall through to built-in
        return super.capture(params).also { result ->
            // patch the broken behavior here
        }
    }
    // getPermission(), getSupportedFormats(), etc. → fall through to built-in automatically
}

At capsule sync, the CLI detects the overrides declaration and generates registration code in the thin .capsule/android/ wrapper: 

// .capsule/android/CapsuleApp.kt (generated — do not edit)
class CapsuleApp : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        CapsuleBridgeRegistry.registerOverride("camera.capture", CameraFix(this))
        CapsuleShell.initialize(this)
    }
}

What compiles: only the developer's fix file — not the shell, not @capsule/core. TypeScript API: unchanged. camera.capture() still works identically from the web layer. Removal: when the official shell patch ships, delete the folder and the plugins entry.

CLI scaffolding: 

capsule override camera
# Creates capsule-plugins/camera-override/ pre-populated with the built-in source
# (fetched from the open-source shell repo at the currently locked shell version)
# Developer deletes all methods they don't need to override.

What capsule override camera generates (the scaffold IS the documentation): 

// capsule-plugins/camera-override/android/CameraOverride.kt
//
// Core capability override for: camera
// Shell version this was generated from: 1.4.2
//
// HOW TO USE:
//   1. Delete every method you do NOT need to change — they fall through to the
//      built-in implementation automatically. Do not leave empty method bodies.
//   2. Use super.capture(params) to call the original built-in from within your fix.
//   3. When the official shell patch ships: delete this file and remove the
//      plugins entry from capsule.config.ts.
//
// The TypeScript API (camera.capture() etc.) is unchanged — this only affects
// the native layer. No web-side changes needed.

@CapsulePlugin("camera-override")
class CameraOverride(bridge: CapsuleBridge) : CapsuleCoreOverride(bridge) {

    // ← EDIT or DELETE: replace with your fix.
    // Returning super.capture(params) calls the original built-in.
    @BridgeMethod("capture")
    suspend fun capture(params: JsonObject): JsonObject {
        return super.capture(params)
    }

    // ← EDIT or DELETE
    @BridgeMethod("getPermission")
    suspend fun getPermission(params: JsonObject): JsonObject {
        return super.getPermission(params)
    }

    // ... all other camera methods pre-populated ...
    // Delete the ones you don't touch — fall-through is automatic
}

Relationship to capsule eject:

capsule override capsule eject Scope Single core capability Entire community integration Use case Bug fix / surgical patch Long-term customization TypeScript API Unchanged Developer-owned Effort One Kotlin/Swift file Full integration authoring Intended lifetime Temporary (remove after patch) Permanent source dependency

docs.title: Q21 — Database API: Raw SQL Bridge vs. Ergonomic Wrapper
docs.text:
Context: SQLite ships natively on both Android (android.database.sqlite) and iOS (libsqlite3.dylib), making it a core OS API that belongs in @capsule/core by Q16's rule. The question is what shape the TypeScript API should take.

Decision: Decided — closed. Two-layer ergonomic API with a db singleton.

Why not expose raw SQL alone: A bridge that only exposes { sql, values } objects forces every app to manage database handles explicitly, write boilerplate open/close logic on every screen, and wrap every call in a verbose options object. Web developers are not SQLite experts — exposing raw SQL as the only surface raises the floor too high.

Layer 1 — db singleton (covers 95% of apps):

The db export is a pre-opened singleton backed by capsule.db. No open() / close() required. The collection() API auto-manages schema — no migration files needed for simple cases. For raw SQL, use the db.sql tagged template with full parameterization.

import { db } from '@capsule/core'

// Zero-SQL CRUD — auto-schema
const notes = db.collection<Note>('notes')
const note  = await notes.add({ title: 'Hello' })
const all   = await notes.getAll()

// Raw SQL when you need joins or aggregates — values always parameterized
const recent = await db.sql<Note[]>`SELECT * FROM notes ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20`

Layer 2 — db.collection() for zero-SQL CRUD:

For tables with simple access patterns, db.collection<T>('name') returns a typed handle with add, get, getAll, where, update, remove. No SQL written. Falls through to db.sql the moment you need joins or complex filters — the two layers compose naturally.

const notes = db.collection<Note>('notes')
const note = await notes.add({ title: 'Hello' })
const all  = await notes.getAll()
const one  = await notes.get(note.id)

database.open() still available for advanced use:

Multi-database apps and encrypted databases use database.open({ name, encrypted, encryptionKey }), which returns a DatabaseHandle with the same all/first/run/transaction/schema methods. This is the escape hatch — not the default path.

preferences for key-value storage:

The preferences capability (SharedPreferences / UserDefaults) is a separate export for lightweight persistent flags, tokens, and settings. It is not SQLite — it has no query capability and is not a substitute for db.

Rationale: The layered design follows the same principle as @capsule/core overall — zero-config default that works for the common case, with explicit escape hatches for advanced needs. A developer who only needs to store a list of items should never need to know what SQLite is.

Rejected alternatives: - Raw SQL bridge only — Too verbose for simple use cases. Every app writes the same open/close/schema boilerplate. - ORM bundled in the shell — Shell binary size penalty for apps that don't use complex queries. Opinionated schema definition conflicts with code-first and migration-first approaches. Community ORMs (Drizzle, Kysely) can target the db bridge natively. - IndexedDB / localStorage on web layer only — No cross-platform backup, limited query capability, size-constrained by the OS WebView storage quota. Not reliable for production app data.

docs.title: Q22 — AI / LLM Inference & Agents: Ownership and Shape
docs.text:
Context: Every platform is being asked for AI. Q16's rule (OS API → @capsule/core) plus the fact that the OS-native on-device models (Apple Foundation Models, Gemini Nano) only cover recent flagships raises the question of what an ai capability should be, and whether Capsule should also expose agents.

Decision: Proposed — see adr-003 for the full record. Summary:

  • ai is a core capability (@capsule/core, opt-in + tree-shaken per Q16), exposed as an ai singleton via the standard interface → provider → Fake → handler pattern, with a provider behind it like geolocation/camera.
  • Three tiers, one TS surface, hybrid by default: Tier 1 OS-native (flagship-only checkbox) · Tier 2 bundled engine (Cactus primary, llama.cpp escape hatch — universal, offline) · Tier 3 cloud (the Phase-5 billing meter). ai.availability() reports the honest tier.
  • Agents = @capsule/core/agent — a thin layer where the native bridge methods are the tool surface (every Phase-3 API is a free agent tool), the loop runs in QuickJS (inference is a bridge call, never in QuickJS), and agent definitions are OTA-updatable via Server Code Push. We do not build a LangChain-style framework; tool protocol likely MCP.
  • Constraints (inherit the Phase-3 OTA rules): models persist outside the OTA bundle dirs; ai carries a native-capability version for OTA gating; a per-tool permission model for agent tools.
  • Phasing: Tier-1 ai spike in late Phase 3; iOS Tier-1 in Phase 4; Tier 2/3 + agent layer + OTA-updatable agent logic in Phase 6. Gates before Tier 2+: confirm Cactus license + .cact longevity (keep the GGUF/llama.cpp escape hatch), MCP-vs-custom tool protocol, tool-permission UX, model-distribution + default tier-escalation policy.

docs.title: Part 2 — Implementation Decisions
docs.text: Decisions that must be made before the relevant phase starts. Ordered by urgency.

docs.title: D1: APK debug keystore for capsule build android --release
docs.text:
Context: Phase 1 uses a debug keystore for --release builds (real signing lands with publishing in Phase 8+; Fastlane automation in Phase 9 DX). Needs a clear behavior when no keystore is configured.

Options: - A — Delegate to Gradle — Let Gradle use its own auto-generated debug keystore (~/.android/debug.keystore). Zero CLI code. Familiar to Android devs. Capsule just runs ./gradlew assembleRelease without injecting signing config. (Recommended — aligns with "shell is a dependency" philosophy: native tooling handles native things) - B — Auto-generate at ~/.capsule/debug.keystore — CLI generates a debug keystore once on first build if none found. Capsule-managed, consistent path, no dependency on Android Studio having run first. - C — Require explicit config — Developer must add android.signing block in capsule.config.ts. Fails with a clear error if missing. Most explicit, most friction for first build.

Needed before: Implementing capsule build android --release (Step 3.7).

Status: ✅ DECIDED — Option A (Delegate to Gradle) Gradle auto-manages ~/.android/debug.keystore. CLI runs ./gradlew assembleRelease without injecting signing config. No CLI keystore code in Phase 1.

docs.title: D2: WASM runtime (WAMR) — always embedded vs. on-demand
docs.text:
Context: WAMR (~500KB native binary) enables WASM integrations (Q18 above). If always embedded, every app pays the size penalty even if unused.

Options: - A — Always embedded — WAMR is compiled into the AAR for all shells. Simple, one shell variant, no conditional compilation. All apps pay ~500KB regardless. - B — On-demand via config flag — Shell is built with WAMR only when capsule.config.ts declares wasm: { enabled: true }. CLI downloads the correct AAR variant. Two AAR variants exist in the registry (standard, wasm). (Recommended — aligns with tree-shaking philosophy) - C — Separate plugin — WASM runtime ships as a first-party plugin @capsule/wasm that adds WAMR to the build. Developer installs only if needed. Cleanest API surface, but adds complexity to the plugin system before it matures.

Needed before: Building the shell registry and the second AAR publish (Phase 2).

Status: ✅ DECIDED — Option C (@capsule/wasm first-party plugin) WASM runtime (WAMR) ships as @capsule/wasm, not in the shell. Aligns with the core architectural principle: shell = native OS capabilities only; code-logic integrations = plugins. Community WASM plugin authors declare @capsule/wasm as a peer dependency.

docs.title: D3: Plugin override — fallthrough semantics for partial overrides
docs.text:
Context: capsule override camera scaffolds a patch class. If the override only implements some methods, what happens to unimplemented ones?

Options: - A — Silent fallthrough — Unimplemented methods in the override delegate automatically to the built-in handler. No error. Developer gets partial patch behavior by default. (Recommended — lowest friction, least surprising) - B — Explicit delegation required — Override must call super.methodName(call) to delegate. Unimplemented methods → error 1002 METHOD_NOT_FOUND. Explicit, but breaks anything not consciously delegated. - C — Runtime warning + fallthrough — Silently falls through (like A) but logs a warning in debug mode: [Capsule] Override for camera.capture not found — falling back to built-in. Best of both worlds for discoverability.

Needed before: Implementing capsule override CLI command and the registry dispatch system.

Status: ✅ DECIDED — Option A (silent fallthrough) + full scaffold capsule override <capability> scaffolds a class with ALL capability methods listed (so developer sees the full surface and TypeScript enforces signatures). Developer deletes methods they don't want to touch — deleted methods fall through to the built-in at runtime silently. Methods kept in the class run as the override. No runtime warnings.

docs.title: D4: Encrypted database — key management model
docs.text:
Context: The db API (../reference/core-api.md) supports encryption, but key derivation, storage, and rotation are unspecified. This is a security contract that cannot be retrofitted after apps ship.

Options: - A — Developer-supplied key — Developer provides the key explicitly: database.open('secure.db', { key: derivedKey }). Capsule stores nothing. Developer is responsible for key derivation and secure storage (e.g., using the biometrics API). (Recommended — most flexible, no opinion on key derivation) - B — Capsule-managed key via secure storage — CLI generates a per-app key stored in Android Keystore / iOS Secure Enclave. Transparent to developer. db is encrypted by default with zero config. No rotation support without a migration. - C — Two-tier — db (unencrypted, default) + database.open('path', { key }) (developer-supplied key for sensitive data). Q21 already implies this split — just needs the key contract documented explicitly.

Needed before: Implementing the database capability in Phase 3.

Status: ✅ DECIDED — Combined A+B API + Option C for encryption

db exposes two complementary APIs on the same SQLite engine: - db.collection<T>() — zero-SQL CRUD with query builder + sync hooks (changesSince / applyChanges). Auto-manages table schema. No migrations needed for simple cases. - db.sql tagged template literal — full SQLite access for joins, aggregates, DDL. Values always parameterized (no injection risk). Collection tables and raw SQL tables share the same database file. - db.schema() — manual migrations only for raw SQL managed tables. - db.transaction() — atomic operations spanning both APIs.

database.open(name, { key }) = encrypted named database via SQLCipher. Same combined API. Developer supplies the key (Capsule never derives or stores it). Key typically retrieved via biometrics or secure preferences API.

See ../reference/core-api.md § db (planned additions) for the full TypeScript interface.

docs.title: D5: Differential update algorithm
docs.text:
Context: The roadmap mentions "80% size reduction via delta bundles" but the algorithm is unspecified. The CodeSync server architecture depends on this choice.

Options: - A — bsdiff/bspatch — Binary diff at the bundle level. Industry standard (Chrome, Android OTA). ~80% reduction for incremental web changes. Mature implementations exist. Server generates the diff; client applies it. Complexity: medium (server must store previous bundle to diff against). - B — File-level content-addressed storage — Bundle is a ZIP. Server only transfers files with changed hashes. Simple to implement, no diff algorithm. Works well for many small changed files. Less effective for large minified bundles with small logical changes. - C — No differential (Phase 6 MVP) — Full bundle always. Decide delta strategy in Phase 6 after measuring real bundle sizes. Don't over-engineer before data exists. (Pragmatic choice for the initial OTA cloud)

Needed before: Designing the CodeSync server storage model (Phase 6).

Status: ✅ DECIDED — Option B (file-level, content-addressed) CodeSync is a service pack / hotfix mechanism — not a full app update channel. A typical hotfix changes 1–3 Vite output chunks out of a 2MB bundle. Vite's content-hashed output (e.g. chunk-abc123.js) means unchanged files have identical hashes. Server stores all bundle files by content hash. Devices request only files they don't already have. In practice this transfers 10–50KB for a hotfix instead of 2MB. bsdiff (A) offers marginal additional gains (~5–10KB) at major complexity cost — not justified for this use case.

docs.title: D6: Safe area insets — timing contract
docs.text:
Context: Q6 above specifies that the shell injects --sai-* CSS custom properties. The timing relative to WebView loading is not defined. App CSS that reads --sai-* before injection = wrong layout on first paint.

Options: - A — Inject before navigation — Shell writes --sai-* via a <style> tag injected into the WebView configuration before the URL loads. Guaranteed available before any app CSS runs. Zero race condition. - B — Inject via evaluateJavascript + capsule.ready() promise — Shell fires the injection after onPageFinished. @capsule/core exposes capsule.ready() that resolves after insets are set. App code awaits capsule.ready() before reading --sai-*. Explicit contract. - C — Both — Inject known safe defaults (0px) before navigation, then update to real values after onPageFinished. No race condition, no capsule.ready() needed. First paint uses 0px; correct values arrive before any user interaction.

Needed before: Implementing safe area support in the shell (Phase 3 shell; iOS in Phase 4).

Status: ⬜ Undecided

docs.title: Part 3 — Embedded Runtime Decisions
docs.text:
These were decided together in 0001-embedded-runtime.md, which is the authoritative source — read it there. (This section previously restated those decisions inline as R1–R14; removed to avoid drift per ../_core/conventions.md.)

adr-001 covers: embedded server as router/SSR (not static serving) · /capsule vs /api namespace split · TypeScript + QuickJS route language · HTTP = data, bridge = events · the QuickJSBridge (4th Bridge impl) · splash + timeout readiness · deterministic port hash from appId · two-process / one-command dev mode · file-based routing · server is optional · two bundles deployed atomically · invisible infrastructure · the CapsuleRuntime coordinator · interfaces + fakes as a mandatory pattern.

docs.title: AI (ai) — Implementation
docs.text:
Phase 3 spike + Phase 4 interface of adr-003. Status: built 2026-10-24. Android Tier 1 runs on Gemini Nano (ML Kit GenAI Prompt API, beta); iOS has the same contract with an Apple Foundation Models provider that still needs a macOS build to verify. Tiers 2 (bundled model) and 3 (cloud) and the agent layer are Phase 6 — not built here.

The device-coverage cliff, loudly: Tier 1 exists only on flagships with an OS model — Pixel 8+ / Galaxy S24+ with AICore, iPhone 15 Pro+ / 16+ / M1+ with Apple Intelligence. On every other device ai.availability() answers unavailable, and generate/stream reject with AI_UNAVAILABLE. Apps must check availability before offering an AI feature. Universal coverage arrives with Tiers 2/3.

docs.title: 1. TypeScript surface — core/src/ai.ts
docs.text:
import { ai } from '@capsule/core'

const a = await ai.availability()   // { tier, status, reason? }
if (a.status === 'downloadable' || a.status === 'downloading') await ai.prepare()

const { text, finishReason } = await ai.generate({ prompt: 'Summarise this note', maxTokens: 256 })

for await (const piece of ai.stream({ prompt })) output.textContent += piece
Field Values tier os-native · bundled · cloud · unavailable status ready · downloadable (call prepare()) · downloading · unavailable reason Why it is not ready — e.g. "os-native: Gemini Nano (AICore) is not available on this device; bundled: …" finishReason stop · length (maxTokens hit) · other

Deviation from adr-003's sketch: availability() returns an object, not the bare tier string — status is needed for the OS model's download step, and reason makes "unavailable" actionable.

docs.title: Bridge methods
docs.text:
Method Params Result ai.availability — AiAvailability ai.prepare — AiAvailability after downloading the model (Android; iOS downloads on its own) ai.generate { prompt, maxTokens?, temperature? } { text, finishReason } ai.stream { prompt, maxTokens?, temperature?, streamId } { text, finishReason }, after pushing every piece as an ai.streamChunk notification { streamId, text }

stream() is real token streaming (the model's own stream, not a split string). AiModule generates the streamId, subscribes to ai.streamChunk before calling, and ends the async generator when the final response arrives. Breaking out of for await stops listening; the device still finishes the reply.

Errors: AI_UNAVAILABLE (7001, reason in data), AI_GENERATION_FAILED (7002).

Browser fallback (WebBridge): honest unavailable with a reason; generate/stream reject with AI_UNAVAILABLE. No fake "echo" replies — browser dev exercises the path most devices take.

docs.title: 2. Native design (Android dev.capsule.ai, iOS Sources/dev/capsule/ai)
docs.text:
Piece Role AiProvider One backend: availability(), prepare(), generate(), stream(onChunk) TieredAiProvider Preference order is the policy (on-device first, cloud last). First ready provider serves; otherwise the most promising (downloadable/downloading beats unavailable) is reported and prepared UnavailableAiProvider A tier this build lacks — Tiers 2/3 today — with the reason AndroidGeminiNanoProvider Tier 1 — com.google.mlkit:genai-prompt (see §3) AppleFoundationModelsProvider Tier 1 iOS 26+ — #if canImport(FoundationModels), unverified until built on macOS AiHandlers.kt ai.availability / ai.prepare / ai.generate / ai.stream (emits via BridgeEventEmitter) FakeAiProvider (Kotlin + Swift) Scripted availability + reply chunks; records requests

Capability: ai = version 1 in CapabilityRegistry (OTA gating). Tier-1 models belong to the OS, so nothing is persisted; Tier-2 model files must live outside the OTA bundle dirs (adr-003 §3).

iOS has no bridge registry yet (Phase 4): TieredAiProvider.standard() is ready for CapsuleBridge.

docs.title: 3. Tier 1 on Android — ML Kit GenAI Prompt API
docs.text:
• Artifact: com.google.mlkit:genai-prompt:1.0.0-beta4 (2026-07-21, built against the Kotlin 2.3 stdlib — needs a Kotlin ≥ 2.3 compiler; ours is 2.4). Docs: https://developers.google.com/ml-kit/genai/prompt/android/get-started. minSdk 26 (matches ours).
  • Moved up from beta2 at the 2026-10-24 upkeep sweep. The surface used here — Builder(TextPart), maxOutputTokens, temperature, checkStatus(), download(), generateContent/generateContentStream — is unchanged between the two AARs (javap diff); beta4 only adds (system instructions, multi-part Content, typed output, thinking mode).
  • Mapping: checkStatus() AVAILABLE/DOWNLOADABLE/DOWNLOADING/UNAVAILABLE → ready/downloadable/ downloading/unavailable; download() flow → prepare(); generateContent / generateContentStream (each streamed response carries the next piece) → generate / stream; FinishReason.MAX_TOKENS → length.
  • First use on a freshly set-up device can fail while AICore initialises — the error surfaces as AI_GENERATION_FAILED; retrying later works.

docs.title: 4. Not in this build (Phase 6, per adr-003)
docs.text:
• Tier 2 (Cactus / llama.cpp, model download outside bundle dirs) and Tier 3 (OTA-cloud inference, billing meter) — modelled as UnavailableAiProviders so availability() explains them.
  • Agent layer (defineAgent, tool registry, tool-permission model, MCP decision). The earlier core/src/agent.ts draft was removed: adr-003 places it in Phase 6 and it had no tested loop behind it.
  • A capsule.config.ts tier preference — the order is fixed in the shell until Tier 2/3 exist.

docs.title: 5. Tests
docs.text: Tier Where JS (vitest) core/src/__tests__/ai.test.ts — module calls, streaming (order, errors, early break, distinct ids), WebBridge fallback Kotlin (pure JVM) test/.../ai/TieredAiProviderTest.kt, test/.../handlers/ai/AiHandlersTest.kt Swift (Linux Docker) Tests/CapsuleTests/ai/TieredAiProviderTests.swift On device androidTest/.../ai/AndroidGeminiNanoProviderTest.kt — availability contract everywhere; generation + streaming only where Gemini Nano is ready (structure, never exact text)

docs.title: Alert Styling
docs.text:
alerts.show() accepts an optional style object that controls the visual appearance of the native dialog. Every property maps to a specific, tested native API — this is not a CSS layer. Properties not listed in AlertStyle are not supported on any platform and are intentionally absent.

import { alerts } from '@capsule/core'
import type { AlertStyle } from '@capsule/core'

await alerts.show({
  title: 'Confirm',
  message: 'Do you want to continue?',
  buttons: [
    { label: 'Cancel', role: 'cancel' },
    { label: 'Continue', role: 'default' },
  ],
  style: {
    accentColor: '#0A84FF',
    backgroundColor: '#1C1C1E',
    titleColor: '#FFFFFF',
    messageColor: '#EBEBF5',
    titleSize: 17,
    messageSize: 14,
    cornerRadius: 16,
    buttonAllCaps: false,
    dimAmount: 0.8,
  },
})

docs.title: Supported properties
docs.text:
Property Type Android iOS accentColor string (hex) button text color tintColor backgroundColor string (hex) window background not supported titleColor string (hex) title TextView color NSAttributedString messageColor string (hex) message TextView color NSAttributedString titleSize number (sp / pt) setTextSize(SP) NSAttributedString font messageSize number (sp / pt) setTextSize(SP) NSAttributedString font buttonAllCaps boolean Button.isAllCaps ignored (iOS is always mixed-case) cornerRadius number (dp / pt) GradientDrawable.cornerRadius not supported dimAmount number (0.0 – 1.0) Window.setDimAmount() not supported

Properties marked not supported are silently ignored — they do not throw, but they have no visual effect on that platform.

Colors accept #RGB, #RRGGBB, or #AARRGGBB (alpha-first). Sizes are in sp on Android and pt on iOS. Lengths (cornerRadius) are in dp on Android and pt on iOS.

docs.title: Style presets pattern
docs.text:
Capsule intentionally ships no built-in presets — the framework is unopinionated about your app's visual language. The recommended pattern is to define your own preset map, keyed to your design tokens, and reuse it across calls:

// lib/alert-styles.ts
import type { AlertStyle } from '@capsule/core'

export const alertStyles = {
  dark: {
    backgroundColor: '#1C1C1E',
    titleColor: '#FFFFFF',
    messageColor: '#EBEBF5',
    accentColor: '#0A84FF',
    cornerRadius: 16,
    buttonAllCaps: false,
    dimAmount: 0.8,
  },
  danger: {
    accentColor: '#FF3B30',
    titleColor: '#FF3B30',
  },
  branded: {
    accentColor: '#34C759',
    cornerRadius: 20,
    buttonAllCaps: false,
  },
} satisfies Record<string, AlertStyle>

// anywhere in your app
import { alerts } from '@capsule/core'
import { alertStyles } from './lib/alert-styles'

await alerts.show({
  title: 'Delete',
  message: 'This cannot be undone.',
  buttons: [
    { label: 'Cancel', role: 'cancel' },
    { label: 'Delete', role: 'destructive' },
  ],
  style: alertStyles.danger,
})

You can also spread a preset and override individual properties per call:

style: { ...alertStyles.dark, accentColor: '#FF9500' }

docs.title: What is not supported
docs.text:
The following are intentionally absent from AlertStyle. They cannot be implemented via the native AlertDialog / UIAlertController APIs without replacing the dialog with a fully custom view:
