  • Per-button colors (all buttons share accentColor)
  • Custom fonts / typefaces
  • Button background colors or shapes
  • Dialog width or height
  • Entry / exit animations
  • Custom layout or additional views (icons, images, inputs)

If you need any of these, the escape hatch is to implement a custom AlertsProvider on the native side while keeping the same TypeScript API.

docs.title: Database (db) — SQLite
docs.text: Status: implemented — Android (AndroidDbProvider) + iOS provider (SqliteDbProvider, bridge wiring lands with the iOS bring-up) + @capsule/core db. Capability db, version 1. Design source: the db section of core-api.md. This page records what shipped and where it deliberately differs.

docs.title: What shipped
docs.text:
import { db } from '@capsule/core'

// Migrations for the tables you manage — run in order, each in its own transaction,
// before the next database operation. Never edit a version that has shipped.
db.schema(1, async (tx) => {
  await tx.sql`CREATE TABLE notes (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL, ts INTEGER)`
})

// Reads resolve to rows…
const recent = await db.sql<{ id: number; title: string }[]>`
  SELECT id, title FROM notes WHERE ts > ${Date.now() - 86_400_000} ORDER BY ts DESC
`

// …statements without columns to { rowsAffected, insertId? }
const { insertId } = await db.sql<{ rowsAffected: number; insertId?: number }>`
  INSERT INTO notes (title, ts) VALUES (${'Hello'}, ${Date.now()})
`

// Atomic: committed when the callback resolves, rolled back when it throws.
await db.transaction(async (tx) => {
  await tx.sql`UPDATE notes SET title = ${'Renamed'} WHERE id = ${insertId!}`
  await tx.sql`DELETE FROM notes WHERE ts < ${0}`
})
Piece Contract db.sql Tagged template. Each ${value} becomes a ? bound parameter — values are never spliced into SQL text. One statement per call (anything after the first is ignored). Resolves to rows when the statement returns columns (SELECT, PRAGMA, RETURNING), else { rowsAffected, insertId? }. Values in null, number, string, boolean (stored 1/0), Uint8Array / ArrayBuffer (BLOB). Anything else (undefined, NaN, Date, bigint, objects) rejects with a TypeError naming the parameter. Values out null, number, string, Uint8Array (BLOB). Integers beyond 2^53 lose precision in JS. Alias duplicate column names (a.id AS aId) — rows are objects. rowsAffected / insertId Rows inserted/updated/deleted by the statement, including by triggers (0 for DDL). insertId is the rowid of the last row the statement inserted; absent if it inserted none. db.transaction(fn) BEGIN IMMEDIATE … COMMIT, or ROLLBACK + rethrow. Resolves to fn's result. db.schema(version, fn) Version kept in PRAGMA user_version. A database newer than every registered version fails all operations with SCHEMA_VERSION_REGRESSION (e.g. an OTA rollback to an older bundle — ship a migration-compatible bundle instead).

One thing at a time. The database has one connection and runs one operation at a time. While a transaction is open, other db.sql / db.transaction calls wait for it — so inside the callback use tx.sql. Awaiting db.sql or a nested db.transaction there waits for the transaction it is part of: a deterministic hang you will see the first time the code runs.

Storage. One database per app — Android databases/capsule.db, iOS Application Support/Capsule/capsule.db — outside the OTA bundle dirs, so a code push never touches it. Not available in the browser fallback (METHOD_NOT_FOUND).

Errors. SQL_ERROR (8001; SQLite's message in error.data), SCHEMA_VERSION_REGRESSION (8002). 021's draft numbers (3010–3012, 4010) sat inside the location and media ranges.

docs.title: Deferred from the 021 design
docs.text:
• db.collection<T>() — zero-SQL CRUD with an auto-managed table and query builder.
  • Encrypted database.open(name, { key }) — needs SQLCipher on both platforms; also brings DATABASE_NOT_OPEN and ENCRYPTION_ERROR.
  • Collection sync helpers (changesSince / applyChanges).

All three build on the shipped db.sql + transaction primitives without changing them.

docs.title: Native side
docs.text:
Bridge methods: db.sql ({ sql, params }), db.begin, db.commit, db.rollback. Wire values are JSON null / number / string, or { "$blob": "<base64>" }. The JS module serialises every operation, so the native providers need no transaction ids; db.begin first rolls back a transaction left open by a JS context that died mid-way (page reload).

Android iOS Provider dev.capsule.db.AndroidDbProvider over SQLiteDatabase SqliteDbProvider over the SQLite3 C API Threading One dedicated thread — SQLiteDatabase binds a transaction to its thread, and a Capsule transaction spans several bridge calls. Process-wide, survives Activity recreation. One connection behind a lock Typed binds Cursor factory binds on the SQLiteQuery (rawQuery would bind every value as text) sqlite3_bind_* Handlers dev.capsule.handlers.db.dbHandlers(provider) DbHandler (JSON in / out) Tests DbHandlerTest (JVM, fake), AndroidDbProviderTest (device) DbHandlerTests (Linux, fake), SqliteDbProviderTests (real SQLite)

docs.title: Hello World Example
docs.text: Here is the minimal code you need to display “Hello, World!” in a Capsule app.

docs.title: src/App.tsx
docs.text:
import { CapsuleText } from '@capsule/core';

export default function App() {
  return (
    <CapsuleText center>
      Hello, World!
    </CapsuleText>
  );
}

docs.title: Running the example
docs.text:
1. Follow the quick start steps to create a new app.
  2. Replace the generated src/App.tsx with the code above.
  3. Run pnpm dev and pnpm dev:android (or pnpm dev:ios when iOS support is ready).
  4. You should see a centered “Hello, World!” text on the screen.

Feel free to experiment with other components from @capsule/core such as CapsuleButton, CapsuleImage, etc.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: To get started with Capsule Framework, follow these steps:

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Node.js (>= 22.12)
  • pnpm (>= 8.x)
  • Java Development Kit (JDK) 17 (for Android builds)
  • Android Studio (including SDK and emulator) or Xcode (for iOS, when available)
  • Git

docs.title: Clone the repository
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/your-org/capsule-framework.git
cd capsule-framework

docs.title: Install dependencies
docs.text: pnpm install

docs.title: Set up environment
docs.text:
Machine paths (JDK, Android SDK, emulator) live in a git-ignored .env.local at the repo root — the same on Windows, macOS and Linux:

cp .env.example .env.local   # then set JAVA_HOME, ANDROID_HOME, AVD_NAME, …
pnpm dev:env                 # print the resolved environment

docs.title: Verify the setup
docs.text:
pnpm run version   # should print the current version

You are now ready to develop with Capsule Framework.

docs.title: Mobile CSS Reset
docs.text: A ~150-byte CSS reset injected automatically into every built app's index.html, so Capsule apps feel like native apps by default — no developer action required.

docs.title: What it fixes
docs.text: Property Effect box-sizing: border-box Consistent element sizing across browsers (padding/border included in width) -webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent Removes the blue/gray tap flash on touch devices touch-action: manipulation Disables double-tap zoom delay; keeps pinch-zoom overscroll-behavior: none Prevents rubber-band/bounce at scroll boundaries

docs.title: The shipped reset
docs.text:
Injected as a single <style data-capsule-reset> block before </head>:

*, *::before, *::after {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}
* {
  -webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent;
}
html {
  touch-action: manipulation;
  overscroll-behavior: none;
}

docs.title: How it's applied
docs.text:
During capsule build, after the web bundle is produced, the CLI injects the reset into dist/index.html (before it is copied to assets/www/). The injection:

  • is skipped when no dist/index.html exists;
  • is skipped when the reset is disabled (see below);
  • goes before </head>; without a </head>, before </body>; without either, at the end;
  • is idempotent — the data-capsule-reset marker is checked first, so running the step again over the same file (a rebuild reusing dist/) never injects a second copy. The same marker lets downstream tooling find or strip it.

docs.title: Opt-out
docs.text:
Set web.mobileReset: false in capsule.config.ts:

export default {
  // …
  web: {
    mobileReset: false,
  },
}

docs.title: What it intentionally does not do
docs.text:
The reset is deliberately minimal. It does not:

  • zero margin/padding (use Tailwind preflight — capsule init --css tailwind wires it up);
  • disable focus outlines (style :focus-visible in your own CSS for accessibility);
  • block image drag or text selection (app-specific concern).

Component styling (radius, spacing, typography presets) is Capsule UI territory — the ui-kit class builders, which take a preset (ios | material) per call; see capsule add-ui in cli.md.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
Internal to the CLI — packages/cli/src/mobile-css-reset.ts, not part of the @capsule/core runtime API (the build runs in Node, the runtime in the WebView):

Function Purpose getMobileResetCss() The raw reset CSS string hasMobileReset(config) Whether the reset is enabled for a given config (default: true) applyMobileReset(html, config) Injects the <style data-capsule-reset> block into an HTML string (no-op if disabled or already present)

capsule build calls applyMobileReset; tests: packages/cli/src/__tests__/mobile-css-reset.test.ts.

docs.title: Over-the-air updates (CodeSync)
docs.text:
Ship web-layer fixes to installed apps without a store review. This page is the how-to for app developers. The protocol, server and on-device internals are in codesync-internals.md.

CodeSync replaces the web bundle an installed app runs: everything in www/ (HTML, JS, CSS, assets) plus the QuickJS route bundle server/bundle.js. Both always travel together as one ZIP, so the client and its /api routes can never drift apart.

Anything native needs a store release instead: the Capsule shell version, permissions, plugins, native SDK changes. See publishing.md for the two release layers, and ota-policy-and-liability.md for what the stores allow you to change over the air.

docs.title: Status: what works today
docs.text:
CodeSync is being built in pieces. Each piece below exists and is tested on its own, but an update does not reach a device end to end yet. The gaps are listed in codesync-internals.md § Known gaps.

Piece State codeSync block in capsule.config.ts Built. enabled, url and apiKey are read by capsule codesync publish; the other fields are typed but not read yet. capsule codesync publish Built: builds, zips and uploads one bundle. Self-hosted server @capsule/codesync-api Built: a file-based server for one app (publish, channels, rollback, pause). On-device client (Android) Built and unit-tested: check, rollout, download, SHA-256 check, atomic install. Not switched on in apps that capsule sync generates. On-device client (iOS) Client core built and tested on Linux; not wired into the iOS bridge yet. Automatic crash-loop rollback Built (Android). codesync JS module Built: checkForUpdate(), getStatus(), applyUpdate(). Hosted service (Capsule Cloud), dashboard, staged rollouts from the CLI, targeting, mandatory updates, differential updates Planned (Phase 6).

docs.title: 1. Pick a server
docs.text:
You need a CodeSync server the app can reach and the CLI can publish to.

  • Self-host: run @capsule/codesync-api from this repo (licensed AGPL-3.0). It stores bundles on local disk, so one small instance is enough for development and small fleets.
  • Hosted: a managed Capsule Cloud service is planned (Phase 6). The server is open source, so you can always run your own instead.

Run the self-hosted server locally:

pnpm --filter @capsule/codesync-api run build
CODESYNC_API_KEY=dev-local pnpm --filter @capsule/codesync-api run start   # listens on :3000

On Windows PowerShell set the key first: $env:CODESYNC_API_KEY='dev-local'. Bundles and the release manifest land in packages/codesync-api/storage/, or in CODESYNC_STORAGE_DIR when set.

docs.title: 2. Configure the app
docs.text:
Add a codeSync block to capsule.config.ts:

export default {
  appId: 'com.example.myapp',
  appName: 'My App',
  version: { name: '1.0.1', buildNumber: 2 },

  codeSync: {
    enabled: true,
    url: process.env.CODESYNC_URL,         // e.g. http://localhost:3000 or your own server
    apiKey: process.env.CODESYNC_API_KEY,  // publish-time only, never shipped in the app
  },
}

Keep the key out of git. Put it in .env.local (already in the template's .gitignore) or in your CI secrets:

# .env.local
CODESYNC_URL=http://localhost:3000
CODESYNC_API_KEY=dev-local

The API key is used only by the CLI when you publish. It is never compiled into the app: devices read updates without a key.

Every field, with its type: config reference (codeSync.*). channel, strategy, checkOnForeground and mandatory are accepted today but have no effect yet. They are reserved for the update strategies described under Mandatory updates and strategies.

docs.title: 3. Publish an update
docs.text:
capsule codesync publish --channel staging --notes "Fix checkout button"

The command:

  1. builds the web app (vite build, or your web.buildCommand);
  2. bundles the QuickJS routes into server/bundle.js when src/server/routes/ exists;
  3. writes a capsule-bundle.json manifest from version.name and version.buildNumber;
  4. zips www/, server/ and the manifest, and uploads the ZIP to the server.

Bump the version before every publish. The server keeps one bundle per version.name and rejects a name it already has (HTTP 409). Raise version.buildNumber too: devices only install a bundle whose build number is higher than the one they run.

All flags: CLI reference (capsule codesync publish).

docs.title: 4. Use channels
docs.text:
A channel is a named release line, such as production or staging. Each publish goes to one channel (--channel, default production), and the server tracks the latest bundle per channel.

A typical flow is to publish to staging, test on internal builds that follow staging, then publish the same version to production. A one-step capsule codesync promote is planned.

docs.title: 5. Roll back or pause
docs.text:
Automatic. If the app fails to start three times within 60 seconds after an update, the shell restores the previous bundle on the next launch. A launch counts as healthy once the WebView finishes loading the page, so your code needs no extra call. You never write rollback logic.

Manual. The self-hosted server rolls a channel back to its previous release, or pauses it. There is no CLI command for this yet, so call the server directly:

curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/rollback -H "x-api-key: $CODESYNC_API_KEY" \
     -H "content-type: application/json" -d '{"channel":"production"}'
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/pause    -H "x-api-key: $CODESYNC_API_KEY" \
     -H "content-type: application/json" -d '{"channel":"production"}'
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/resume   -H "x-api-key: $CODESYNC_API_KEY" \
     -H "content-type: application/json" -d '{"channel":"production"}'

GET /releases?channel=production lists what was published. The full endpoint list is in codesync-internals.md § Self-hosted server.

docs.title: 6. Check for updates from app code
docs.text:
The shell checks on its own. Use the codesync module when you want your UI to react:

import { codesync } from '@capsule/core'

const update = await codesync.checkForUpdate()   // CodeSyncUpdate | null
if (update) {
  console.log(`Version ${update.version} (build ${update.buildNumber}) is ready`)
  await codesync.applyUpdate()                   // takes effect on the next resume
}

const status = await codesync.getStatus()        // 'idle' | 'checking' | 'downloading' | …

The methods exist only when the shell was built with CodeSync enabled. Otherwise, and in the browser during development, the call fails with METHOD_NOT_FOUND (1002). Types: core API reference.

docs.title: Mandatory updates and strategies
docs.text:
Planned. These options are defined in the config type but not implemented yet:

Option Planned behaviour strategy: 'background' Download silently, apply on the next resume. strategy: 'immediate' Prompt the user and reload now. strategy: 'on-next-launch' Apply on the next cold start only. checkOnForeground Check every time the app returns to the foreground. mandatory Treat updates as required unless a bundle says otherwise.

The device already receives a per-bundle mandatory flag and rollout percentage from the check response (see codesync-internals.md), so these options build on data that is already on the wire.

docs.title: Self-hosting or hosted: what changes
docs.text:
Self-hosted @capsule/codesync-api Capsule Cloud (planned) Runs on Your machine or server, one process Managed service Storage Local disk (storage/) Object storage and CDN Access One shared API key (CODESYNC_API_KEY) Per-organization keys from the portal Rollouts, targeting, dashboard Not available Planned License AGPL-3.0 Service terms

The portal and cloud control-plane design is in server-design/overview.md.

docs.title: Capsule Framework — Community Integration System (Deep Technical Reference)
docs.text: How community integrations (third-party SDK wrappers) work at every layer: bridge wire protocol, native dispatch, code generation, threading, language feasibility, and what already exists to reuse.

docs.title: Scope: Community Integrations vs. Core SDK
docs.text:
Core platform capabilities (camera, GPS, push, NFC, Bluetooth, haptics, biometrics, filesystem, barcode, etc.) are built into @capsule/core. They are not plugins — they ship with the framework and are tree-shaken if unused. Developers import them directly, no installation required.

Community integrations are what this document covers: third-party SDK wrappers (@capsule-community/google-maps, @capsule-community/stripe, etc.) and custom local integrations that require SDKs the Capsule team does not own or control.

The same bridge protocol, dispatch system, and language support documented here applies to both layers. The distinction is ownership and distribution, not technical architecture.

docs.title: Two Integration Modes
docs.text:
Mode 1 — Binary (npm)                    Mode 2 — Source (inline)
──────────────────────────────────────   ──────────────────────────────────────
npm install @capsule-community/maps      capsule-plugins/
                                           my-integration/
Pre-compiled AAR + XCFramework             android/MyIntegration.kt
Distributed via npm + Maven/SPM            ios/MyIntegration.swift
No modification                            web/index.ts
                                           image-processor/
                                             android/proc.c    ← NDK
                                             game-logic.lua    ← scripting VM

Both modes register through the same JSON-RPC 2.0 bridge. From the web layer they are identical.

docs.title: Part 1 — The Bridge: How JS Calls Reach Native Code
docs.text: This is the core mechanism everything else builds on. Understanding it precisely is required before designing plugins.

docs.title: Android: addJavascriptInterface vs addWebMessageListener
docs.text:
Option A — addJavascriptInterface (API 1+, minSdk 26 safe)

// CapsuleBridge.kt
// Name "__capsule_host" to avoid colliding with the JS-side runtime object "__capsule"
webView.addJavascriptInterface(BridgeHost(this), "__capsule_host")

class BridgeHost(private val bridge: CapsuleBridge) {
    @JavascriptInterface                // required annotation — exposes method to JS
    fun postMessage(json: String) {
        bridge.handleCall(json)         // runs on a WebView background thread, NOT main thread
    }
}

JavaScript side: 

// window.__capsule_host is the native Java object (Android only)
// window.__capsule is the JS runtime object (defined by @capsule/core)
window.__capsule_host.postMessage(JSON.stringify({
    jsonrpc: '2.0',
    id: 'uuid-abc',
    method: 'barcode.scan',
    params: { quality: 0.8 }
}))

Naming convention: __capsule_host is the raw native interface exposed by addJavascriptInterface. __capsule is the high-level JS runtime object defined by @capsule/core that manages Promises and events. They are distinct objects. Using the same name for both would cause addJavascriptInterface to overwrite the JS runtime object during WebView initialization.

Critical threading fact: @JavascriptInterface methods execute on an arbitrary WebView background thread, never the main thread. Plugins must dispatch to the right thread explicitly if they need UI access (bridge.activity.runOnUiThread { ... }).

Option B — addWebMessageListener (API 24+, Chromium WebView only)

webView.addWebMessageListener(
    "__capsule_msg",
    setOf("https://localhost"),   // allowed origins
    object : WebViewCompat.WebMessageListener {
        override fun onPostMessage(view: WebView, message: WebMessageCompat, ...) {
            bridge.handleCall(message.data!!)
        }
    }
)

JavaScript side: 

window.__capsule_msg.postMessage(JSON.stringify({ ... }))

Comparison:

addJavascriptInterface addWebMessageListener API level 1+ 24+ (Android 7) WebView type Any Chromium WebView only Origin restriction No (security risk in mixed content) Yes (set of allowed origins) Object exposure Full JS object with methods Single postMessage only Used by Capacitor Yes (primary) No Recommendation Use — minSdk 26 removes legacy risks Future-proof but not necessary now

Decision for Capsule: Use addJavascriptInterface. It is what Capacitor, Cordova, and every production WebView bridge uses. minSdk 26 eliminates the pre-4.2 vulnerability. addWebMessageListener offers no meaningful advantage for this use case.

docs.title: Android: Native → JS (calling back into the WebView)
docs.text:
// Runs on main thread (evaluateJavascript REQUIRES main thread)
// Calls into the JS-side runtime object __capsule (managed by @capsule/core)
activity.runOnUiThread {
    webView.evaluateJavascript(
        "window.__capsule._resolve('${callId}', ${resultJson})",
        null
    )
}

This is how call.resolve(data) works internally. Every plugin response follows this path. window.__capsule here is the JS-side runtime (defined by @capsule/core), NOT the native host object __capsule_host.

For events (native pushes to web unprompted): 

activity.runOnUiThread {
    webView.evaluateJavascript(
        "window.__capsule._event('push.messageReceived', ${dataJson})",
        null
    )
}

docs.title: iOS: WKScriptMessageHandler vs WKScriptMessageHandlerWithReply
docs.text:
Option A — WKScriptMessageHandler (iOS 8+, universal)

// Register in WKWebViewConfiguration
config.userContentController.add(bridge, name: "capsule")

// Called on main thread — guaranteed
func userContentController(
    _ userContentController: WKUserContentController,
    didReceive message: WKScriptMessage
) {
    guard let body = message.body as? String else { return }
    bridge.handleCall(body)
}

JavaScript side: 

window.webkit.messageHandlers.capsule.postMessage(JSON.stringify({ ... }))

Limitation: No return value — response must be sent back via evaluateJavaScript. This means managing a callId-to-Promise mapping in JS.

Option B — WKScriptMessageHandlerWithReply (iOS 14+)

config.userContentController.addScriptMessageHandler(bridge, contentWorld: .page, name: "capsule")

func userContentController(
    _ userContentController: WKUserContentController,
    didReceive message: WKScriptMessage,
    replyHandler: @escaping (Any?, String?) -> Void
) {
    // message.body received on main thread
    // but replyHandler can be called from any thread
    bridge.handleCall(message.body as! String) { result, error in
        replyHandler(result, error)
    }
}

JavaScript side uses await: 

const result = await window.webkit.messageHandlers.capsule.postMessage(payload)

Threading hazard with Option B: The replyHandler closure captures WebKit internal state. It must be called exactly once — never twice, never dropped. Calling it from a background thread is allowed, but accessing message.body after the handler's scope is not. Swift's strict concurrency (@MainActor) conflicts with the protocol's non-isolated signature — use MainActor.assumeIsolated(_:) to assert main thread access.

Decision for Capsule: - Primary: WKScriptMessageHandler (Option A) — iOS 8+, simpler threading model, proven in production (Capacitor, Cordova, Ionic all use this) - Enhancement: Adopt WKScriptMessageHandlerWithReply for iOS 14+ as a progressive enhancement that eliminates the JS-side callId bookkeeping

docs.title: iOS: Native → JS
docs.text:
// Called on main thread
webView.evaluateJavaScript(
    "window.__capsule._resolve('\(callId)', \(resultJson))",
    completionHandler: nil
)

For modern WKWebView, prefer the async variant: 

Task { @MainActor in
    try? await webView.evaluateJavaScript(
        "window.__capsule._resolve('\(callId)', \(resultJson))"
    )
}

docs.title: JS-Side Bridge Runtime (@capsule/core)
docs.text:
The web layer manages the Promise lifecycle:

// packages/core/src/bridge.ts

type PendingCall = {
  resolve: (data: unknown) => void
  reject:  (err: CapsuleError) => void
}

const pending = new Map<string, PendingCall>()

// Called by Capsule to receive responses from native
window.__capsule = {
  _resolve(id: string, data: unknown) {
    pending.get(id)?.resolve(data)
    pending.delete(id)
  },
  _reject(id: string, code: number, message: string) {
    pending.get(id)?.reject(new CapsuleError(code, message))
    pending.delete(id)
  },
  _event(method: string, data: unknown) {
    eventBus.emit(method, data)
  }
}

export function call<T>(method: string, params: unknown): Promise<T> {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const id = crypto.randomUUID()
    pending.set(id, { resolve: resolve as any, reject })

    const message = JSON.stringify({ jsonrpc: '2.0', id, method, params })

    // Android path — __capsule_host is the Java object from addJavascriptInterface
    if ((window as any).__capsule_host?.postMessage) {
      (window as any).__capsule_host.postMessage(message)
      return
    }

    // iOS path — webkit.messageHandlers.capsule is from WKScriptMessageHandler
    ;(window as any).webkit?.messageHandlers?.capsule?.postMessage(message)
  })
}

What already exists: Capacitor's @capacitor/core package (packages/core/src/bridge.ts in the Capacitor monorepo) is MIT-licensed and solves exactly this. Study it rather than reinventing. The Capsule bridge will differ only in the JSON-RPC envelope format.

docs.title: Part 2 — Plugin Dispatch: How Bridge Calls Reach Plugin Methods
docs.text: Once the native layer receives a JSON-RPC call, it needs to route barcode.scan to the scan method on BarcodeScanner. There are two approaches.

docs.title: Approach A — Reflection (simple, slight perf cost)
docs.text:
// BridgeRouter.kt
class BridgeRouter {
    private val registry = mutableMapOf<String, CapsulePlugin>()

    fun register(name: String, plugin: CapsulePlugin) {
        registry[name] = plugin
    }

    fun route(call: BridgeCall) {
        val parts      = call.method.split(".")          // "barcode.scan" → ["barcode", "scan"]
        val pluginName = parts[0]                        // "barcode"
        val methodName = parts[1]                        // "scan"
        val plugin     = registry[pluginName] ?: return call.reject(1001, "Plugin not found")

        // Reflection: find method by name on the plugin class
        val method = plugin.javaClass.methods
            .firstOrNull { it.name == methodName && it.isAnnotationPresent(BridgeMethod::class.java) }
            ?: return call.reject(1002, "Method not found")

        try {
            method.invoke(plugin, call)
        } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) {
            call.reject(1003, e.cause?.message ?: "Plugin error")
        }
    }
}

What Capacitor does: Reflection with a small cache layer. Fully production-proven.

docs.title: Approach B — Generated Dispatch Table (no reflection, faster)
docs.text:
At capsule sync time, the CLI generates:

// .capsule/android/src/.../CapsulePluginRegistry.kt  (AUTO-GENERATED)
object CapsulePluginRegistry {
    fun register(bridge: CapsuleBridge) {
        bridge.registerDispatch("barcode") { call ->
            val plugin = BarcodeScanner(bridge)
            when (call.method) {
                "scan"          -> plugin.scan(call)
                "onScanResult"  -> plugin.onScanResult(call)
                else            -> call.reject(1002, "Method not found: ${call.method}")
            }
        }
        bridge.registerDispatch("imageProcessor") { call ->
            val plugin = ImageProcessor(bridge)
            when (call.method) {
                "grayscale"  -> plugin.grayscale(call)
                else         -> call.reject(1002, "Method not found: ${call.method}")
            }
        }
    }
}

No reflection at runtime. Generated from annotations at build time.

How the CLI generates this — two feasible approaches:

  1. KSP (Kotlin Symbol Processing): Processes @CapsulePlugin and @BridgeMethod annotations at compile time. Google uses KSP for Hilt, Room, Dagger. Fast, correct, integrates with Gradle naturally. Requires writing a KSP processor as a separate module.

  2. CLI pre-scan (simpler): The Capsule CLI reads and parses the Kotlin source files with a TypeScript regex/AST parser before the Gradle build, then writes the registry file. Slower to implement correctly but requires no Gradle plugin.

Recommendation: Start with Approach A (reflection) — it is what Capacitor uses and it works fine. Graduate to Approach B with KSP when performance profiling shows it matters (it usually won't for plugin dispatch — plugin method execution time dominates).

What already exists: The KSP processor infrastructure exists in Capacitor's android/annotation-processor module. It is MIT-licensed and can be studied directly.

docs.title: Kotlin / Java — FULLY FEASIBLE ✅
docs.text:
How it works: Source files added to android { sourceSets { main { java.srcDirs += [...] } } } in the generated build.gradle. They compile as part of the same Gradle build as the capsule shell. Full access to Android SDK.

What exists: This is standard Android development. Capacitor plugins written in Kotlin/Java follow exactly this model. Zero novel engineering required.

Gotchas: - Package name collisions — the CLI must enforce that plugin packages don't clash with dev.capsule.* - ProGuard/R8 rules — plugins that use reflection need -keep rules in the generated proguard-rules.pro

docs.title: Swift / Objective-C — FULLY FEASIBLE ✅
docs.text:
How it works: Swift/ObjC files are added to the Xcode project target's sources list in the generated .xcodeproj or via Swift Package Manager's sources: array. They compile into the same app binary as the capsule shell.

What exists: Standard iOS development. Capacitor iOS plugins follow this model exactly.

Gotchas: - Swift plugins need access to the capsule's bridge types — the CapsuleBridge module must be importable - If mixing Swift and ObjC in the same plugin, a bridging header is needed — the CLI must generate it - Swift 5.9+ strict concurrency warnings in WKScriptMessageHandlerWithReply implementations (see Part 1)

docs.title: C / C++ (Android NDK) — FEASIBLE, SIGNIFICANT COMPLEXITY ⚠️
docs.text:
How it works:

C source file → NDK (clang cross-compiler) → libmyplugin.so
                                                    ↓
            Java/Kotlin calls via JNI → System.loadLibrary("myplugin")

The JNI boundary requires a specific function signature: 

// Android NDK: function name must match Java package + class + method
// Package: com.yourapp.plugins  Class: ImageProcessor  Method: grayscale
JNIEXPORT jstring JNICALL
Java_com_yourapp_plugins_ImageProcessor_grayscale(
    JNIEnv* env,
    jobject thiz,
    jstring paramsJson
) {
    // process and return result JSON
    const char* params = (*env)->GetStringUTFChars(env, paramsJson, NULL);
    // ... do work ...
    return (*env)->NewStringUTF(env, resultJson);
}

OR use a Kotlin wrapper that calls into a pure-C shared library (cleaner):

// ImageProcessor.kt — thin Kotlin wrapper
@CapsulePlugin(name = "imageProcessor")
class ImageProcessor(bridge: CapsuleBridge) : CapsulePluginBase(bridge) {

    init { System.loadLibrary("image_processor") }

    @BridgeMethod
    fun grayscale(call: BridgeCall) {
        val result = nativeGrayscale(call.getString("path", ""))
        call.resolve(mapOf("path" to result))
    }

    private external fun nativeGrayscale(path: String): String  // JNI call
}

// image_processor.c — pure C implementation
JNIEXPORT jstring JNICALL
Java_com_yourapp_plugins_ImageProcessor_nativeGrayscale(JNIEnv* env, jobject thiz, jstring path) {
    // actual image processing
}

The CLI generates CMakeLists.txt and the externalNativeBuild block in build.gradle:

# .capsule/android/src/main/cpp/CMakeLists.txt  (auto-generated)
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.22.1)
project("capsule_plugins")

add_library(image_processor SHARED
    ../../../../capsule-plugins/image-processor/android/image_processor.c
)
target_link_libraries(image_processor android log)

What already exists: Android NDK is mature and production-ready. The CMakeLists.txt generation is not difficult — about 20 lines of CLI code per C plugin.

Real complexity: The JNI layer is error-prone. Memory management (GetStringUTFChars must be matched with ReleaseStringUTFChars), exception handling, and thread safety are all developer responsibilities. The CLI cannot protect against these.

Recommendation: Support C/C++ plugins but document the JNI complexity clearly. Provide a Kotlin wrapper template that hides the raw JNI. Most developers should prefer Kotlin.

docs.title: C / C++ (iOS) — FULLY FEASIBLE, SIMPLER THAN ANDROID ✅
docs.text:
On iOS, C/C++ is a first-class citizen — Xcode projects have always mixed Objective-C, C, C++, and Swift. No JNI layer. A C function callable from Swift via a bridging header:

// capsule-plugins/my-plugin/ios/fast_hash.c
#include "fast_hash.h"

const char* compute_hash(const char* input) {
    // xxHash or similar
}

// MyPlugin.swift — calls C directly after importing header
import Foundation
import CapsuleBridge

@objc(MyPlugin)
class MyPlugin: CapsulePlugin {
    @objc func hash(_ call: CapsuleBridgeCall) {
        let input  = call.getString("input") ?? ""
        let result = String(cString: compute_hash(input))   // direct C call
        call.resolve(["hash": result])
    }
}

The CLI adds the .c file to the Xcode target and generates the bridging header.

docs.title: Lua — PARTIALLY FEASIBLE, PLATFORM SPLIT ⚠️
docs.text: This is the most nuanced case. The feasibility differs significantly between platforms.

docs.title: Lua on Android — FULLY FEASIBLE ✅
docs.text:
Option 1 — LuaJ (pure Java, recommended)

LuaJ is a Lua 5.2 interpreter written in pure Java. No NDK, no native compilation, no .so files. Just a Maven dependency.

// build.gradle (auto-added by CLI when a .lua plugin is detected)
implementation 'org.luaj:luaj-jse:3.0.1'

// LuaPluginHost.kt — hosts all .lua plugins
class LuaPluginHost(private val bridge: CapsuleBridge) : CapsulePluginBase(bridge) {

    private val globals = JsePlatform.standardGlobals()

    fun loadScript(name: String, assetPath: String) {
        val source = bridge.context.assets.open(assetPath).bufferedReader().readText()
        globals.load(source, name).call()
    }

    fun call(pluginName: String, method: String, params: Map<String, Any>, call: BridgeCall) {
        val onCall = globals.get("onCall") as? LuaFunction
            ?: return call.reject(4001, "Lua plugin missing onCall function")

        val luaParams = LuaTable()
        params.forEach { (k, v) -> luaParams.set(k, CoerceJavaToLua.coerce(v)) }

        val resolveFn = object : TwoArgFunction() {
            override fun call(a: LuaValue, b: LuaValue): LuaValue {
                call.resolve(CoerceLuaToJava.coerce(b, Map::class.java) as Map<String, Any>)
                return LuaValue.NIL
            }
        }

        val rejectFn = object : TwoArgFunction() {
            override fun call(a: LuaValue, b: LuaValue): LuaValue {
                call.reject(4002, a.tojstring())
                return LuaValue.NIL
            }
        }

        onCall.call(
            LuaValue.valueOf(method),
            luaParams,
            resolveFn,
            rejectFn
        )
    }
}

Option 2 — LuaJIT NDK (higher performance)

LuaJIT compiles Lua to native machine code (JIT compilation). Faster for CPU-intensive scripts. Requires NDK build for each ABI (arm64-v8a, x86_64). Pre-built NDK binaries exist in the open-source community but are not official.

Decision: Start with LuaJ (pure Java). Offer LuaJIT as an opt-in for performance-critical plugins.

docs.title: Lua on iOS — BUNDLED ONLY, NO OTA UPDATES ⚠️
docs.text:
The App Store 2.5.2 rule directly restricts this:

"Apps may not download, install, or execute code which introduces or changes features or functionality of the app, including other apps." — Apple App Store Review Guidelines 2.5.2

Scenario Allowed on iOS? .lua files bundled inside the app binary ✅ Yes — interpreted at runtime but bundled at build time Downloading new .lua scripts from a server ❌ No — violates 2.5.2 Updating .lua via CodeSync OTA ❌ No — same violation Using JavaScript in WKWebView (the web bundle) ✅ Yes — explicit WebKit exemption

This means: On iOS, Lua plugins are static. They ship with the app binary and can only change with a new app store release. There is no OTA update path for Lua on iOS.

On Android: No such restriction exists. Lua scripts can be included in the CodeSync bundle and updated OTA freely.

Implementation: - On iOS, use the C Lua 5.4 interpreter compiled into the Xcode project (Lua is a C library, ~300KB) - Scripts are read from Bundle.main (bundled assets) only — the host explicitly refuses to load scripts from external paths - The LuaPluginHost.swift enforces this at runtime

class LuaPluginHost: CapsulePlugin {
    private var luaState: OpaquePointer?

    func loadBundledScript(name: String) {
        // ONLY loads from app bundle — never from Documents or network paths
        guard let url = Bundle.main.url(forResource: name, withExtension: "lua"),
              let source = try? String(contentsOf: url) else { return }
        luaL_dostring(luaState, source)
    }
}

Summary for Lua:

Android iOS Bundled scripts ✅ LuaJ (pure Java) ✅ Lua 5.4 C library OTA script updates ✅ Via CodeSync ❌ App Store violation JIT performance ✅ Optional LuaJIT NDK ❌ No JIT (Apple forbids writable+executable memory)

Correction to previous doc: The claim that "Lua plugins can be updated via CodeSync OTA on iOS" was incorrect. OTA Lua updates on iOS violate App Store guidelines. This capability is Android-only.

docs.title: Part 4 — Code Generation: TypeScript Types from Native Annotations
docs.text: This eliminates handwritten TypeScript bridges. The developer annotates Kotlin/Swift; the CLI generates the .ts file.

docs.title: Android: KSP Processor
docs.text:
// @BridgeMethod and @BridgeParam are processed by the Capsule KSP processor

@CapsulePlugin(name = "barcode")
class BarcodeScanner {

    @BridgeMethod
    @Returns(BarcodeResult::class)
    fun scan(
        @BridgeParam("quality") quality: Float,
        @BridgeParam("facing")  facing: String
    ): Unit

    @BridgeEvent
    @Emits(BarcodeResult::class)
    fun onScanResult(): Unit
}

@BridgeType
data class BarcodeResult(
    val value: String,
    val format: String
)

KSP processor output: 

// AUTO-GENERATED — do not edit. Run `capsule generate types` to regenerate.

export interface BarcodeResult {
  value: string
  format: string
}

export const barcode = {
  scan(params: { quality?: number; facing?: 'front' | 'back' }): Promise<BarcodeResult> {
    return capsuleBridge.call('barcode.scan', params)
  },
  onScanResult(handler: (data: BarcodeResult) => void): () => void {
    return capsuleBridge.subscribe('barcode.onScanResult', handler)
  }
}

What exists: Writing a KSP processor is ~300 lines of Kotlin. Google's KSP documentation is comprehensive, and Capacitor's existing annotation processor (KAPT-based) is a direct reference to port to KSP.

docs.title: iOS: Swift Macros (Swift 5.9+)
docs.text:
@CapsulePlugin("barcode")      // Swift attached macro
class BarcodeScanner: CapsulePlugin {

    @BridgeMethod               // macro marks this for TS generation + dispatch registration
    func scan(quality: Float, facing: String) async throws -> BarcodeResult { ... }
}

The Swift macro generates: 1. The Objective-C @objc exposure needed for the runtime bridge 2. A .d.ts snapshot file that capsule generate types collects into the final TypeScript output

What exists: Swift macros are new (Xcode 15+, Swift 5.9). No existing framework does this yet. Sourcery is the mature alternative — it uses SwiftSyntax to parse Swift files and generate code from templates. Sourcery is used in 40,000+ projects (Airbnb, Bumble, NYT). Either approach works; Swift macros are more elegant but require Xcode 15.

docs.title: Part 5 — Plugin Threading Model
docs.text: Getting threading wrong causes random crashes and ANR (Application Not Responding) errors. This must be defined as an explicit contract.

docs.title: Android Threading Rules
iOS Threading Rules
docs.text: Context Thread Rule WKScriptMessageHandler.didReceive Main thread Safe for UI; dispatch off main for heavy work call.resolve() / call.reject() Any thread Safe Heavy computation Background DispatchQueue.global(qos: .userInitiated).async { } Camera / permissions Main thread required Must dispatch back

docs.title: Part 6 — Error Boundaries and Plugin Crashes
docs.text: An uncaught exception inside a plugin method must not crash the entire app.

docs.title: Android
docs.text:
The BridgeRouter wraps every plugin invocation:

fun route(call: BridgeCall) {
    try {
        dispatch(call)
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        // Plugin threw — reject the call, log, do not rethrow
        Log.e("CapsuleBridge", "Plugin error in ${call.method}", e)
        call.reject(4999, "Plugin error: ${e.message}")
    }
}

Additionally, Kotlin coroutine exceptions need a CoroutineExceptionHandler: 

val exceptionHandler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, throwable ->
    Log.e("CapsuleBridge", "Unhandled plugin coroutine error", throwable)
    // notify developer in debug mode; silence in production
}

docs.title: iOS
docs.text:
func route(_ call: CapsuleBridgeCall) {
    do {
        try dispatch(call)
    } catch {
        NSLog("CapsuleBridge: Plugin error in \(call.method): \(error)")
        call.reject(.pluginError, error.localizedDescription)
    }
}

Objective-C exceptions (from legacy ObjC plugins) require a separate @try/@catch wrapper since Swift does not catch ObjC exceptions by default.

docs.title: Part 7 — The capsule eject Command (Forking an npm Plugin)
What "eject" actually means
docs.text:
An npm binary plugin ships an AAR (which is just a zip file of compiled .class files, resources, and a manifest). Decompiling it with tools like jadx produces readable Java — but that's a workaround, not a first-class path.

The correct approach: Require all official and community plugins to publish source code. The capsule-plugin.json manifest includes a sourceRepo field:

{
  "name": "@capsule/camera",
  "sourceRepo": "https://github.com/capsule-framework/plugin-camera",
  "sourceBranch": "main"
}

capsule eject @capsule/camera then: 

1. Read capsule-plugin.json from node_modules/@capsule/camera/
2. Read sourceRepo field
3. git clone --depth=1 {sourceRepo} capsule-plugins/camera
4. Remove @capsule/camera from capsule.config.ts plugins array
5. Add ./capsule-plugins/camera to plugins array
6. Run capsule sync to rebuild registry

The developer now owns the full source. Modifications compile from source at every capsule build.

For closed-source third-party plugins with no sourceRepo: eject is not available. The CLI should say so explicitly rather than attempting decompilation.

docs.title: Part 9 — Plugin Lifecycle
docs.text:
App cold start
     │
     ▼
CapsuleShell.onCreate()
     │
     ├─ Load all plugin instances (eager, synchronous)
     │    Plugin.load() called — reserve resources, open DB connections
     │
     ├─ WebView created and configured
     │    addJavascriptInterface / WKScriptMessageHandler registered
     │
     ├─ Web bundle loaded
     │    Phase 1: file:///android_asset/www/ (dev server in debug mode)
     │    Phase 2+: CapsuleRuntime starts the server, navigates WebView to
     │              http://127.0.0.1:{port}/ after server is ready
     │    DOMContentLoaded fires
     │    Web code imports plugins from @capsule/core
     │
     └─ App is live — bridge calls can now flow


App goes to background
     │
     └─ Plugin.pause() called — release camera, pause sensors

App returns to foreground
     │
     └─ Plugin.resume() called — reacquire resources, re-check permissions

App destroyed
     │
     └─ Plugin.destroy() called — close DB, release memory

Plugins that do not override pause()/resume()/destroy() get no-op defaults.

docs.title: Capsule Framework — Store Publishing
docs.text:
Automated pipeline from capsule build to live in the Play Store and App Store. How the APIs work, what credentials are needed, and how Fastlane bridges the gap.

Different "publish": this doc is about shipping apps built with Capsule to the app stores. For publishing the framework itself (git repos + npm/Maven packages, de-Windows, license, docs split) see release.md.

docs.title: Two Release Layers
docs.text:
Before diving in, the distinction matters:

Layer 1 — Store Release (this document)
  Full APK/IPA → Play Store / App Store review
  Required when: native shell update, new permissions, new native plugins
  Time: hours to days (review)
  Controlled by: capsule publish android|ios

Layer 2 — CodeSync OTA (ota-updates.md)
  JS bundle only → direct to devices, no review
  Required when: web code changes (JS, CSS, HTML, assets)
  Time: seconds
  Controlled by: capsule codesync publish

These are complementary, not competing. A typical release cycle: - Ship a new store version to add a native feature (Layer 1) - Then iterate the UI weekly via CodeSync (Layer 2) without touching the store

docs.title: How the API Works
docs.text:
Google exposes the Google Play Developer API (REST + gRPC). It manages: - Uploading APK / AAB (Android App Bundle) - Assigning builds to tracks (internal → alpha → beta → production) - Staged rollouts (0–100% of production users) - Release notes per language - Listing current live versions

Authentication: A service account with a JSON key file. The service account is granted access to your app in the Play Console. It uses OAuth 2.0 with JWT assertion — no browser login required, fully automated.

docs.title: Setting Up Play Store Access
docs.text:
Step 1 — Create a service account in Google Cloud Console: 

Google Cloud Console → IAM & Admin → Service Accounts
→ Create Service Account
→ Role: not needed here (Play grants its own permissions)
→ Create Key → JSON → download to secure location

Step 2 — Grant the service account access in Play Console: 

Play Console → Setup → API access
→ Link to Google Cloud project
→ Grant access to service account
→ Permissions: Release manager (or App manager for full control)

Step 3 — Store the key securely: 

# Never commit the JSON key. Use environment variables or a secrets manager.
export PLAY_STORE_JSON_KEY=/path/to/service-account.json
# Or base64-encode it for CI:
export PLAY_STORE_JSON_KEY_DATA=$(base64 -w0 service-account.json)

docs.title: Tracks and Staged Rollouts
docs.text:
internal   →   alpha   →   beta   →   production
  (team)    (invited)   (opt-in)    (all users)

Production supports staged rollout: 10% → 50% → 100%

The API call to promote a build to production at 10%: 

PUT /androidpublisher/v3/applications/{packageName}/edits/{editId}/tracks/production
{
  "releases": [{
    "versionCodes": ["42"],
    "status": "inProgress",
    "userFraction": 0.10,
    "releaseNotes": [{ "language": "en-US", "text": "Bug fixes" }]
  }]
}

docs.title: AAB vs APK
docs.text:
Always use AAB (Android App Bundle) for Play Store uploads: - Google generates optimized APKs per device configuration - ~20-30% smaller downloads vs universal APK - Required for new apps since Aug 2021

# In capsule build pipeline:
./gradlew bundleRelease    # produces .aab
# vs
./gradlew assembleRelease  # produces .apk (for sideloading / direct install only)

docs.title: How the API Works
docs.text:
Apple provides the App Store Connect API (REST). It manages: - Uploading IPA builds - Submitting for TestFlight beta testing - Submitting for App Store review - Managing phased releases - App metadata, screenshots, pricing

Authentication: An API key (.p8 private key file) combined with a Key ID and Issuer ID. Generates a short-lived JWT for each API request. No Apple ID login required, fully headless.

docs.title: Three Key Pieces of iOS Identity
docs.text:
Understanding this is critical before any automation:

1. Distribution Certificate (.p12)
   → Proves the binary was built by your team
   → Issued by Apple, stored in macOS Keychain or encrypted file
   → Expires every year — must be renewed

2. Provisioning Profile (.mobileprovision)
   → Ties: app ID + certificate + allowed devices (for dev) or "any" (for distribution)
   → App Store distribution profile: no device restriction
   → Expires, must be regenerated when cert changes

3. App Store Connect API Key (.p8)
   → Used only for API calls (upload, submit, metadata)
   → Does NOT replace certificate or provisioning profile
   → Never expires, but can be revoked

docs.title: Setting Up App Store Connect API Access
docs.text:
Step 1 — Generate API Key: 

App Store Connect → Users and Access → Keys
→ Generate API Key
→ Select role: Admin (for full publishing) or App Manager
→ Download .p8 file (ONE TIME — cannot re-download)
→ Note: Key ID (10-char string) and Issuer ID (UUID)

Step 2 — Store securely: 

# The .p8 file is a private key — treat like a password
export APP_STORE_CONNECT_KEY_ID=XXXXXXXXXX
export APP_STORE_CONNECT_ISSUER_ID=xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx
export APP_STORE_CONNECT_KEY_CONTENT=$(cat AuthKey_XXXXXXXXXX.p8 | base64)

Step 3 — Certificate + Profile management via Fastlane Match:

Fastlane Match solves the multi-developer certificate problem by storing encrypted certificates in a private git repo or S3 bucket. Every developer and CI machine fetches from the same source:

# First time setup
fastlane match init
# → Choose storage (git / s3 / google_cloud)
# → Enter git repo URL (private repo)

# Generate and store distribution cert + profile
fastlane match appstore

# On CI: read-only mode (never regenerate, just fetch)
fastlane match appstore --readonly

Match encrypts with a passphrase (MATCH_PASSWORD env var). The private key never leaves the machine unencrypted.

docs.title: TestFlight vs Production
docs.text:
TestFlight (beta)
  → Upload IPA → automatic processing (~10 min)
  → Internal testers: instant, no review
  → External testers: one-time beta review (1-2 days)
  → CLI: capsule publish ios --track testflight

App Store (production)
  → Upload IPA → App Store review (24-48 hrs typical, can be longer)
  → Phased release: roll out to 1%→2%→5%→10%→20%→50%→100% over 7 days
  → Manual override to pause or accelerate
  → CLI: capsule publish ios --track production

docs.title: Fastlane as the Integration Layer
docs.text: Capsule wraps Fastlane. Developers never write a Fastfile. The CLI generates it from capsule.config.ts and then invokes it.

docs.title: Why Fastlane
docs.text:
• Battle-tested (used by Airbnb, Twitter, Google, etc.)
  • Handles the gnarly parts: signing, build number increment, upload retry on network error, screenshot upload
  • MIT licensed, active maintenance
  • Supports both Play Store (supply action) and App Store (deliver + pilot actions)

docs.title: What capsule publish android Does Internally
docs.text:
capsule publish android --track production --rollout 10

1. capsule build android --release
   └─ Vite build → dist/
   └─ gradlew bundleRelease → app-release.aab

2. CLI generates Fastfile in .capsule/fastlane/
   └─ lane :publish_android do
        supply(
          track: 'production',
          rollout: '0.1',
          aab: '.capsule/android/app-release.aab',
          json_key: ENV['PLAY_STORE_JSON_KEY'],
          package_name: 'com.yourcompany.app',
          skip_upload_apk: true,
          release_status: 'inProgress'
        )
      end

3. fastlane publish_android
   └─ Authenticates with service account JSON
   └─ Creates Play edit (transaction)
   └─ Uploads AAB
   └─ Assigns to production track at 10% rollout
   └─ Commits the edit → goes live

docs.title: What capsule publish ios Does Internally
docs.text:
capsule publish ios --track testflight

1. capsule build ios --release
   └─ Vite build → dist/
   └─ xcodebuild archive → .xcarchive
   └─ xcodebuild exportArchive → .ipa

2. CLI generates Fastfile in .capsule/fastlane/
   └─ lane :publish_ios do
        pilot(
          ipa: '.capsule/ios/MyApp.ipa',
          api_key_path: '.capsule/fastlane/app_store_connect_key.json',
          skip_waiting_for_build_processing: true,
          changelog: ENV['RELEASE_NOTES'] || 'New build'
        )
      end

3. fastlane publish_ios
   └─ Authenticates with App Store Connect API key
   └─ Uploads IPA via Transporter protocol
   └─ Triggers TestFlight distribution (or production submission)

The app_store_connect_key.json is a temp file the CLI writes from env vars — never persisted to disk after the session.

docs.title: capsule.config.ts — Full Publishing Config

docs.title: CLI Publishing Commands in Full
docs.text:
# Android
capsule publish android                          # upload to defaultTrack (internal)
capsule publish android --track alpha            # upload to alpha
capsule publish android --track production       # submit to production
capsule publish android --track production --rollout 10   # 10% staged rollout
capsule publish android --rollout 50             # increase existing rollout to 50%
capsule publish android --rollout 100            # full rollout (complete staged release)
capsule publish android --pause                  # halt staged rollout

# iOS
capsule publish ios                              # upload to TestFlight (defaultTrack)
capsule publish ios --track testflight           # TestFlight internal testing
capsule publish ios --track testflight-external  # TestFlight external (needs beta review)
capsule publish ios --track production           # submit for App Store review
capsule publish ios --track production --phased  # enable 7-day phased release
capsule publish ios --pause-phased               # pause phased release
capsule publish ios --resume-phased              # resume paused phased release

# Version management
capsule version                                  # show current version codes
capsule version bump patch                       # 1.4.2 → 1.4.3
capsule version bump minor                       # 1.4.2 → 1.5.0
capsule version set 2.0.0                        # explicit version

docs.title: Version Code Management
docs.text:
Both platforms require a monotonically increasing integer build number alongside the human-readable version string.

Platform Human version Build number Notes Android versionName (e.g. "1.4.2") versionCode (e.g. 47) versionCode must increase with every upload iOS CFBundleShortVersionString (e.g. "1.4.2") CFBundleVersion (e.g. 47) Same requirement

Capsule stores both in capsule.config.ts and auto-increments versionCode/CFBundleVersion on each capsule publish:

// capsule.config.ts (managed by CLI — do not hand-edit build numbers)
version: {
  name: '1.4.2',
  buildNumber: 47   // auto-incremented by `capsule publish`
}

The CLI commits the bumped buildNumber back to capsule.config.ts after a successful upload. In CI, configure git so this commit is created by a bot account.

docs.title: CI/CD Pipeline — Full End-to-End
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/release.yml

name: Release

on:
  push:
    tags: ['v*']

jobs:
  # ─── Android ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  release-android:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    container:
      image: ghcr.io/capsule/build-android:latest

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Restore keystore from secret
        run: echo "${{ secrets.KEYSTORE_BASE64 }}" | base64 -d > /tmp/keystore.jks

      - name: Build + publish to Play Store (internal track)
        run: capsule publish android --track internal
        env:
          CAPSULE_KEYSTORE_PATH:      /tmp/keystore.jks
          CAPSULE_KEYSTORE_PASS:      ${{ secrets.KEYSTORE_PASS }}
          CAPSULE_KEY_ALIAS:          ${{ secrets.KEY_ALIAS }}
          CAPSULE_KEY_PASS:           ${{ secrets.KEY_PASS }}
          PLAY_STORE_JSON_KEY_DATA:   ${{ secrets.PLAY_STORE_JSON_KEY_DATA }}

  # ─── iOS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  release-ios:
    runs-on: macos-15    # required — Xcode only runs on macOS

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22' }

      - run: npm install -g @capsule/cli

      - name: Install signing via Fastlane Match
        run: bundle exec fastlane match appstore --readonly
        env:
          MATCH_GIT_URL:      ${{ secrets.MATCH_GIT_URL }}
          MATCH_PASSWORD:     ${{ secrets.MATCH_PASSWORD }}
          APPLE_TEAM_ID:      ${{ secrets.APPLE_TEAM_ID }}

      - name: Build + publish to TestFlight
        run: capsule publish ios --track testflight
        env:
          APP_STORE_CONNECT_KEY_ID:      ${{ secrets.ASC_KEY_ID }}
          APP_STORE_CONNECT_ISSUER_ID:   ${{ secrets.ASC_ISSUER_ID }}
          APP_STORE_CONNECT_KEY_CONTENT: ${{ secrets.ASC_KEY_CONTENT }}

docs.title: Staged Rollout Coordination: Store + CodeSync
docs.text:
Both layers support gradual rollouts. Here is how they work together:

Day 0: capsule publish android --track production --rollout 5
       → 5% of users get the new native binary
       → They also run the new JS bundle (included in the APK)

Day 1: capsule codesync publish --rollout 10
       → All users on the OLD native version get the new JS bundle
       → The 5% on the new native also get it (compatible)

Day 3: capsule publish android --rollout 25
       → 25% of users now on new native

Day 5: capsule publish android --rollout 100
       → All users on new native
       capsule codesync rollout 100
       → All devices running the latest JS bundle

Key rule: CodeSync bundles must declare minNativeVersion. If a new JS bundle requires a new native feature:

// Only deliver this bundle to devices on native v2.0+
capsule codesync publish --min-native-version 2.0.0

Devices still on native v1.x keep running the previous JS bundle until they update from the store.

docs.title: Direct APK Distribution (No Store)
docs.text:
For enterprise apps, internal tooling, or beta testers outside TestFlight/Play:

# Build a signed APK (not AAB — direct install requires APK)
capsule build android --release --format apk

# Output: .capsule/android/app-release.apk
# Distribute via:
#   - MDM (Mobile Device Management): Intune, Jamf, VMware Workspace ONE
#   - Internal download page (HTTPS required on Android 8+)
#   - ADB: adb install app-release.apk

iOS direct distribution (no App Store) requires: - Enterprise Distribution Certificate (Apple Developer Enterprise Program — $299/yr) - In-house provisioning profile (no device limit, no App Store review) - Distributed via MDM or HTTPS manifest plist

capsule build ios --release --distribution enterprise
# Generates: .capsule/ios/MyApp.ipa + manifest.plist
# Host on HTTPS server → users open itms-services://?action=download-manifest&url=...

docs.title: Secrets Management Reference
docs.text:
Never hardcode any of these. Use environment variables, a secrets manager, or GitHub/GitLab/Azure secrets.

Secret Platform How to get How to store KEYSTORE_BASE64 Android keytool -genkey (first time) Base64-encode .jks, store as repo secret KEYSTORE_PASS Android You set this Repo secret KEY_ALIAS Android You set this Repo secret KEY_PASS Android You set this Repo secret PLAY_STORE_JSON_KEY_DATA Android Google Cloud service account Base64-encode JSON, repo secret MATCH_GIT_URL iOS Private git repo you create Repo secret MATCH_PASSWORD iOS You set this (encrypts the cert repo) Repo secret APPLE_TEAM_ID iOS Apple Developer portal (10-char) Repo secret ASC_KEY_ID iOS App Store Connect → Keys Repo secret ASC_ISSUER_ID iOS App Store Connect → Keys Repo secret ASC_KEY_CONTENT iOS Base64-encode the .p8 file Repo secret

First-time keystore generation (run once, store the result): 

keytool -genkey -v \
  -keystore my-release-key.jks \
  -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000 \
  -alias my-key-alias \
  -dname "CN=My App, OU=Mobile, O=My Company, L=City, S=State, C=US"

# Then base64-encode and store:
base64 -w0 my-release-key.jks > keystore.b64
# → paste keystore.b64 content into KEYSTORE_BASE64 repo secret
# → DELETE the .jks and .b64 files from your machine
# → The canonical copy is the repo secret

Android keystore warning: If you lose this keystore, you can never update your app on the Play Store. The Play Store ties your app's identity to the keystore forever. Fastlane Match solves the iOS equivalent. For Android, store the keystore in at minimum two independent secure locations.

docs.title: What Fastlane Actually Calls
docs.text: For transparency — here is the raw API flow Fastlane executes on your behalf.

docs.title: Play Store upload flow
docs.text:
1. POST /auth/token  (OAuth2 JWT assertion)
   → access_token

2. POST /androidpublisher/v3/applications/{pkg}/edits
   → editId  (like a database transaction)

3. POST /androidpublisher/v3/applications/{pkg}/edits/{editId}/bundles
   (upload AAB as multipart/form-data)
   → versionCode

4. PUT /androidpublisher/v3/applications/{pkg}/edits/{editId}/tracks/{track}
   → assign versionCode to track with rollout fraction

5. POST /androidpublisher/v3/applications/{pkg}/edits/{editId}:commit
   → edit goes live (equivalent to "save and submit")

docs.title: App Store Connect upload flow
docs.text:
1. Generate JWT from .p8 private key (expires in 20 min)

2. POST /v1/apps/{appId}/appStoreVersions  (create new version record)

3. POST /v1/builds  (Transporter-based upload — uses Apple's binary protocol, not REST)
   Note: the actual .ipa upload uses Apple's Transporter tool or its REST equivalent
   Fastlane uses `xcrun altool` (Xcode ≤14) or `xcrun notarytool` + direct REST (Xcode 15+)

4. PATCH /v1/builds/{buildId}  (attach build to version, set release notes)

5. POST /v1/appStoreVersionSubmissions  (submit for review)
   → status: WAITING_FOR_REVIEW → IN_REVIEW → APPROVED → READY_FOR_SALE

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Task Command Time Review? Upload to internal track (Play) capsule publish android --track internal ~5 min No Upload to production (Play), staged capsule publish android --track production --rollout 10 ~5 min No (if previously approved) Upload to TestFlight internal capsule publish ios --track testflight ~15 min processing No Submit to App Store capsule publish ios --track production 24–48 hrs Yes Push JS update to all devices capsule codesync publish ~30 sec No

docs.title: Push Notifications (FCM / APNs) — Implementation Design
docs.text:
Phase 3 · API #4. Status: Slice 1 built (2026-06-24), Slice 2 not started. This doc is the execution plan — a fresh session can build the Android slice from it without re-deriving anything.

Slice 1 delivered: core/src/push.ts + index export + WebBridge fallback (+__capsulePushSimulate) + errors.ts PUSH_REGISTRATION_FAILED (6001); Kotlin PushProvider/PushController/PushHandlers + FakePushProvider + BridgeError.PushRegistrationFailed; pure-JVM PushControllerTest + PushHandlerTest; PushScreen.tsx + registry. Deviation: CapsuleActivity wiring (§4) moved to Slice 2 — it is inseparable from the AndroidPushProvider instance it must construct, and adding a throwaway no-op provider to main/ would violate the no-placeholder bar. Slice 1's gate (offline tiers + browser dev via WebBridge) is fully satisfied without it; capabilities.has('push') is honestly true only in the browser until Slice 2 registers the native capability alongside the real provider.

Prerequisites met: App lifecycle + deep links (#3 — provides the cold/warm tap-routing seam this design reuses) and Network status (#4-prereq — introduced the shared BridgeEventEmitter this design emits through). TS surface already specified in the core API reference (push). Firebase ownership settled in ../decisions/log.md Q19. Server-side delivery job is Phase 6 (../project/server-design/workers.md).

docs.title: 2. TypeScript surface — core/src/push.ts
docs.text:
Mirror network.ts structure (types → method-name constants → module class). Types come verbatim from the core API reference (push): PushToken, PushMessage, NotificationChannel, PermissionStatus.

export const PushMethods = {
  // request/response
  REGISTER:                'push.register',
  CREATE_CHANNEL:          'push.createChannel',
  REMOVE_CHANNEL:          'push.removeChannel',
  LIST_CHANNELS:           'push.listChannels',
  REMOVE_ALL_DELIVERED:    'push.removeAllDeliveredNotifications',
  CHECK_PERMISSIONS:       'push.checkPermissions',
  REQUEST_PERMISSIONS:     'push.requestPermissions',
  GET_LAUNCH_NOTIFICATION: 'push.getLaunchNotification',   // D2, mirrors app.getLaunchUrl
  // native → JS events (over BridgeEventEmitter)
  MESSAGE:                 'push.message',                  // foreground arrival
  NOTIFICATION_TAP:        'push.notificationTap',          // warm tap
  REGISTRATION_ERROR:      'push.registrationError',
} as const

PushModule methods: register, createChannel, removeChannel, listChannels, removeAllDeliveredNotifications, checkPermissions, requestPermissions, getLaunchNotification, and the three subscription sugar methods onMessage, onNotificationTap, onRegistrationError — each returning an unsubscribe fn, exactly like network.onStatusChange / app.onUrlOpen.

Error codes (already in 021): 2001 NOTIFICATIONS_PERMISSION_DENIED, 3001 PUSH_REGISTRATION_FAILED.

docs.title: 3. Kotlin seam — push/PushProvider.kt
docs.text:
interface PushProvider {
    /** Register for remote push. Async — token (or error) arrives via the callbacks. */
    fun register(onToken: (PushToken) -> Unit, onError: (PushError) -> Unit)

    fun checkPermissions(): PermissionStatus
    fun requestPermissions(onResult: (PermissionStatus) -> Unit)

    // Android-only channel ops (no-op on iOS)
    fun createChannel(channel: NotificationChannel)
    fun removeChannel(id: String)
    fun listChannels(): List<NotificationChannel>
    fun removeAllDeliveredNotifications()

    /** Begin delivering foreground messages + warm taps to the controller. */
    fun start(onMessage: (PushMessage) -> Unit, onTap: (PushMessage) -> Unit)
    fun stop()

    companion object {
        const val CAPABILITY = "push"
        const val CAPABILITY_VERSION = 1
    }
}

Serializable data classes (@Serializable, lowercase wire enums — same convention as NetworkStatus): PushToken(value, platform), PushMessage(id, title?, body?, data, badge?, sound?, launchNotification), NotificationChannel(...), PermissionStatus, PushError(message, code).

docs.title: PushController (emit + cold-launch hold) — mirrors NetworkStatusController + AppLifecycleController
docs.text:
• Holds the shared BridgeEventEmitter.
  • onMessage(msg) → emit(MESSAGE, msg).
  • onTap(msg) → emit(NOTIFICATION_TAP, msg) (warm).
  • onRegistrationError(err) → emit(REGISTRATION_ERROR, err).
  • setLaunchNotification(msg) / consumeLaunchNotification(): PushMessage? — consume-once, copied straight from AppLifecycleController.setLaunchUrl / consumeLaunchUrl (D2).

docs.title: handlers/push/PushHandlers.kt
docs.text: One handler per request method (factory pushHandlers(provider, controller) returning the list, like networkHandlers). PushGetLaunchNotificationHandler returns { message: <msg|null> } (always-present, null-safe key — same shape as AppGetLaunchUrlHandler).

docs.title: fakes/FakePushProvider.kt
docs.text: Injectable modes, mirroring FakeNetworkProvider.push(...): registrationFails: PushError?, tokenReturns(token), messageArrives(msg) (fires the foreground listener), tapArrives(msg) (fires the warm-tap listener), settable permission. Lets PushControllerTest + PushHandlerTest cover the whole contract with zero device.

docs.title: 4. CapsuleActivity wiring (edit) — moved to Slice 2
docs.text:
Deferred from Slice 1: the wiring constructs an AndroidPushProvider, which is a Slice-2 artifact. Doing it in Slice 1 would need a throwaway no-op provider in main/. Build this together with AndroidPushProvider in Slice 2. Steps below are unchanged.

Mirror the Network block:

  1. capabilities chain → add .register(PushProvider.CAPABILITY, PushProvider.CAPABILITY_VERSION).
  2. Init pushController = PushController { method, params -> bridge.sendNotification(method, params) }.
  3. Handlers → add pushHandlers(pushProvider, pushController).
  4. Lifecycle → pushProvider.start(onMessage = { pushController.onMessage(it) }, onTap = { pushController.onTap(it) }); stop() on teardown.
  5. Cold tap (Slice 2): in onCreate, if the launch intent carries push extras (set by CapsulePushService when it posts the tray notification), parse → pushController.setLaunchNotification(msg). Reuses the existing singleTask + onNewIntent path App-lifecycle already added — a warm tap arriving via onNewIntent routes to pushController.onTap(msg).

docs.title: 5. WebBridge dev fallback (browser)
docs.text: Add push.* to web-bridge.ts so the example runs in capsule dev without a device: - register() → resolves a fake token { value: 'web-dev-token', platform: 'android' }. - channel ops → in-memory list; checkPermissions/requestPermissions → map the Notification.permission Web API where present, else 'granted'. - getLaunchNotification() → { message: null }. - Expose a dev-only window.__capsulePushSimulate(msg) to fire push.message / push.notificationTap from the console (mirrors how online/offline are simulated). - Declare push: 1 in the WebBridge capability map so capabilities.has('push') matches native.

docs.title: 6. Slice 2 — Firebase (isolated build-system + CLI surface)
docs.text:
Only this slice touches the Gradle build and the CLI. Keep it a separate set of commits.

  • AndroidPushProvider: FirebaseMessaging.getInstance().token for register; NotificationManager for channels + removeAllDeliveredNotifications; Android 13+ POST_NOTIFICATIONS runtime permission for requestPermissions.
  • CapsulePushService : FirebaseMessagingService (manifest-registered): onNewToken → forward to provider's token callback; onMessageReceived → if app foreground, deliver to the message listener; if background, post a tray notification whose tap intent re-launches the Activity with push extras (→ cold/warm tap routing per §4.5). Messages can arrive with no Activity/QuickJS alive — the Service is the entry point, the Activity is not.
  • Gradle: add com.google.firebase:firebase-messaging to the capsule module + com.google.gms.google-services plugin. This changes the AAR build → stale-AAR rule applies (assembleRelease before any build android).
  • CLI sync: copy android.push.googleServicesFile (from capsule.config.ts, per Q19) → .capsule/android/app/google-services.json. google-services.json is app-specific (project id / api key / app id) — never bundled in the shell; the developer supplies the path. Add config typing + a capsule doctor check that warns if push is used without it.

docs.title: 7. iOS (APNs) seam — Phase 4, defined now (D6)
docs.text: Same PushProvider interface. iOS impl: UNUserNotificationCenter for permissions/channels (channels are a no-op — iOS has no channel concept), registerForRemoteNotifications + application(_:didRegisterForRemoteNotificationsWithDeviceToken:) → PushToken{platform:'ios'}, didReceiveRemoteNotification / userNotificationCenter(_:didReceive:) → message + tap. Cold tap arrives via launchOptions[.remoteNotification] → setLaunchNotification (the APNs analogue of the Android launch-intent extras). No third-party SDK — APNs is pure platform (Q19). Declared in capsule.config.ts ios.capabilities: ['push-notifications'] (already in publishing.md).

docs.title: 8. Test plan (run ALL tiers at the end)
docs.text:
Tier Slice 1 Slice 2 core vitest push.ts module shape, method-name wire constants, unsubscribe semantics; WebBridge fallback — CLI vitest — google-services.json copy on sync; doctor warning when path missing Kotlin JVM PushControllerTest (emit MESSAGE/TAP/ERROR; consume-once launch notification), PushHandlerTest (each request handler over FakePushProvider, incl. modes) — Instrumented — AndroidPushProviderTest — channel CRUD against real NotificationManager; tokenLivesOutsideOtaBundleDir assertion (D5) Device smoke Push screen renders, register button returns the fake token, console-simulated message/tap update the log real FCM: send a test message from Firebase console → foreground arrival logs live; background → tray notification → tap cold/warm-routes to the Push screen

Example screen (PushScreen.tsx): register button + token display, permission status + request button, channel create/list (Android), and a live event log of messages + taps (cold tap shown via getLaunchNotification() on mount, warm via onNotificationTap) — follows the NetworkScreen get-then-subscribe pattern. Registry entry: { id: 'push', title: 'Push', icon: '🔔', group: 'Native APIs', Component: PushScreen }.

docs.title: 9. Build-order checklist for a fresh session
docs.text:
1. ✅ Slice 1 — core/src/push.ts + index export + WebBridge fallback + errors.ts → pnpm run build (core).
  2. ✅ PushProvider.kt (interface + data classes) → PushController.kt → FakePushProvider.kt → PushHandlers.kt (+ BridgeError.PushRegistrationFailed).
  3. ✅ PushControllerTest.kt + PushHandlerTest.kt → gradlew test (JVM, offline — must stay green).
  4. ⏭️ Wire CapsuleActivity.kt — moved to Slice 2 (needs AndroidPushProvider; see §4).
  5. ✅ PushScreen.tsx + registry entry → core vitest + CLI vitest.
  6. Commit Slice 1 (English Conventional Commits across capsule + examples + docs).
  7. Slice 2 — AndroidPushProvider.kt + CapsulePushService.kt + CapsuleActivity wiring (§4)
  8. Gradle/google-services + CLI sync + config typing → assembleRelease (stale-AAR rule) → AndroidPushProviderTest.kt → instrumented + device smoke → commit Slice 2.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: Let's create a simple capsule app and run it on an emulator or device.

docs.title: 1. Create a new app
docs.text:
capsule create my-first-app --template react-ts
cd my-first-app

docs.title: 2. Install app dependencies
docs.text: pnpm install

docs.title: 3. Start the development server
docs.text:
# This starts Vite (client) and the Node.js server for QuickJS
pnpm dev

In another terminal, run the Android dev command:

pnpm dev:android

You should see the app launch in the emulator or attached device.

docs.title: 4. Make a change
docs.text: Edit src/App.tsx and save – the changes will hot‑reload instantly.

docs.title: 5. Build a release APK
docs.text:
pnpm build:android --release

The signed APK will be located at android/app/build/outputs/apk/release/app-release.apk.

That's it! You’ve just built and run a Capsule app.

docs.title: Step 5 — QuickJSBridge: @capsule/core routes in QuickJS ✅
docs.text:
What was built:

File Role packages/core/src/router.ts addRoute(method, handler) + dispatch(requestJson) — returns object \| null (not string) packages/core/tsup.config.ts Added src/router.ts entry → produces dist/router.{js,mjs,d.ts} packages/core/package.json Added "./routes" export pointing to dist/router.* packages/cli/src/commands/build.ts bundleRoutes() — esbuild IIFE bundle (globalName: 'capsuleRouter') + appends var dispatch = capsuleRouter.dispatch; var addRoute = capsuleRouter.addRoute; to routes.js capsule-android/.../runtime/QuickJSBridge.kt Loads assets/www/routes.js into engine, routes JSON-RPC via engine.call("dispatch", "[quoted]") capsule-android/.../CapsuleBridge.kt Tries QuickJS first (quickJsBridge?.handleRequest(raw)), falls through to Kotlin on null capsule-android/.../CapsuleActivity.kt Creates QuickJSEngineImpl + QuickJSBridge, wires both into CapsuleRuntime

Deleted: handlers/quickjs/QuickJSPingHandler.kt (superseded by real bridge)

Instrumented tests: 4 passing in QuickJSBridgeTest.kt - handleRequest_unregisteredMethod_returnsNull ✓ - handleRequest_registeredMethod_returnsJsonRpcResponse ✓ - handleRequest_handlerThrows_returnsErrorResponse ✓ - handleRequest_jsHandlerTakesPriorityOverKotlin ✓

Critical QuickJS JNI constraints discovered (required for correctness):

  1. globalThis is the only reliable persistent namespace across evaluate() → call() boundaries. Top-level var bindings and function-object properties (e.g. fn._routes = {}) are NOT reliably visible inside functions called via engine.call(). The C helper uses globalThis[fn] — use globalThis.__capsule_routes for shared state.

  2. JS functions called via engine.call must return plain objects, not JSON strings. The C __capsule_call helper wraps every return value in JSON.stringify(). If JS dispatch() returns a pre-serialised string (from JSON.stringify({...})), the result is double-encoded: "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",...}". The correct pattern is to return the object directly: return { jsonrpc: '2.0', id, result }.

  3. router.ts: dispatch() return type is object | null (was string | null)

  4. Test routerScript: return { jsonrpc: "2.0", id, result } (not JSON.stringify(...))
  5. Exception: production esbuild IIFE bundle is fine — all routes registered inside the IIFE before it returns, closures work correctly within a single evaluate() call.
