docs.title: Capsule — Business Model (Server Code Push as the Funding Engine)
docs.text:
The framework is free and open source. The money is a managed cloud for OTA delivery + governance + analytics. This is open-core SaaS — the same model as Expo EAS, Appflow, and the (now-dead) CodePush. This doc captures the commercial strategy decided in the 2026-06-15 strategy session.

Technical specs for the server itself live in ../server-design/overview.md (control plane), ../server-design/file-storage.md (bundle delivery/CDN), and ../../guide/publishing.md (codesync publish vs publish). This doc is the why and the who-pays, not the how.

docs.title: The model in one line
docs.text: Free, open, no-lock-in framework + Ionic/F7 migration on-ramp = the funnel. A managed "safe-deploy" OTA cloud whose flagship is canary + auto-rollback = the revenue. Sold first to agencies. Gated on iOS shipping.

docs.title: Why open source the framework at all
docs.text:
Lock-in fear is the #1 reason developers refuse hybrid OTA tooling (Appflow is the cautionary tale). Open-sourcing the runtime, CLI, and sync protocol — and shipping a self-hostable server — makes the anti-lock-in pitch real and removes adoption friction. The cloud (convenience, scale, governance, analytics, multi-tenant) is the moat, not the protocol.

This also defuses the CodePush death trap: CodePush offered unlimited free hosted OTA and the bandwidth bill helped kill it. With a self-hostable server, "free + unlimited" = bring your own infra — you're never on the hook for someone else's egress.

docs.title: Market timing (lead with this)
docs.text:
• Microsoft App Center retired (March 2025); CodePush deprecated → many RN/Cordova/hybrid apps orphaned and actively shopping for a new OTA provider.
  • Appflow is expensive and Ionic-locked.
  • Wedge sentence: "CodePush is dead, Appflow is a tax. Capsule gives you OTA with automatic crash-rollback, an open-source runtime, and no lock-in."

docs.title: ICP — agencies first, freelancers as the funnel
docs.text:
Three buyers want opposite things; do not design for all three at once:

Buyer Wants Role in strategy Freelancers / indie devs Free + simple Funnel. Served by the free tier + OSS. Cheapest acquisition channel — they recommend Capsule into agencies. Keep them happy; don't design the product around them. Agencies (many client apps) Multi-tenant, many apps, per-client channels Primary ICP. Most apps, clearest multi-tenant pain, budget, most CodePush-orphaned. Land these first. Enterprises Canary, SSO, audit, on-prem, SLA Upmarket pull. Agencies pull you here; high-ticket, but heavier sales.

docs.title: Free vs paid — what's the line
docs.text:
Meter on MAU + bandwidth, NOT on deploy count. Deploys are nearly free to serve and frequent small deploys are the behavior to encourage. The original "1 codesync/day / 100 test versions/day" axes were wrong — dropped. (Pricing table: pricing.md.)

Free tier shape: unlimited production deploys, unmetered dev/staging channels, 1,000 MAU, 3 seats, 30-day / last-10-version retention, basic metrics. Plus a self-hostable OSS server with no caps (your infra). The premium modules (canary/auto-rollback, multi-tenant, advanced analytics, SSO, managed signing) are the open-core "closed" parts — absent from the free hosted tier and the OSS server.

docs.title: Paid feature priorities (graded)
docs.text: Feature Verdict Canary / pilot rollout + auto-rollback on crash signal 🥇 Flagship. Enterprises pay for safe deploys. The on-device crash-loop guard already exists (Phase 2 Step 7) — the server side reports crashes → halts rollout → auto-rolls-back. Monetizes work already done. Multi-app / multi-tenant per company 🥇 Enterprise gold. Exactly the agency + white-label-SaaS pain. Per-tenant channels + RBAC = top tier. Device segmentation (geo, version) ✅ Substrate canary/targeting rides on. Scheduled sync ✅ Easy paid lever. Metrics + logs portal + crash analytics ✅ Closes the loop with auto-rollback (data-driven decisions). Unlimited devices/deploys/seats ✅ Standard scaling lever. MCP server for AI ⚠️ Distribution channel, not a SKU. Make read/deploy-status MCP free (gets Capsule into every AI dev workflow); gate only scoped automation (CI deploys, agent-triggered prod rollout) behind paid. AI app-builder + online VSCode 🛑 Scope creep, wrong customer. Serves greenfield/new apps, not the migrate-off-Ionic ICP. A whole separate product (IDE infra, sandboxes, hosting). Defer, or run a stripped version purely as lead-gen — never a revenue line now.

docs.title: Features the original list missed (enterprises pay for these)
docs.text:
1. Compatibility gating — minNativeVersion / bridge-contract version per bundle so a new OTA refuses to activate on an old shell before it crashes (already in publishing.md). Feature + safety story. See ota-policy-and-liability.md.
  2. Mandatory vs optional updates + forced-update screens.
  3. Differential / binary-diff updates — cuts your bandwidth bill and sells as "instant updates." Pure margin (see ../server-design/file-storage.md).
  4. Compliance tier — SSO/SAML, audit log, RBAC.
  5. On-prem / self-managed Enterprise license — banks/gov/health. High-ticket; it's the OSS server + license + support SLA.
  6. Bundle signing / integrity — tamper protection on the OTA payload.

docs.title: Store positioning (the superpower)
docs.text:
Two update paths (full detail in ota-policy-and-liability.md and publishing.md):

  • capsule codesync publish → OTA, instant, no store review (most updates: JS/web bundle + QuickJS logic).
  • capsule publish → automated store submission via Fastlane/store APIs (native-shell changes only).

Headline: most updates never touch the store. The store becomes an occasional event, not a per-release tax. Never market this as "bypass review" — see the liability doc.

docs.title: Open risks tracked
docs.text:
1. iOS is the gate. Almost nobody pays for Android-only OTA. Monetization is sequenced after iOS. See roadmap re-sequencing in ../roadmap.md and bring-up plan in ../../contributing/ios-bring-up.md.
  2. Apple/Google OTA policy + the QuickJS-vs-JavaScriptCore clause → ota-policy-and-liability.md.
  3. Trust / reliability. A startup running production OTA infra must earn trust: uptime, SLA, CDN reliability. Infra economics in ../infrastructure.md.

docs.title: OTA Policy & Liability (Apple / Google)
docs.text: Where Capsule's responsibility ends and the customer's begins, how store policy bounds OTA, and the one clause to keep an eye on. Decided in the 2026-06-15 strategy session.

docs.title: Liability posture: you are a tool vendor
docs.text:
If a customer uses OTA to change their app's behavior in violation of store policy, that is the customer's problem, not Capsule's. The customer holds the developer account, signs the binary, agreed to Apple's/Google's developer terms, and submits the app. Stores enforce against the app/account, not the tool that produced the bundle. CodePush, Expo Updates, and Appflow all enable exactly this — none is liable for what customers push. Same posture for Capsule.

That default only holds if you don't undermine it:

  1. Terms of Service + Acceptable Use Policy (non-negotiable before charging): the customer is solely responsible for store compliance; Capsule may suspend accounts pushing policy-violating updates. Standard SaaS shield.
  2. Never market "bypass review." Position = "ship fixes and content fast, within policy" — never "skip the store." Marketing language is legally and reputationally load-bearing.
  3. Warn + require acknowledgment (below).

docs.title: Deterministic — capability gating (BUILD THIS; it's also a feature)
docs.text:
You can detect exactly when an OTA needs something the installed shell doesn't have: a new permission, a new native plugin, or a bridge-contract / minNativeVersion bump. This is deterministic. The tool blocks the OTA and says "this needs a new store release — run capsule publish."

  • Same mechanism as minNativeVersion gating in ../../guide/publishing.md.
  • Doubles as the strongest safety guardrail and a sellable governance feature.

docs.title: Best-effort — semantic policy warning (warn + acknowledge, don't promise)
docs.text:
You cannot auto-detect a "primary purpose change" — that's semantic. So the diff tool surfaces signals (new top-level routes, large bundle delta, anything resembling an added payment flow or external-purchase link — Apple's hot button) and shows a one-time "Confirm this update complies with store policy" acknowledgment.

  • Moves responsibility explicitly onto the customer.
  • Creates an audit-trail entry (who acknowledged what, when) — itself an enterprise feature.

docs.title: The clause to keep an eye on: QuickJS vs JavaScriptCore
docs.text:
Apple's developer agreement permits OTA interpreted code as long as it doesn't change the app's primary purpose — but historically references code run by Apple's WebKit / JavaScriptCore.

Capsule surface Engine Status Web bundle (UI) WKWebView (WebKit) ✅ Squarely allowed Server route runtime QuickJS (third-party JS engine) ⚠️ The gray edge of the clause

Reassuring precedent: React Native's Hermes engine is also not JavaScriptCore, and CodePush OTA-updated Hermes/RN bundles for years with no Apple action. In practice Apple tolerates non-JSC interpreted code over OTA as long as the primary-purpose rule holds.

Conservative framing to maintain: position QuickJS server routes as handling logic/data, not the app's nature. Keep an eye on the clause; don't build messaging that depends on its loosest reading.

docs.title: Google
docs.text: Looser than Apple on OTA, but watching for: dynamic code that circumvents the permission model, or behavior that materially differs from the reviewed listing. The same capability-gating guardrail (no new permissions/native via OTA) keeps you onside.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Customer owns compliance. Protect the default with a ToS/AUP and non-evasion marketing.
  • Build the deterministic capability gate (real guardrail + governance feature).
  • Treat the semantic policy check as best-effort + acknowledgment + audit log.
  • Watch the QuickJS-OTA clause; Hermes/CodePush precedent says it's been fine.

docs.title: Capsule — Pricing, Payments & Trial
docs.text: Illustrative pricing decided in the 2026-06-15 strategy session. Validate against 5–10 customer interviews before locking numbers. Strategy context: business-model.md.

docs.title: Pricing principle
docs.text:
Meter on MAU (monthly active devices) + bandwidth — never on deploy count. Deploys are cheap to serve; frequent small deploys are the behavior to encourage. Bandwidth is the real cost driver (see ../infrastructure.md).

Anchors: Appflow Live Updates ~$499+/mo; Expo EAS has a free tier + usage; the dead-CodePush gap is the opening.

docs.title: Tiers
docs.text:
Tier Price MAU Seats Apps Key features Community (self-host) Free, OSS Unlimited (your infra) n/a n/a Run the OSS server. No canary/analytics/multi-tenant/SSO modules. Free (hosted) $0 1,000 3 1 Unlimited deploys, unmetered staging, 30-day / last-10 retention, basic metrics Pro ~$49/mo 10,000 5 3 Scheduled sync, basic canary, device segments, metrics + logs portal Team ~$199/mo 50,000 15 10 Canary + auto-rollback, multi-tenant channels, audit log, priority support Business ~$499/mo 200,000 unlimited unlimited SSO/SAML, RBAC, differential updates, managed signing Enterprise Custom unlimited unlimited unlimited On-prem / self-managed license, SLA, data residency, support contract
  • Overage: ~$10–20 per additional 1,000 MAU. (Meter the bandwidth axis, not deploys.)
  • Annual billing: 2 months free (~17% off) — pulls cashflow forward for a self-funded project.

docs.title: Trial
docs.text:
• Free tier forever (product-led growth — the freelancer/indie on-ramp).
  • 14-day trial of Team-tier features, no credit card. Converts agencies who hit multi-tenant / canary needs.

docs.title: Payment processor
docs.text:
Start with a Merchant-of-Record (Paddle or Lemon Squeezy), not raw Stripe.

  • The hard part of international SaaS isn't taking payments — it's global sales-tax / VAT compliance. Raw Stripe makes you the merchant: you owe VAT registration/filing across many jurisdictions.
  • Paddle / Lemon Squeezy are the merchant of record — they collect and remit VAT/tax worldwide for you, for ~5% + fees. Worth it for a solo founder until there's finance headcount.
  • Migrate to Stripe Billing later at scale, when you want fine-grained usage-based metering (MAU/bandwidth) control and can absorb tax compliance.
Need Pick Solo founder, global sales, no tax team Paddle / Lemon Squeezy (MoR) Scale, usage-based metering, own the stack Stripe Billing

docs.title: Metering implementation note
docs.text: MAU and bandwidth are computed from CodeSync check-in / download events already flowing through the control plane (see ../server-design/workers.md job queues and ../server-design/database.md). Bill on the metered axis; expose current usage in the dashboard so customers self-serve upgrades before hitting hard caps.

docs.title: Embedded Server Startup — Bind-Race Analysis & Fix Plan
docs.text: Status: analysis complete (2026-10-15); SR-1, SR-3 and SR-4's error-screen catch-all shipped; resolved 2026-10-24 by replacing the server — see Resolution below. D2/D3 (probe + bind retry) were removed with NanoHTTPD. Symptom source: cold-start testing on emulator + real device — the splash ("loader") does not wait for the server and reveals an error page (reported as a 404; the WebView error page for this failure is actually net::ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED — same user-visible UX). Owns: the startup contract for the embedded loopback server (adr-001 #6, serving transport per adr-004).

docs.title: Resolution 2026-10-24: CivetWeb
docs.text:
The server itself was replaced on both platforms by CivetWeb (adr-004 amendment, primer: civetweb.md). That changes how each part of the fix design holds:

Design item Now D1 contract — start() returns only when the port accepts Unchanged, and now true by construction: mg_start2 returns only after the listening socket is bound and listening. Stated on the Kotlin CapsuleServer interface and the Swift CapsuleServer protocol (SR-5). D2 readiness probe, D3 bind retry Removed — nothing to wait for. A bind failure is reported by CivetWeb directly and surfaces as a typed error: Android ServerStartupException ("Port N is already in use by another process" when the port is held), iOS ServerStartupError.portInUse. D4 WebView main-frame retry Kept as defense in depth (WebViewRetryPolicy, WebViewRetryPolicyTest). D5 error surfacing Unchanged (CapsuleActivity catch-all → error screen).

Stop/start semantics (new). stop() returns at once and releases the port on a background thread: mg_stop joins CivetWeb's workers, and a worker can be inside an /api route that waits on the main thread, so joining on the caller's thread could deadlock. The next start() on the same port waits for that shutdown before binding — an Activity/scene recreation never sees "port in use" from its own previous instance.

Where the contract is pinned:

  • Android — CivetwebServerTest (instrumented, src/androidTest/): a GET immediately after start() with no sleep or retry; port-in-use → typed exception; a new server starts on the same port right after stop(); plus assets, 404s, a 1 MB streamed asset, /api through JNI, HEAD. These moved from the JVM tier to the instrumented tier because the native server cannot load on a plain JVM; the routing rules stay on the JVM (RequestRouterTest, ParseHeadersTest).
  • iOS — CivetwebServerTests (7 tests, real sockets — run on Linux in Docker) mirrors the Android cases; RequestRouterTests (10) mirrors RequestRouterTest.

SR-4 with the new server (2026-10-24, API 36 emulator, examples/react-ts release build): 20 cold starts + 10 quick relaunches, every launch rendered, no startup error. Still to repeat on a physical device. S2 (below) is still open: the server still serves the bundled www/ only, not the OTA-installed bundle.

docs.title: Root cause — verified against the nanohttpd-2.3.1 bytecode, not guessed
docs.text:
CapsuleRuntime.start() (runtime/CapsuleRuntime.kt) runs:

withTimeout(timeoutMs) { server.start() }        // NanoHttpdServer.start()
quickJsBridge?.load()
navigator.navigateTo("http://127.0.0.1:${server.port}/")

NanoHttpdServer.start() calls httpd.start(SOCKET_READ_TIMEOUT, false). Decompile of fi.iki.elonen.NanoHTTPD#start(int, boolean) (2.3.1, from the resolved jar):

getServerSocketFactory().create()      // UNBOUND ServerSocket — no bind here
myServerSocket.setReuseAddress(true)
createServerRunnable(timeout)          // the Runnable performs the bind
new Thread(runnable).start()           // bind runs on the new thread…
// …and start() RETURNS — before the socket is bound or accepting

ServerRunnable.run() then calls ServerSocket.bind(...) on that thread and records failures in a private bindException field — there is no public API in 2.3.1 to observe bind success or failure.

So CapsuleServer.start() returns before the server can accept a single connection. The documented contract — adr-001 #6 "binds NanoHTTPD … on ready → navigate" and the runtime KDoc "if the server does not bind within timeoutMs" — is not enforced anywhere. Consequences:

# Failure chain User-visible F1 Fast device: renderer connects before bind() completes ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED error page ("404" as remembered) F2 withTimeout(3s) { server.start() } — start() already returned, so the timeout never bounds the bind; it only guards a hung withContext(IO) the documented 3s guard is dead code for this failure mode F3 Quick relaunch in the dev loop: the previous process still holds the deterministic port → bind() throws inside the thread, stored in private bindException, never surfaced; server never comes up splash hangs until readyTimeoutMs (10s), then reveals the error page; the 3s timeout never fires F4 A refused load never reaches notifyAppReady → CrashLoopGuard records it as an unconfirmed launch — the right reaction, but F1's root cause can manufacture crash loops spurious rollback risk on fast cold-restarts

Why it is intermittent: the race window is (thread start → bind()), a few milliseconds — slow devices lose the race less often than fast emulators. Matches the emulator + device reports.

docs.title: Secondary finding (related, separate task)
docs.text: NanoHttpdServer.serve() serves static files only from assets/www/. OTA bundles installed by BundleStore (filesDir/bundles/active) are never served — on-device CodeSync updates cannot apply. Tracked as its own roadmap item (S2 below); the startup fix does not depend on it.

docs.title: D1 — Contract: CapsuleServer.start() returns only when the server accepts connections
docs.text: The honest interface. KDoc on CapsuleServer states it; implementations enforce it. The runtime's existing withTimeout(timeoutMs) finally becomes the real bind deadline it always claimed to be. (Recorded as an amendment to adr-001 #6.)

docs.title: D2 — Enforcement: readiness probe in NanoHttpdServer
docs.text: After httpd.start(...): loop-connect a local socket to 127.0.0.1:{port} (backoff 20–50ms, deadline ≈ 2s — inside the runtime's 3s), close immediately. A successful connect is the definitive "bound + accepting" proof (what production health checks do) — it sidesteps NanoHTTPD 2.3.1's private hasBinded/bindException. On deadline: throw a typed ServerStartupException, diagnosed by attempting a bind (distinguishes "port in use" from other failures).

docs.title: D3 — Hardening: bind retry with backoff
docs.text: Retry httpd.start() up to 3 times (200ms apart) before failing — absorbs the quick-relaunch race (F3). Failures after the last attempt surface as D2's typed exception.

docs.title: D4 — Defense in depth: WebView main-frame retry
docs.text: In CapsuleWebViewClient: on main-frame connection-type errors (ERROR_CONNECT, ERROR_CONNECTION_REFUSED… — not ERROR_UNKNOWN, not sub-frame), retry the load up to 3 times (150/300/600ms) before surfacing the error screen. The retry decision (shouldRetryLoad(errorCode, attempt)) is a pure function + unit test, per the repo's pure-logic discipline.

docs.title: D5 — Error surfacing
docs.text: CapsuleActivity catches ServerStartupException/IOException alongside TimeoutCancellationException → the same error screen. No silent thread-internal death (F3).

docs.title: Explicitly rejected
docs.text:
• Ephemeral port (port 0) — adr-001 #7's deterministic port stays (dev-server consistency, adb reverse, deep-link stability).
  • Holding the splash for "server ready" instead of "page ready" — the splash already waits for page render; the bug is load-before-bind, not splash timing.
  • A third "loading" HTML page served by the server — the server is the thing not ready.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text: Phase Deliverable Done-when SR-1 D1 contract: CapsuleServer.start() KDoc + ServerStartupException type; FakeCapsuleServer unchanged (StartsAfter already models a slow bind) compiles; all 168 existing tests green SR-2 D2+D3 in NanoHttpdServer: probe loop, bind retry, typed failure new real-socket test: a GET / immediately after start() returns succeeds (ephemeral port); probe-deadline test asserts the typed exception SR-3 D4: pure shouldRetryLoad(errorCode, attempt) + wiring in CapsuleWebViewClient JVM unit test pins the decision table; existing CapsuleWebViewClientTest green SR-4 D5: Activity catch-all → error screen manual e2e: 20× cold start on emulator + device with zero error pages; 10× quick-relaunch with a clear error (if a stale holder is simulated) SR-5 iOS parity: the same contract recorded for the future Swift CapsuleServer (Phase 4) — GCDWebServer-class impl must bind-before-return contract text in adr-001 + this doc; iOS CapsuleServer protocol (when created) carries it

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
• Emulator + real device: 20× cold start — no error pages; 10× rapid relaunch — clean failure mode (no silent hang past 3s).
  • pnpm --filter @capsule/core test + Kotlin testDebugUnitTest stay green.

docs.title: Planning Brainstorm — 2026-06-24
docs.text: Sequencing + scope decisions raised after Push Slice 1 shipped. Captures what's decided (low-risk, I can act on it), what's open (your call), and the consolidated questions at the end. Once you answer, the outcomes fold into 000-Roadmap.md (and an ADR if the Phase-4 sequencing changes). This doc is transient — delete it once the roadmap is updated.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: # Topic Status One-line outcome 1 Firebase config ownership ✅ Decided Customer owns google-services.json; Capsule only makes wiring frictionless. 2 Defer Push Slice 2 (Firebase) ✅ Decided Yes — Local Notifications goes next; Slice 2 slots in later, smaller. 3 Emulator vs real device ℹ️ Info Emulator covers #5–#8 and Push; device only for NFC/Bluetooth/on-device-AI-perf. 4 Missing native APIs 🔄 Open Gap list below (+ live competitive scan pending). Pick which to adopt. 5 Move Server Code Push to Phase 4 ❗ Open — needs your call Viable; hinges on "product-to-launch vs system-to-master." Middle path recommended. 6 Primer docs (Kotlin/C·C++/NanoHTTPD/QuickJS) ✅ Decided Yes — 4 primers under ../Primers/, anchored to your C#/TS background.

docs.title: 1. Firebase config — customer owns it (hard boundary)
docs.text:
Capsule must never ship a shared google-services.json. That file encodes a specific Firebase project + API key + sender ID + GCP billing account; FCM tokens are scoped to that sender. A shared config = cross-app push, quota collisions, and Capsule carrying abuse/billing liability. Every peer (Capacitor, RN, Flutter) requires the developer's own file.

Capsule's job: CLI sync copies the dropped-in file → .capsule/android/app/google-services.json; capsule doctor warns if push is declared without it; config typing points at its path. A capsule firebase scaffolding helper is a fine future nicety. A Phase-5 cloud managed push-relay (dev uploads their FCM service-account key, sends through Capsule's API) is possible later — but even then the client config stays the dev's.

docs.title: 2. Defer Push Slice 2 (Firebase) — yes
docs.text: Slice 1 (the seam) is done, committed, proven offline + browser. Slice 2 was designed to be liftable (022 D3); nothing else depends on real FCM. Better still: Local Notifications (#6) is pure-platform (no Google) and reuses the same NotificationManager + channels + POST_NOTIFICATIONS infra — so doing it next lets it own a shared channel manager, making Firebase Slice 2 smaller when you get to it. Defer on motivation, not blockers.

docs.title: 3. Emulator coverage — you can stay on the emulator a long time
docs.text:
API Emulator? Push / FCM ✅ Yes — use a Google Play / Google APIs AVD; FCM delivers to emulators. Local notifications · Status bar · Keyboard · Share · SQLite ✅ Yes Biometrics ✅ Yes — enroll a fake fingerprint (adb emu finger touch / extended controls). Telecom / SMS ⚠️ Partial — emulator simulates calls/SMS via extended controls. NFC ❌ Real device Bluetooth ❌ Real device (emulator BT unreliable/absent) On-device AI (Gemini Nano/AICore) ⚠️ Logic via FakeAiProvider; real perf needs Pixel 8+/compatible

The device-only items (NFC, Bluetooth, on-device AI perf) are all late in the order. Daily-drive a Play-Store AVD.

docs.title: 4. Missing native APIs (from-knowledge — live scan appended below when it lands)
docs.text:
Against the Capacitor baseline, table-stakes APIs not on the roadmap, cheapest/highest-value first:

Capability Priority Note Browser / In-App Browser (Custom Tabs / SFSafariViewController) High External URLs / OAuth flows. Secure storage (Keystore/Keychain-backed) High Distinct from plain storage; needed for tokens. Security-relevant. App Launcher (canOpenUrl, open tel:/mailto:/maps) High Common, trivial. Toast High Ubiquitous, trivial. Splash Screen control API (splash.hide/show) Med Splash exists internally; no JS control yet. Screen Orientation (lock/unlock) Med — File / Document picker Med Distinct from camera/gallery. Barcode / QR scanning (ML Kit) Med Huge in the community. Motion/sensors · Calendar · Contacts · Background geolocation Low Common community plugins.

Framework7 is a UI framework (components/router/theming) that leans on Capacitor/Cordova for native — not a native-API competitor. The lesson for Capsule isn't "match F7's native APIs" (it has none) but "Phase 7's migration on-ramp must absorb F7/Ionic UI + routing conventions." (F7 v9, Nov 2025: iOS-26 visual redesign, React 19 / Svelte 5 adapters — pure UI-layer, no native or AI moves.)

docs.title: Live competitive scan (Capacitor/Ionic, 2025-2026) — findings
docs.text:
Correction: the scan flagged "Filesystem" as a gap because my prompt omitted it — Capsule has Filesystem (✅ done). Ignore that row. Confirmed/refined gaps below.

Capability Stakes Note (from scan) Browser + In-App Browser High Capacitor split these into two official plugins (@capacitor/browser + @capacitor/inappbrowser). External URLs / OAuth / embedded webviews. Capsule has none. Secure storage (Keystore/Keychain) High Two community plugins at ~80–103k/wk. Encrypted tokens, distinct from storage. Splash Screen control High Official; Capsule has splash internally, no JS control API. App Launcher (outbound) High Official; Capsule has inbound deep-links but not outbound app launch / canOpenUrl. Toast + Action Sheet High / Med-High Both official; pair with our alerts. Barcode / QR (ML Kit) Med-High Capacitor promoted this to an official plugin — strong table-stakes signal. File / document picker Med-High @capawesome/capacitor-file-picker ~87k/wk; distinct from camera. App Badge Med ~126k/wk — pairs directly with our push/local-notifications; cheap, high-value. Native HTTP (CORS bypass) Med Official @capacitor/http + @capacitor/cookies. Our network is connectivity-status only — native fetch is a real gap. TTS / Speech recognition Med Natural companion to our on-device-AI direction (voice + LLM). Privacy Screen Med Now official — blur in task-switcher + block screenshots. Security/compliance. Motion · Screen Orientation · Contacts · Calendar · In-app review · In-app update · Social/OAuth login · Background geolocation Low-Med Common community plugins; adopt per app need.

docs.title: Strategic news that nudges YOUR open questions
docs.text:
1. Appflow is winding down (sales stopped 2025-02-11, EOL 2027-12-31; Live Updates folding into paid OutSystems cloud). Independent OTA (Capawesome Cloud, Capgo) is filling the vacuum right now. → Directly validates "Server Code Push as funding engine" — the incumbent vacated the open/independent OTA market exactly as you'd enter it. This is a real tailwind for Q-B option (B)/(A): pull OTA forward. Caveat: it doesn't change the iOS-market logic (agencies want both platforms), but it means the window for the independent-OTA wave is open now and narrows as Capawesome/Capgo entrench.
  2. Ionic shipped an official on-device LLM plugin (capacitor-local-llm v1.0.0, 2026-05-11): unified TS API over Apple Foundation Models + Gemini Nano, incl. image gen + multi-turn sessions. → Capsule's Tier-1 ai is now parity catch-up, not pioneering; the bar rose to "unified cross-platform TS surface + sessions (+ voice companion)." The moat is still OTA-updatable agents, not raw inference.
  3. Capacitor Skills (2026-06-03): reusable AI-agent primitives — the same "native capabilities as composable agent tools" thesis as our adr-003. Convergent validation; our OTA-updatable-agents angle is arguably ahead of their static-skills approach.
  4. Platform churn to anticipate: Capacitor 8 (2025-12-08) made SPM the iOS default + added Android edge-to-edge/SystemBars; ~6-month release cadence tracking annual OS releases. Feed this into Phase 4 (iOS) + the upkeep routine.

docs.title: 5. Move Server Code Push to Phase 4 (before iOS)? — the big call
docs.text:
Technically viable. OTA has no hard iOS dependency; the capability-versioning it needs (CapabilityRegistry) already exists. The bulk — capsule codesync publish, control plane, portal, DB, billing UI — is platform-agnostic web/backend work in your wheelhouse (C#/TS), and the on-device fetch/apply half is emulator-testable. Fits both "play to my strengths" and "stay on emulator."

The tension: advancing OTA freezes the native layer at ~9 APIs (no local-notif, biometrics, secure storage…), and the biz model wrote OTA cloud as "gated on iOS" (agencies want both platforms; Android-only halves the market). But you're explicitly not racing for funds (the whole re-sequence was capability-first) — so "gated on iOS" may be over-conservative for a personal build. The AI agent layer + Tier-2/3 inference are also bundled into Phase 6 with OTA (adr-003: OTA-updatable agents = the moat) — pulling OTA forward raises the question of whether AI comes too.

Recommended middle path: finish a thin, high-value Phase 3 first — Local Notifications → Biometrics → Status bar/Keyboard/Share + Toast + Browser (all emulator-friendly, each a few days, no Google) — so the Android framework feels complete and gives you tools to showcase. Then make Server Code Push your Phase 4; defer iOS + hardware APIs (NFC/BT) + on-device AI perf. Push Slice 2 (Firebase) slots in whenever you feel like touching Google.

→ See Q-A / Q-B / Q-C below.

docs.title: 6. Primer docs — yes (../Primers/)
docs.text:
Capsule-specific primers anchored to your C#/OO + TS/web background (not generic tutorials), each linked to real Capsule files:

  • kotlin-for-csharp-devs.md — null-safety (?/!!), data class (≈ records), sealed class (≈ discriminated unions → BridgeError), object/companion object (≈ static), coroutines/suspend (≈ async/await → suspendCancellableCoroutine in PushHandlers), fun interface (≈ delegates → BridgeEventEmitter), extension functions.
  • jni-and-cpp.md — the Kotlin ↔ C/C++ ↔ QuickJS boundary; what JNI is; QuickJSEngineImpl's single-thread dispatcher + 4 MB stack; why strings must be objects.
  • nanohttpd.md — why an embedded HTTP server exists; NanoHttpdServer serving assets/www/ at 127.0.0.1:{port}; the /api/* → QuickJS route; lifecycle.
  • quickjs.md — JS engine vs V8; why Capsule embeds QuickJS-ng; the dispatch() contract; globalThis as the only reliable store; the vendoring model.

→ See Q-E below.

docs.title: Open Questions — your answers drive the next moves
docs.text:
• Q-A (the pivotal one): Is Capsule, right now, a product you intend to launch (→ iOS matters early, keep OTA gated on it) or a system you're building to master/use yourself (→ Android-only OTA is fine, pull it forward freely)? Scan input: the Appflow wind-down opens the independent-OTA window now — a point for "launch", but only if you move before Capawesome/Capgo entrench.
  • Q-B — Sequencing: Pick one:
  • (A) Middle path (recommended): thin Phase 3 (Local notif → Biometrics → Status bar/Keyboard/Share/Toast/Browser) → OTA = Phase 4 → iOS → AI/hardware.
  • (B) Your instinct: OTA right now (Phase 4) → fill the rest later.
  • (C) Status quo: finish all of Phase 3 → iOS → OTA+AI (Phase 6).
  • Q-C — AI: If OTA moves to Phase 4, does the AI agent layer + Tier-2/3 inference move with it, or stay in Phase 6? Scan input: Ionic now ships an official on-device-LLM plugin, so Tier-1 ai is parity-catch-up; the durable moat is OTA-updatable agents (which live with OTA) — a mild nudge to keep AI paired with OTA.
  • Q-D — Native gaps: Which of §4's gap APIs do you want on the roadmap? Refined top picks after the scan: Browser/In-App Browser, Secure storage, App Launcher, Toast + two the scan elevated — App Badge (pairs with push, ~126k/wk) and Barcode/ML-Kit (Capacitor just made it official).
  • Q-E — Primers: Write all four now, or one sample (kotlin-for-csharp-devs.md) first to check tone/depth?
  • Q-F — Firebase: For whenever Slice 2 happens — do you already have (or will you create) a Firebase project + google-services.json? (Free; runs on a Play-Store emulator, no device needed.)

docs.title: Immediate next action (pending your answers)
docs.text: Default if you just say "go": Local Notifications (#6) next — pure-platform, emulator-friendly, builds the shared channel manager that shrinks Push Slice 2. Everything else waits on Q-A/Q-B.

docs.title: ChatGPT first impressions
docs.text:
This is a surprisingly coherent architecture. The thing that stands out is that you've actually chosen hard boundaries and enforced them consistently:

  • Native shell = OS APIs only
  • Plugins = third-party SDKs
  • HTTP = request/response
  • Bridge = events
  • Native project = generated artifact
  • Runtime components = interface-first

Most frameworks become messy because they violate those boundaries over time.

Go ahead with your questions.

Some areas where I'd be especially interested to discuss because they're the highest-risk parts of the design:

docs.title: 1. The "all OS APIs in core" promise
docs.text:
• Technically possible.
  • The challenge isn't implementation.
  • It's keeping Android/iOS API surface evolution manageable without turning @capsule/core into a giant maintenance burden.

docs.title: 2. Tree-shaking native code
docs.text:
• JS tree-shaking is easy.
  • Native tree-shaking is trickier.
  • R8 can strip unused classes, but permissions, manifest entries, service declarations, broadcast receivers, and iOS entitlements often require explicit build-time management.

docs.title: 3. QuickJS route handlers
docs.text:
• This is probably the most differentiated feature.
  • It's also the feature most likely to create unexpected edge cases around:
  • memory limits
  • async execution
  • database access
  • background execution
  • OTA bundle compatibility

docs.title: 4. Embedded HTTP server
docs.text:
• Strong idea.
  • Solves many file:// problems.
  • But you'll need a very clear story for:
  • service workers
  • localhost security
  • app lifecycle
  • deep linking into routes
  • startup latency

docs.title: 5. Binary dependency model
docs.text:
• This is arguably the biggest innovation.
  • If developers never touch Android Studio or Xcode, you've eliminated one of the biggest pain points of hybrid development.
  • The challenge becomes providing enough escape hatches without breaking the abstraction.

docs.title: 6. Override registry
docs.text:
• This is actually more interesting than most people realize.
  • If done correctly, it gives you:
  • hotfixes
  • enterprise customizations
  • experimental APIs
  • vendor-specific patches

without shell forks.

docs.title: 7. CodeSync + server bundle
docs.text:
• Atomic deployment is the correct choice.
  • I'd strongly recommend versioning the bridge contract separately from bundle versions so a newer OTA bundle can detect an older shell and refuse activation before a crash occurs.

Ask whatever you're wondering about—architecture, performance, business viability, comparison with Capacitor/Ionic, QuickJS design, plugin model, or whether some assumption is likely to break at scale.

docs.title: Fundamental Principle
docs.text:
Do not attempt to become a Capacitor or Cordova runtime.

Bad direction:

Capsule Runtime
 └── Capacitor Runtime
      └── Cordova Runtime

This creates:

  • duplicated bridge layers
  • duplicated lifecycle systems
  • duplicated plugin systems
  • permanent compatibility debt

Instead:

Capacitor Plugin
       │
       ▼
Importer
       │
       ▼
Capsule Plugin ABI
       │
       ▼
Capsule Runtime

The goal is:

Make plugin migration cheap, not plugin execution universal.

docs.title: What the importer does
docs.text:
Example:

capsule plugin import capacitor @capacitor/filesystem

The importer:

  1. Reads plugin metadata
  2. Detects methods
  3. Detects permissions
  4. Detects events
  5. Detects lifecycle requirements
  6. Generates Capsule plugin scaffolding

Example output:

capsule-plugins/
└── filesystem/
    ├── capsule-plugin.json
    ├── android/
    │   └── FilesystemAdapter.kt
    ├── ios/
    │   └── FilesystemAdapter.swift
    └── web/
        └── index.ts

docs.title: Why a universal importer is impossible
docs.text: Not all plugins are simple RPC wrappers.

docs.title: Simple Plugin
docs.text:
@CapacitorPlugin(name = "Camera")
class CameraPlugin : Plugin() {

    @PluginMethod
    fun getPhoto(call: PluginCall) {
        ...
    }
}

Importer can map this automatically.

Camera.getPhoto()
        │
        ▼
camera.capture()

docs.title: Activity Lifecycle Plugin
docs.text:
registerActivityResultLauncher(...)

Requires:

  • activity result callbacks
  • permission callbacks
  • lifecycle integration

Importer must generate additional adapter code.

docs.title: Deep Runtime Plugin
docs.text:
bridge.getWebView()
bridge.getConfig()
pluginHandle.load()

Now plugin depends on Capacitor internals.

Example:

class CustomPlugin : Plugin() {

    fun doSomething() {
        val webView = bridge.webView
        ...
    }
}

Importer cannot safely translate this automatically.

Manual work required.

docs.title: Level 1 — Certified
docs.text:
Guaranteed support.

Examples:

@capacitor/filesystem
@capacitor/preferences
@capacitor/device
@capacitor/share

Characteristics:

✓ CI tested
✓ Official support
✓ Version compatibility guarantees
✓ Fully automated import

docs.title: Level 2 — Importable
docs.text:
Importer can generate working adapters.

Characteristics:

✓ Mostly automatic
✓ Community maintained
✓ Not guaranteed

Example:

capsule plugin import capacitor some-plugin

Result:

✓ Methods imported
✓ Permissions imported
✓ Events imported

Warnings:
 - Unsupported lifecycle hook

docs.title: Level 3 — Manual Port
docs.text:
Importer generates scaffolding.

Example:

capsule plugin import capacitor enterprise-plugin

Output:

Generated:
  android/Adapter.kt
  ios/Adapter.swift

TODO:
  Replace Bridge.getWebView()
  Replace PluginManager references
  Replace ActivityResult integration

Developer completes the migration.

docs.title: Capsule Plugin ABI
docs.text:
The ABI is not the importer.

The ABI is the internal format all plugins become.

docs.title: Weak ABI (Not Recommended)
docs.text:
{
  "methods": [
    {
      "name": "capturePhoto"
    }
  ]
}

Supports only simple RPC plugins.

Many plugins become impossible.

docs.title: Strong ABI (Recommended)
docs.text:
Should support:

Methods
Events
Permissions
Activity Results
Lifecycle Hooks
Background Services
Foreground Services
Deep Links
Notifications
Native Views
Broadcast Receivers
Assets
Configuration

Conceptually:

Capacitor Plugin
Cordova Plugin
Custom Plugin
        │
        ▼
   Capsule ABI
        │
        ▼
 Capsule Runtime

docs.title: Example ABI Manifest
docs.text:
{
  "name": "filesystem",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "permissions": ["READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE"],
  "methods": [
    {
      "name": "readFile",
      "params": [
        {
          "name": "path",
          "type": "string"
        }
      ],
      "returns": "string"
    }
  ],
  "events": [],
  "nativeViews": [],
  "backgroundServices": []
}

docs.title: Generated Plugin Structure
docs.text:
plugin/
├── capsule-plugin.json
├── android/
│   └── Filesystem.kt
├── ios/
│   └── Filesystem.swift
└── web/
    └── index.ts

Runtime only understands this format.

No Capacitor concepts.

No Cordova concepts.

docs.title: Capacitor Compatibility
docs.text:
Capacitor plugins are generally easier.

Typical Capacitor plugin:

import { registerPlugin } from "@capacitor/core";

export const Camera = registerPlugin("Camera");

Native:

@CapacitorPlugin(name = "Camera")
class CameraPlugin : Plugin()

Importer can usually map:

registerPlugin("Camera")
          │
          ▼
Capsule ABI Method

Many modern plugins fit this model.

docs.title: Cordova Compatibility
docs.text:
Cordova is harder.

Typical Cordova JS:

cordova.exec(success, error, "Camera", "getPicture", []);

Native:

public class CameraLauncher extends CordovaPlugin

Cordova plugins often depend on:

CordovaPlugin
CordovaInterface
CordovaWebView
CordovaPreferences
CordovaActivity

These are runtime-level dependencies.

A generic importer becomes much harder.

docs.title: Why Not Full Cordova Runtime Compatibility
docs.text:
Suppose Capsule decides to run Cordova plugins directly.

Now Capsule needs:

Capsule Runtime
├── CordovaPlugin
├── CordovaWebView
├── CordovaActivity
├── CordovaBridge
├── CordovaPreferences
└── CordovaLifecycle

This creates:

Capsule
 └── Cordova

which violates Capsule's core principle:

The shell is a dependency, not a framework stack.

docs.title: Recommended Architecture
docs.text:
Capacitor Plugin
       │
       ▼
Importer
       │
       ▼
Capsule ABI
       │
       ▼
Capsule Runtime

and

Cordova Plugin
       │
       ▼
Importer
       │
       ▼
Capsule ABI
       │
       ▼
Capsule Runtime

The runtime never understands Capacitor or Cordova.

Only the importer does.

docs.title: Long-Term Goal
docs.text:
Do not build:

A system that executes every Capacitor plugin.

Build:

A system that makes Capacitor plugins cheap to port.

Target migration flow:

Capacitor Plugin
       │
       ▼
Importer
       │
       ▼
80% generated
20% manual fixes
       │
       ▼
Capsule Plugin

This is achievable.

A fully universal compatibility layer is not.

docs.title: CodeSync Server — Database
docs.text: PostgreSQL data model for the CodeSync backend. Covers schema, indexes, migrations, and data lifecycle.

docs.title: Database Choice
docs.text:
PostgreSQL 16 — chosen for: - JSONB columns (device metadata, rollout rules, bundle manifests) - Row-level security (RLS) for multi-tenant isolation - pg_cron for scheduled cleanup without external workers - Proven at scale for time-series update-check data

Self-hosted: runs as the postgres container in docker-compose.yml. Cloud: managed RDS/CloudSQL/Supabase — connect via DATABASE_URL env var.

Migration tool: Knex.js — co-located with the codesync-api Node.js service. Run with pnpm migrate:latest.

docs.title: organizations
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE organizations (
  id          UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  slug        TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,           -- URL-safe name: "acme-corp"
  name        TEXT NOT NULL,
  plan        TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'free',   -- 'free' | 'pro' | 'enterprise'
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  deleted_at  TIMESTAMPTZ                     -- soft delete
);

CREATE INDEX organizations_slug_idx ON organizations(slug) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

docs.title: apps
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE apps (
  id              UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  org_id          UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES organizations(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  slug            TEXT NOT NULL,              -- "my-app" (unique within org)
  name            TEXT NOT NULL,
  bundle_id       TEXT NOT NULL,             -- reverse-domain: "com.example.myapp"
  platform        TEXT NOT NULL,             -- 'android' | 'ios' | 'both'
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  deleted_at      TIMESTAMPTZ,

  UNIQUE(org_id, slug)
);

CREATE INDEX apps_org_id_idx ON apps(org_id) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

docs.title: api_keys
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE api_keys (
  id              UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  org_id          UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES organizations(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  name            TEXT NOT NULL,              -- human label: "CI/CD key"
  key_hash        TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,       -- SHA-256 of the raw key (never store plaintext)
  key_prefix      TEXT NOT NULL,              -- first 8 chars shown in UI: "csk_abc1"
  scopes          TEXT[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',  -- ['publish', 'read', 'admin']
  last_used_at    TIMESTAMPTZ,
  expires_at      TIMESTAMPTZ,
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  revoked_at      TIMESTAMPTZ
);

CREATE INDEX api_keys_key_hash_idx ON api_keys(key_hash) WHERE revoked_at IS NULL;
CREATE INDEX api_keys_org_id_idx ON api_keys(org_id);

Key generation: CLI generates a random 32-byte key, prefixed with csk_. Raw key is shown once to the user and never stored. Only SHA-256(rawKey) is stored.

docs.title: channels
docs.text:
Update channels within an app (e.g. production, staging, beta).

CREATE TABLE channels (
  id              UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  app_id          UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES apps(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  name            TEXT NOT NULL,              -- 'production' | 'staging' | 'beta'
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),

  UNIQUE(app_id, name)
);

docs.title: bundles
docs.text:
A bundle = one complete web build (dist/ ZIP). Content-addressed — the ZIP is stored in file storage by its SHA-256 hash. See file-storage.md.

CREATE TABLE bundles (
  id              UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  app_id          UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES apps(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  channel_id      UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES channels(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,

  version         TEXT NOT NULL,              -- semver from capsule.config.ts: "1.4.2"
  build_number    INTEGER NOT NULL,           -- monotonic: 47
  label           TEXT,                       -- optional human label: "hotfix-login-crash"
  notes           TEXT,                       -- release notes (markdown)

  -- Content-addressed storage
  zip_hash        TEXT NOT NULL,              -- SHA-256 of bundle.zip
  zip_size_bytes  INTEGER NOT NULL,
  file_count      INTEGER NOT NULL,           -- number of files inside the ZIP

  -- Individual file hashes for differential downloads
  -- Stored as JSONB: { "assets/main-abc123.js": "sha256:...", ... }
  file_manifest   JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',

  status          TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
  -- 'pending'   → uploaded, not yet processed
  -- 'active'    → current live bundle for the channel
  -- 'archived'  → superseded by newer bundle
  -- 'failed'    → processing failed (see processing_error)
  -- 'rolled_back' → manually rolled back

  processing_error TEXT,                     -- set if status = 'failed'
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  activated_at    TIMESTAMPTZ,               -- when status changed to 'active'
  archived_at     TIMESTAMPTZ
);

CREATE INDEX bundles_app_channel_idx ON bundles(app_id, channel_id, status);
CREATE INDEX bundles_zip_hash_idx ON bundles(zip_hash);  -- dedup check

docs.title: bundle_files
docs.text:
Content-addressed file store — each unique file content is stored once. Multiple bundles can reference the same file (e.g. unchanged vendor-react.js).

CREATE TABLE bundle_files (
  sha256          TEXT PRIMARY KEY,           -- SHA-256 of file content
  size_bytes      INTEGER NOT NULL,
  first_seen_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  last_seen_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

How differential downloads work: 1. Bundle upload: server extracts ZIP, computes SHA-256 of each file, upserts into bundle_files 2. Device check-in: device sends its current file manifest ({ filename: sha256 }) 3. Server diffs: finds which files the device is missing 4. Response: only URLs for missing files — unchanged files skipped entirely 5. Result: a hotfix changing 2 JS chunks out of a 2MB bundle transfers ~30KB

docs.title: rollouts
docs.text:
Controls which devices receive a bundle and at what percentage.

CREATE TABLE rollouts (
  id              UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  bundle_id       UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES bundles(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  channel_id      UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES channels(id),

  strategy        TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'percentage',
  -- 'percentage' → random cohort by device_id hash
  -- 'manual'     → specific device IDs (test devices)
  -- 'immediate'  → 100% instantly

  percentage      INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 100 CHECK (percentage BETWEEN 0 AND 100),
  rollout_seed    INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 42,   -- MurmurHash3 seed for cohort assignment

  -- Manual targeting: device IDs that always get this bundle
  target_device_ids TEXT[] DEFAULT '{}',

  -- Mandatory: device cannot skip this update
  mandatory       BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false,

  -- Scheduling
  starts_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  paused_at       TIMESTAMPTZ,               -- rollout paused
  completed_at    TIMESTAMPTZ,              -- reached 100%

  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE INDEX rollouts_channel_bundle_idx ON rollouts(channel_id, bundle_id);

docs.title: devices
docs.text:
Anonymous device registry — no PII stored.

CREATE TABLE devices (
  id              UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  app_id          UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES apps(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,

  device_id       TEXT NOT NULL,              -- UUID generated by shell on first launch
  platform        TEXT NOT NULL,             -- 'android' | 'ios'
  shell_version   TEXT NOT NULL,             -- '1.4.0' — native capsule version
  app_version     TEXT NOT NULL,             -- '2.1.0' — store build version
  os_version      TEXT NOT NULL,             -- 'Android 14' | 'iOS 17.2'

  current_bundle_id  UUID REFERENCES bundles(id),   -- what the device currently has loaded
  current_zip_hash   TEXT,                   -- SHA-256 of the currently loaded bundle

  -- File-level cache: what individual files the device already has
  -- { "assets/main-abc123.js": "sha256:...", ... }
  file_cache      JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',

  -- Custom metadata provided by the app at device enrollment (locale, timezone, etc.)
  metadata        JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',

  first_seen_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  last_seen_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),

  UNIQUE(app_id, device_id)
);

CREATE INDEX devices_app_id_idx ON devices(app_id);
CREATE INDEX devices_device_id_idx ON devices(device_id);
CREATE INDEX devices_last_seen_idx ON devices(app_id, last_seen_at DESC);

docs.title: update_checks
docs.text:
Append-only log of every device check-in. Used for analytics and rollout tracking.

CREATE TABLE update_checks (
  id              UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  app_id          UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES apps(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  device_id       TEXT NOT NULL,
  channel_id      UUID REFERENCES channels(id),

  -- What the device had
  current_bundle_id  UUID REFERENCES bundles(id),
  current_zip_hash   TEXT,

  -- What we decided to send
  response_type   TEXT NOT NULL,
  -- 'no_update'       → device is current
  -- 'update_available' → bundle URL(s) returned
  -- 'mandatory_update' → must update
  -- 'rollback'        → device rolled back to previous bundle

  bundle_id_offered  UUID REFERENCES bundles(id),  -- NULL if no_update
  bytes_to_transfer  INTEGER,              -- estimated download (differential)

  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- Partition by month for query performance (Postgres declarative partitioning)
-- CREATE TABLE update_checks_2025_01 PARTITION OF update_checks
--   FOR VALUES FROM ('2025-01-01') TO ('2025-02-01');

CREATE INDEX update_checks_app_created_idx ON update_checks(app_id, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX update_checks_device_idx ON update_checks(device_id, created_at DESC);

docs.title: update_check_daily_summary
docs.text:
Pre-aggregated daily metrics for dashboard charts. Populated by the aggregate-analytics worker job (see workers.md). Avoids full-table scans on update_checks for dashboard queries.

CREATE TABLE update_check_daily_summary (
  app_id              UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES apps(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  date                DATE NOT NULL,
  total_checks        BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  updates_delivered   BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  no_update           BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  bytes_transferred   BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,

  PRIMARY KEY (app_id, date)
);

CREATE INDEX update_check_daily_summary_date_idx
  ON update_check_daily_summary(app_id, date DESC);

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text:
Managed by Knex.js in packages/codesync-api/src/db/migrations/.

# Apply all pending migrations
pnpm --filter codesync-api migrate:latest

# Rollback one migration
pnpm --filter codesync-api migrate:rollback

# Check migration status
pnpm --filter codesync-api migrate:status

Migration file naming: YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_description.ts

// packages/codesync-api/src/db/migrations/20250101000000_initial_schema.ts
import type { Knex } from 'knex'

export async function up(knex: Knex): Promise<void> {
  await knex.raw(`CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS "pgcrypto"`)

  await knex.schema.createTable('organizations', (t) => {
    t.uuid('id').primary().defaultTo(knex.raw('gen_random_uuid()'))
    t.text('slug').notNullable().unique()
    t.text('name').notNullable()
    t.text('plan').notNullable().defaultTo('free')
    t.timestamp('created_at', { useTz: true }).notNullable().defaultTo(knex.fn.now())
    t.timestamp('deleted_at', { useTz: true }).nullable()
  })
  // ... rest of tables
}

export async function down(knex: Knex): Promise<void> {
  await knex.schema.dropTableIfExists('organizations')
}

docs.title: Connection Configuration
docs.text:
// packages/codesync-api/src/db/knex.ts
import Knex from 'knex'

export const db = Knex({
  client: 'pg',
  connection: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
  pool: {
    min: 2,
    max: 20,                    // tune per worker count
    acquireTimeoutMillis: 5000,
    idleTimeoutMillis: 30000,

Environment: 

DATABASE_URL=postgres://codesync:password@postgres:5432/codesync

docs.title: Data Retention
docs.text: Table Retention Mechanism update_checks 90 days pg_cron job: DELETE FROM update_checks WHERE created_at < now() - interval '90 days' devices 180 days since last_seen_at pg_cron weekly job bundles (archived) 365 days Soft — archived_at set; files in storage cleaned separately bundle_files Until no bundle references it Cleanup job in workers.md organizations (deleted) 30 days Grace period before hard delete cascade

docs.title: Multi-Tenancy
docs.text:
Row-level security is NOT used in the initial MVP — all queries include explicit WHERE org_id = $orgId and WHERE app_id = $appId clauses enforced at the API layer. RLS is a Phase 8 (Ecosystem) hardening item.

The api_keys table scopes every request to an org: SELECT org_id FROM api_keys WHERE key_hash = $hash AND revoked_at IS NULL.

docs.title: CodeSync Server — File Storage
docs.text: Content-addressed bundle storage for the CodeSync backend. Covers storage architecture, MinIO/S3 setup, CDN, and the differential download protocol.

docs.title: Storage Model
docs.text: CodeSync uses content-addressed storage — every file is stored by its SHA-256 hash, never by name. This is the same model used by Git and npm's package cache.

docs.title: Why content-addressed
docs.text:
A typical Vite build produces 15–40 files with content-hashed names (main-a1b2c3.js). Between releases, only 1–3 files change. Content-addressed storage means:

  • Unchanged files are stored once — vendor-react-3f8d2a.js from v1.0 and v1.1 is the same hash → same single object in storage
  • Differential downloads are automatic — device sends its file cache ({ filename: sha256 }), server finds missing hashes, returns only those
  • No deduplication logic needed — the hash IS the identity

docs.title: What is stored
docs.text:
/bundles/
  {sha256}/           ← one directory per unique file hash
    content           ← raw file bytes (compressed at rest by S3/MinIO)

No folder structure beyond the hash. No filenames. No version directories.

docs.title: Self-hosted: MinIO
docs.text:
MinIO is S3-compatible and ships in docker-compose.yml. Zero config for local development.

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  minio:
    image: minio/minio:RELEASE.2024-11-07T00-52-20Z
    command: server /data --console-address ":9001"
    environment:
      MINIO_ROOT_USER:     minioadmin
      MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD: minioadmin
    volumes:
      - minio_data:/data
    ports:
      - "9000:9000"    # S3 API
      - "9001:9001"    # Web console (minioadmin/minioadmin)
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:9000/minio/health/live"]
      interval: 10s

volumes:
  minio_data:

Bucket provisioning (runs on first start): 

# packages/codesync-api/scripts/setup-minio.sh
mc alias set local http://localhost:9000 minioadmin minioadmin
mc mb --ignore-existing local/capsule-bundles
mc anonymous set none local/capsule-bundles    # private — all access via signed URLs

docs.title: Cloud: S3 / R2 / GCS
docs.text:
Same S3 API — just change the endpoint and credentials:

# AWS S3
STORAGE_ENDPOINT=https://s3.amazonaws.com
STORAGE_BUCKET=capsule-bundles-prod
STORAGE_ACCESS_KEY=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE
STORAGE_SECRET_KEY=wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY
STORAGE_REGION=us-east-1

# Cloudflare R2 (recommended — free egress)
STORAGE_ENDPOINT=https://<account-id>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com
STORAGE_BUCKET=capsule-bundles-prod
STORAGE_ACCESS_KEY=<r2-access-key-id>
STORAGE_SECRET_KEY=<r2-secret>
STORAGE_REGION=auto

docs.title: Storage Client
docs.text:
// packages/codesync-api/src/storage/client.ts
import { S3Client, PutObjectCommand, GetObjectCommand, HeadObjectCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3'
import { getSignedUrl } from '@aws-sdk/s3-request-presigner'

export const s3 = new S3Client({
  endpoint:        process.env.STORAGE_ENDPOINT,
  region:          process.env.STORAGE_REGION ?? 'auto',
  credentials: {
    accessKeyId:     process.env.STORAGE_ACCESS_KEY!,
    secretAccessKey: process.env.STORAGE_SECRET_KEY!,
  },
  forcePathStyle: true,   // required for MinIO + most non-AWS S3
})

const BUCKET = process.env.STORAGE_BUCKET!

export async function fileExists(sha256: string): Promise<boolean> {
  try {
    await s3.send(new HeadObjectCommand({ Bucket: BUCKET, Key: objectKey(sha256) }))
    return true
  } catch {
    return false
  }
}

export async function putFile(sha256: string, body: Buffer): Promise<void> {
  await s3.send(new PutObjectCommand({
    Bucket:      BUCKET,
    Key:         objectKey(sha256),
    Body:        body,
    ContentType: 'application/octet-stream',
    // Immutable — content hash never changes
    CacheControl: 'public, max-age=31536000, immutable',
  }))
}

export async function signedDownloadUrl(sha256: string, expiresInSeconds = 300): Promise<string> {
  const command = new GetObjectCommand({ Bucket: BUCKET, Key: objectKey(sha256) })
  return getSignedUrl(s3, command, { expiresIn: expiresInSeconds })
}

// Object key: first 2 chars as prefix prevents hot partition on large buckets
function objectKey(sha256: string): string {
  return `bundles/${sha256.slice(0, 2)}/${sha256}`
}

docs.title: Bundle Upload Flow
docs.text:
When capsule codesync publish uploads a bundle:

CLI: POST /v1/bundles/upload  (multipart/form-data: bundle.zip)

Server:
  1. Authenticate API key → resolve org + app + channel
  2. Parse multipart stream → buffer bundle.zip
  3. Compute SHA-256 of bundle.zip
  4. Check db.bundles WHERE zip_hash = $hash → reject duplicate
  5. Enqueue 'process-bundle' job → respond 202 Accepted { bundleId, status: 'pending' }

Processing happens asynchronously in a worker (see workers.md):

Worker: process-bundle job
  1. Fetch bundle.zip bytes from queue payload
  2. Extract ZIP in-memory (no disk writes)
  3. For each file in ZIP:
     a. Compute SHA-256
     b. Check if object exists in S3 (HeadObject)  ← skip upload if already stored
     c. If missing: PUT to S3 by hash
     d. Upsert into db.bundle_files { sha256, size_bytes }
  4. Build file_manifest: { "assets/main-abc.js": "sha256:...", ... }
  5. PUT bundle.zip itself to S3 (for full-bundle fallback)
  6. UPDATE db.bundles SET status='active', file_manifest=$manifest, activated_at=now()
  7. Archive previous active bundle (UPDATE status='archived')

docs.title: Update check request (device → server)
docs.text:
GET /v1/check/{appId}/{channel}/{shellVersion}/{appVersion}
Authorization: Bearer <api-key>  (or anonymous with app public token)

Body (JSON) — NOT in headers (headers break CDN caching):
{
  "deviceId": "<uuid>",
  "currentBundleHash": "sha256:abc123...",
  "fileCache": {
    "index.html":             "sha256:aaa...",
    "assets/main-abc123.js":  "sha256:bbb..."
  }
}

Note: Device-specific data (deviceId, fileCache) is in the POST body. Path segments (appId, channel, shellVersion, appVersion) are shared across devices → CDN can cache the response for devices on the same version.

docs.title: Update check response (server → device)
docs.text:
No update: 

{ "status": "no_update" }

Update available: 

{
  "status": "update_available",
  "mandatory": false,
  "bundle": {
    "version": "1.4.3",
    "buildNumber": 48,
    "zipHash": "sha256:xyz789...",
    "files": [
      {
        "path": "assets/main-def456.js",
        "sha256": "sha256:new111...",
        "size": 45200,
        "url": "https://cdn.capsule.dev/bundles/ne/new111...?sig=..."
      }
      // index.html and vendor-react.js NOT included — device already has them
    ],
    "totalBytes": 45200   // only the delta
  }
}

The device downloads only the listed files, patches its local cache, and marks the bundle as current.

docs.title: Full bundle fallback
docs.text:
If fileCache is empty (first install, corrupted cache), or if the diff would be > 80% of the full bundle size, the server returns a single signed URL for the full bundle.zip instead of individual files:

{
  "status": "update_available",
  "bundle": {
    "fullBundleUrl": "https://cdn.capsule.dev/bundles/xy/xyz789...zip?sig=...",
    "fullBundleSize": 380000
  }
}

docs.title: CDN Layer
docs.text:
Signed URLs expire in 5 minutes. For high-traffic production deployments, serve files via CDN:

Cloudflare R2 + Cloudflare Workers (recommended for self-hosted): - Store files in R2 (free egress from R2 to Cloudflare network) - Worker validates the request signature, forwards to R2 - Global edge — no origin egress cost

AWS S3 + CloudFront: - Pre-sign URLs with 5-minute TTL - CloudFront caches by URL — since content-hash is in the key, cached forever - Set Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable on S3 objects

MinIO (self-hosted, no CDN): - 5-minute signed URL directly from MinIO - Fine for internal/enterprise deployments with devices on the same network

docs.title: Retention rules
docs.text: Object Retention When deleted Individual bundle files (bundles/{prefix}/{sha256}) Until no bundle references them Cleanup worker (weekly) Full bundle ZIPs 365 days after archived_at Cleanup worker (monthly) Orphaned objects (failed uploads) 7 days S3 lifecycle rule

docs.title: S3 lifecycle rule (orphan cleanup)
docs.text:
{
  "Rules": [{
    "ID": "delete-orphan-uploads",
    "Status": "Enabled",
    "Filter": { "Prefix": "bundles/staging/" },
    "Expiration": { "Days": 7 }
  }]
}

The S3 lifecycle rule only applies to bundles/staging/ — the temporary prefix used during bundle upload before processing. If a bundle upload fails or is abandoned, the staging object is automatically cleaned up after 7 days.

Active bundle files (bundles/{prefix}/{sha256}) are never touched by the S3 lifecycle rule. They are only deleted by the cleanup-orphaned-files worker job, which checks the database before deleting anything.

docs.title: Cleanup worker logic
docs.text: See workers.md for the cleanup-orphaned-files job implementation.

docs.title: Bucket Configuration
docs.text:
# Capsule Cloud / production setup

# Create buckets
aws s3 mb s3://capsule-bundles-prod --region us-east-1

# Block all public access (all access via signed URLs)
aws s3api put-public-access-block \
  --bucket capsule-bundles-prod \
  --public-access-block-configuration \
    "BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true"

# Enable versioning (protects against accidental deletes)
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning \
  --bucket capsule-bundles-prod \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled

# Server-side encryption
aws s3api put-bucket-encryption \
  --bucket capsule-bundles-prod \
  --server-side-encryption-configuration \
    '{"Rules":[{"ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault":{"SSEAlgorithm":"AES256"}}]}'

docs.title: Capsule Server — Portal & Self-Hosted Infrastructure
docs.text: The Capsule Portal is the management layer for CodeSync: org registration, app management, API key generation, and the device dashboard. It can be self-hosted or used as Capsule Cloud.

docs.title: What the Portal Is
docs.text:
The portal is the control plane for CodeSync. It is not required to build or run Capsule apps — only needed when you want to use CodeSync OTA updates.

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   Capsule Portal                        │
│                                                         │
│  ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐   ┌────────────┐  │
│  │  Org signup  │   │  App mgmt    │   │  API Keys  │  │
│  │  User auth   │   │  Channels    │   │  Webhooks  │  │
│  └──────────────┘   └──────────────┘   └────────────┘  │
│                                                         │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │         CodeSync Dashboard (embedded)              │ │
│  │  Bundle releases · Device fleet · Rollout control  │ │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          ↕  REST API (authenticated by API key)
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              capsule codesync publish                   │
│              (CLI on developer's machine or CI)         │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Two Deployment Modes
docs.text:
Mode Setup Best for Capsule Cloud No setup — sign up at capsule.dev Teams who want zero infrastructure Self-hosted Run Capsule-Server via Docker Compose Enterprises with data residency requirements, offline environments

Both expose the exact same API. Switching between them is one line in capsule.config.ts (codeSync.url).

docs.title: Self-Hosted: What You Run
docs.text:
capsule-server/
  docker-compose.yml     ← full stack definition
  .env                   ← secrets (never committed)
  nginx.conf             ← reverse proxy (optional, for custom domain + TLS)
  migrations/            ← database schema (runs automatically on start)

The stack (defined in ../../contributing/docker.md): - codesync-api — Fastify backend - codesync-dashboard — React dashboard (nginx static) - postgres:16 — primary database - redis:7 — check endpoint cache - minio — S3-compatible bundle storage (or replace with real S3/R2)

docs.title: Step 1 — First Admin Account
docs.text:
On first launch, the portal is unseeded. The first user to register becomes the organization owner.

Self-hosted:  http://your-server:8080/setup
Capsule Cloud: https://capsule.dev/signup

Registration requires: - Email address - Password (min 12 characters) - Organization name (e.g. "Acme Corp")

The organization name becomes part of the API namespace. Multiple organizations can exist on one self-hosted instance (multi-tenant).

docs.title: Step 2 — Invite Team Members
docs.text:
Dashboard → Organization → Members → Invite

Roles:

Role Permissions Owner Full access — billing, org settings, delete org Admin Manage apps, members, API keys, all releases Releaser Publish bundles, promote between channels, roll back. Cannot manage team members or billing. Developer Publish bundles, manage releases, view devices Viewer Read-only access to dashboard and device fleet

All roles authenticate via email + password. SSO (SAML/OIDC) is on the roadmap.

docs.title: Registering an App
docs.text:
Each appId must be registered in the portal before the CLI can publish to it.

Dashboard → Apps → New App
→ App ID:     com.yourcompany.app   (must match capsule.config.ts appId)
→ App Name:   My App
→ Platform:   Android | iOS | Both

docs.title: Channels
docs.text:
After creating the app, create the channels you need:

Dashboard → Apps → [your app] → Channels → Add Channel

Default channels created automatically: - production - staging

Additional channels (e.g. qa, beta, internal) can be added freely. The channel name is just a string — it matches capsule.config.ts codeSync.channel.

docs.title: API Keys
docs.text: API keys authorize the CLI to publish bundles. They are scoped to an organization — one key can publish bundles for any app within the org. To restrict a key to specific apps, use the scopes field when creating the key. API keys are never embedded in the app binary.

docs.title: Generating a Key
docs.text:
Dashboard → Apps → [your app] → Settings → API Keys → Generate Key
→ Key name:  "CI/CD Key" or "Alex's laptop"
→ Scope:     publish (write) | read-only
→ Expiry:    never | 90 days | 1 year (recommended: 1 year with rotation reminder)

The key is shown once — copy it immediately. It looks like: 

csk_live_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx

Prefix csk_live_ for production, csk_test_ for sandbox/staging apps.

docs.title: Using the Key
docs.text:
# .env.local (never commit)
CODESYNC_API_KEY=csk_live_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx

# CI secret (GitHub/GitLab/Azure):
# Name: CODESYNC_API_KEY
# Value: csk_live_...

// capsule.config.ts
codeSync: {
  url:    process.env.CODESYNC_URL,       // https://your-server or https://api.capsule.dev
  apiKey: process.env.CODESYNC_API_KEY,   // from portal
  channel: process.env.CHANNEL || 'production'
}

docs.title: Key Rotation
docs.text:
Dashboard → Apps → [your app] → Settings → API Keys
→ Click "Rotate" on the existing key
→ New key generated, old key immediately revoked
→ Update CI secret before the old key is used again

Rotate keys: - When a team member with key access leaves - After any suspected compromise - On a regular schedule (quarterly recommended)

docs.title: Login
docs.text:
POST /auth/login
{ "email": "alex@company.com", "password": "..." }
→ { "accessToken": "...", "refreshToken": "..." }
  • accessToken — short-lived JWT (15 minutes), used in Authorization: Bearer header
  • refreshToken — longer-lived (30 days), stored in httpOnly cookie, used to get new access tokens
  • After 30 days of inactivity, full re-login required

docs.title: Session Persistence
docs.text: The dashboard stores the refresh token in an httpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie. The access token is in memory only (never localStorage — XSS protection). On page reload, the dashboard silently exchanges the refresh token for a new access token.

docs.title: Password Reset
docs.text:
POST /auth/forgot-password
{ "email": "alex@company.com" }
→ Email sent with reset link (valid 1 hour)

The self-hosted portal sends email via SMTP. Configure in .env: 

SMTP_HOST=smtp.yourcompany.com
SMTP_PORT=587
SMTP_USER=noreply@yourcompany.com
SMTP_PASS=...
SMTP_FROM="Capsule Portal <noreply@yourcompany.com>"

docs.title: Self-Hosted Docker Compose
docs.text:
# capsule-server/docker-compose.yml

services:
  codesync-api:
    image: ghcr.io/capsule/codesync-api:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL:    ${DATABASE_URL}
      REDIS_URL:       ${REDIS_URL}
      STORAGE_ENDPOINT: ${STORAGE_ENDPOINT}
      STORAGE_BUCKET:  ${STORAGE_BUCKET}
      STORAGE_ACCESS_KEY: ${STORAGE_ACCESS_KEY}
      STORAGE_SECRET_KEY: ${STORAGE_SECRET_KEY}
      JWT_SECRET:      ${JWT_SECRET}           # random 64-char string
      SMTP_HOST:       ${SMTP_HOST}
      SMTP_PORT:       ${SMTP_PORT}
      SMTP_USER:       ${SMTP_USER}
      SMTP_PASS:       ${SMTP_PASS}
      SMTP_FROM:       ${SMTP_FROM}
      PUBLIC_URL:      ${PUBLIC_URL}           # https://codesync.yourcompany.com
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_started

  codesync-dashboard:
    image: ghcr.io/capsule/codesync-dashboard:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      VITE_API_URL: ${PUBLIC_URL}   # where the dashboard calls the API
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
    depends_on:
      - codesync-api

  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER:     capsule
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
      POSTGRES_DB:       capsule
    volumes:
      - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U capsule"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - redis-data:/data

  minio:
    image: minio/minio:RELEASE.2024-11-07T00-52-20Z
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: server /data --console-address ":9001"
    environment:
      MINIO_ROOT_USER:     ${MINIO_ROOT_USER}
      MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD: ${MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD}
    volumes:
      - minio-data:/data
    ports:
      - "9000:9000"
      - "9001:9001"

volumes:
  postgres-data:
  redis-data:
  minio-data:

docs.title: Self-Hosted .env Template
docs.text:
# capsule-server/.env
# Copy to .env and fill in values. Never commit .env.

# ── Database ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

docs.title: CodeSync Server — Background Workers
docs.text: Async job processing for the CodeSync backend. Covers queue architecture, job types, and worker deployment.

docs.title: Queue Stack
docs.text:
BullMQ (Redis-backed) — chosen for: - Persistent queues (jobs survive server restart) - Concurrency control per queue - Built-in retry with exponential backoff - Job progress tracking (useful for bundle processing) - Works with any Redis-compatible server (Redis, Valkey, Upstash)

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    command: redis-server --appendonly yes   # persist queue state
    volumes:
      - redis_data:/data
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"

volumes:
  redis_data:

# Environment
REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379

docs.title: Queue Architecture
docs.text:
┌──────────────────────────────────┐
                    │         codesync-api              │
                    │  (Fastify HTTP server)            │
                    └──────────┬───────────────────────┘
                               │ enqueue jobs
                               ▼
                    ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
                    │         Redis (BullMQ)            │
                    │                                   │
                    │  queue: bundle-processing         │
                    │  queue: notifications             │
                    │  queue: device-cleanup            │
                    │  queue: analytics                 │
                    └──────────┬───────────────────────┘
                               │ dequeue + process
                               ▼
                    ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
                    │         codesync-worker           │
                    │  (separate Node.js process)       │
                    └──────────────────────────────────┘

The worker process is a separate Node.js process from the API. In Docker Compose, it runs as a separate service using the same Docker image with a different CMD:

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  codesync-api:
    image: ghcr.io/capsule/codesync-api
    command: node dist/server.js
    environment: *api-env

  codesync-worker:
    image: ghcr.io/capsule/codesync-api    # same image, different entrypoint
    command: node dist/worker.js
    environment: *api-env
    deploy:
      replicas: 2                  # scale workers independently

docs.title: Worker Entry Point
docs.text:
// packages/codesync-api/src/worker.ts
import { Worker } from 'bullmq'
import { connection } from './queue/connection.js'
import { processBundleJob } from './jobs/process-bundle.js'
import { sendNotificationsJob } from './jobs/send-notifications.js'
import { cleanupDevicesJob } from './jobs/cleanup-devices.js'
import { cleanupOrphanedFilesJob } from './jobs/cleanup-orphaned-files.js'
import { aggregateAnalyticsJob } from './jobs/aggregate-analytics.js'

const workers = [
  new Worker('bundle-processing', processBundleJob, {
    connection,
    concurrency: 4,             // process 4 bundles simultaneously
    limiter: { max: 10, duration: 60_000 },  // max 10 per minute
  }),
  new Worker('notifications', sendNotificationsJob, {
    connection,
    concurrency: 20,
  }),
  new Worker('device-cleanup', cleanupDevicesJob, {
    connection,
    concurrency: 1,             // runs on schedule, no concurrency needed
  }),
  new Worker('analytics', aggregateAnalyticsJob, {
    connection,
    concurrency: 2,
  }),
]

// Graceful shutdown
process.on('SIGTERM', async () => {
  await Promise.all(workers.map(w => w.close()))
  process.exit(0)
})

console.log('[worker] Started — listening on all queues')
